#4997. Puking, Passing, Posting: The New Rules of Race Etiquette

More athletes than ever are showing up to starting lines of all kinds.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Race etiquette used to be pretty straightforward: Stay in your lane, don’t cut people off, and be aware of your surroundings when you stop for water. But ever since run clubs and new hybrid competitions like Hyrox have taken off, there's been an influx of athletes who have never been taught race rules. To make matters more complicated, new competition styles mean additional rules have to get ironed out in real time. Best case scenario, this might mean you bump into a few people with cameras trying to get social media content at the finish line. Worst case scenario (in rare, extreme cases), the race may turn into a literal sh*tshow.

“Racing has become much more popularized and mainstream over the years, bringing in more people who may be racing from more of a ‘fun’ standpoint rather than a competitive one,” says kettlebell coach Sarah Warshowsky, CPT, creator of the WH Build & Burn kettlebell plan who’s competed in a Hyrox race and half-marathon. “Newer racers need to respect the history, competition, and elite athletes who may have prize money on the line, while competitive racers should feel inclusive and accepting of new racers coming into their sport because in the end, it does bring more eyes to it.”

Meet the experts: Sarah Warshowsky, CPT, is a New York City–based kettlebell coach and creator of the Build & Burn kettlebell track. Kayla Jeter, CFSC, is a Lululemon athlete, wellness consultant, and veteran half-, full, and ultramarathoner. Sunny Choi, CSCS, is an Olympic breaker who’s competed in a Hyrox race.

Knowing all the ins and outs of how to act during a race isn’t exactly part of your ChatGPT training plan, but race etiquette is essential. That’s why Women’s Health tapped some of our most trusted racing experts to put together a comprehensive list of the new rules of race etiquette—here’s what to know before you head to the starting line.

Be respectful and practice spatial awareness, both when you’re maintaining a steady pace, and passing people. After all, “the point of a race is that you want to pass people and you want people to feel like they can pass you,” says Warshowsky. But you need to check your surroundings, and be strategic about when you can make those passes. For instance, if you’re about to turn a corner down a new street during a half-marathon, you might want to wait a second before you try and squeeze past a bunch of people.

Similarly, some races like Hyrox also have passing lanes for faster athletes. Do your event research ahead of time, know which lane you’re in, keep it moving, and if you need to switch, look around and try not to knock into runners, Warshowsky says.

After all, it’s your race too! “Too many times, I’ve experienced and seen others almost fall from ‘me’-centric runners moving erratically,” says Kayla Jeter, CFSC, a Lululemon athlete, wellness consultant, and veteran half-, full, and ultramarathoner. “If someone starts swerving, I’ll casually start snapping to announce my presence, I’ll also use my arms as a barrier to keep people from bumping into me.”

If you’re in desperate need of water or a walking break, stay on the lookout for an upcoming water station or less crowded area to stop by. Just like you would when riding a bike, stick out your hand to the right or left to signify that you’ll be pulling over, Warshowsky says. Then, start inching your way toward that side of the road “instead of needing to cut across an entire lane of people running,” she adds. If you need a walking break, raise your arm straight up in the air before slowing down.

“Go into every race knowing you’re not the only one on the course and are responsible for how your actions impact someone else’s race,” Jeter reminds. So, if you want to record content, do your best not to include people in the background, whether you’re at the start line, finish line, or mile 10. Want to stop and grab a couple of videos? Look around you and make sure no one is right behind you. “I’ve seen plenty of runners crash into someone crossing the finish line because someone wanted to capture their moment,” she adds.

Ultimately, just be respectful. “A creator filming themselves having their own experience does not have to bother anyone around them, as long as they are not coming in the way of anyone else's experience,” says Warshowsky.

Understand the guidelines and your race order ahead of time. At Hyrox, the stations are numbered pretty clearly, but if you get lost, don’t be afraid to ask a nearby judge for help, says Warshowsky.

After finishing up at one of the machines, participants don’t typically wipe sweat off after leaving it since that can take time off of their score. But you should make sure the station is relatively clean and the weights are in place so you’re not putting the person behind you at a major disadvantage, she adds.

PRing your race is not worth ignoring a bodily emergency. Before getting to the start line, know the nearest exits and bathrooms in each section of the race, Warshowsky says. Then, “if you have any signs of discomfort, listen to your body, because those signs are usually not there for nothing,” says Olympic breaker Sunny Choi, CSCS, who has competed in a Hyrox race. Hit the nearest bathroom, and if you don’t make it, try to find a nearby empty space to stay in until you feel better.

If you start feeling faint during Hyrox or something more serious may be going on but you still have four more stations to go, don’t power through. Tell a volunteer or someone working the course that you may need medical attention. “The only way that you can get help is if you let someone know you actually need help,” Warshowsky adds. “The safety of yourself and others around you should be number-one priority when needing to make the call whether you need to exit the race for any reason.”

Nothing New on Race Day!When it comes to clothing and sneakers, “as tempting as it can be to wear something fresh at the start line, new products are often stiff, which can cause chaffing and be distracting,” says Jeter. The same goes for food: New fuel mixed with nerves may make your stomach feel weird at an inconvenient time during the race, Choi adds. So, make sure you know what feels best in your body pre-race day by testing it ahead of time, like during a taper run.

When you’re running in the middle of the street and you have a water cup in one hand and an energy gel in the other, pulling to the side to throw them in the trash is probably not top of mind. But throwing trash anywhere on the ground can cause it to get trapped underneath athletes’ feet and potentially cause tripping. (Plus, it’s more trash for the people cleaning up afterward.) So, try your hardest to either hold onto your trash until you see a trash can, or store it in your running belt or vest for the time being, says Warshowsky.

“Without them, there is no race,” says Warshowsky. If a volunteer is giving you a directive—asking you not to step off the marathon race course to say hi to your friends, for example—don’t fight back. “It's not just about you, it's about the whole collective and everyone there,” she adds. They’re just doing their job and trying to keep everyone safe.

Remember: When you’re racing recreationally, these races are individual. “It's you versus you,” says Warshowsky. But it’s important to “be mindful of the people around you and how much time, preparation, energy, money, scheduling everyone around you had to go through as well as yourself.”

Run Your Next Race Even Faster With This 4-Week Plan

On a deeper level, remember that unless racing is your profession and there’s money on the line, “it's not always that serious,” Warshowsky adds. “The safety of yourself, your body, and the safety of everyone around you is more important” than a PR. If after a few miles—or workout stations—you know it’s not your day to beat your record, hang back, relax, and enjoy it. Remember why you race, and make it an enjoyable experience for yourself and everyone around you. There will always be another race where you can try your best.

#4996. Raw Denim vs. Regular Denim: Which Is Actually Worth Buying?

Here’s what to know about both kinds of jeans.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

I COME FROM the denim era where streetwear juggernauts like FUBU and Rocawear reigned supreme, along with mall favorites like Abercrombie & Fitch and Hollister. I was in my preteens rocking all these clothing brands and you couldn’t tell me their baggy-stacking-at-the-shoe jeans weren’t the flyest on the market. Since I began working as a fashion editor, I’ve practically worn every pair of jeans in the denim universe. Slim, relaxed, stretch, washed, distressed—you name it, I’ve probably tried it. I’ve even tried my hand at denim-making in Japan, the mecca of old-school, high-quality denim, where I produced my own pair of selvedge jeans. Denim is one of those rare items in a guy’s wardrobe that never goes out of style.

And after years of being in the menswear space, I’ve gotten familiar with the nuances that distinguish one kind of denim from the next. Two worth knowing are regular denim and raw denim. Raw denim usually looks darker, stiffer, and more uniform in color, while regular denim has a softer feel and a more broken-in appearance with visible fading or whiskering from factory washing and finishing. Those differences also affect how each pair feels when you first put it on and how it changes over the years. Here’s what to know about both and which one deserves a spot in your rotation.

Regular jeans are usually made by weaving cotton yarn into denim, then cutting fabric into patterns and sewing them together to create the finished garment. These jeans have already gone through washing or finishing treatments to soften the fabric and give them that broken-in look, so you don’t have to spend weeks waiting for them to feel comfortable. If I want to throw on a pair of jeans and get on with my day, this is the kind I’m reaching for. I also like that you can find them in practically every fit and wash, whether you’re after a clean, dark indigo pair or something faded and lived-in. Most everyday options from brands like Levi’s and Wrangler run roughly $40 to $100, while designer and premium styles can cost considerably more. For me, prewashed denim makes the most sense when you want that comfortable feel from the jump. There’s nothing wrong with skipping the break-in period and getting straight to the good part.

I like raw denim because you get to see how jeans change the more you wear them. Unlike prewashed jeans, raw denim typically hasn’t been washed after the dyeing and manufacturing process, so it typically arrives stiff, dark, and pretty rigid. One thing to watch out for, though, is dye transfer. Indigo can rub off onto lighter-colored clothes, shoes, and other materials, including suede. I’ve had this happen before, so I'd be mindful of what you wear with a fresh pair. But that’s part of the appeal for denim enthusiasts. As you wear it, the fabric softens and develops fades and creases based on how you move, sit, and live in your jeans. You’re essentially breaking them in yourself, which makes the finished look feel uniquely yours. Prices can start around $60 to $100 for entry-level options and climb to $150 to $300 or more for premium denim, particularly Japanese-made styles. I’ll admit, the break-in period takes some patience, but if you enjoy watching your jeans evolve over time, raw denim is worth considering.

Raw denim and selvedge denim get lumped together all the time, but they actually refer to different things. Raw denim describes the fabric’s finishing state: It’s typically sold without a post-production wash that softens the fabric or creates a faded look. Selvedge, on the other hand, refers to how the denim is woven, creating a clean, self-finished edge you can often spot by rolling up the cuff. You can have raw selvedge denim, washed selvedge denim, or raw denim that isn’t selvedge at all. Having made my own pair of selvedge jeans in Japan, I’ve seen firsthand how the construction differs. Once you know what to look for, the distinction is pretty easy to spot.

At the end of the day, I don’t think you need to drop $300 on raw denim to dress well. After years of working in menswear, I’ve learned that a higher price tag doesn’t automatically make something the right choice for your wardrobe. I’ve seen guys look just as good in an affordable pair of Levi’s as they do in premium Japanese denim. What matters more is finding comfortable jeans that fit your body and work with the clothes you already own. I’m always going to appreciate the quality craftsmanship behind a great pair of raw denim, but there’s no single right way to wear jeans. I think every guy should have one dependable pair, whether that’s raw or prewashed. But ultimately, like most things in style, it comes down to personal preference—and knowing what works for you.

#4994. Canton’s CC rises 4% as SEC staff view it as ‘digital commodity’

SEC staff’s no-action letter covers CC earned by running infrastructure and applications, but is not a binding ruling on its legal status.

Canton Network’s native cryptocurrency rose 4% on Wednesday after the US Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) Division of Corporation Finance issued a no-action letter stating it views the token as a “digital commodity.”

Canton Coin (CC) traded at $0.098 at 10:27 am UTC, but was still down roughly 4.2% over the past week, according to CoinMarketCap.

In its Tuesday letter, SEC staff accepted the explanation that CC’s value comes from how the network operates and demand for the token, rather than a central team’s efforts to generate profits for holders.

The division also said it would not recommend enforcement action over CC’s issuance without securities registration, provided the tokens are created under the conditions described by Canton.

In Friday’s letter to the SEC, Canton developer Digital Asset said network participants earn CC by operating infrastructure and applications, with the protocol determining how many tokens they can mint based on their activity.

The SEC issued guidance in March distinguishing digital commodities, such as Bitcoin and Ether, from securities. It said these tokens are not themselves securities, although the way they are offered and sold can still be subject to securities laws.

The SEC’s response reflects its staff’s position and is not a binding ruling on CC’s legal status.

SEC staff previously issued token-related no-action letters to crypto projects, including DoubleZero (2Z) in September 2025 and Solana-native decentralized physical infrastructure network (DePIN) project Fuse in November 2025.

#4989. The 6 Best Undereye Patches, Tested and Reviewed by Dermatologists and Beauty Editors

The entire Women's Health team swears by them.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’m always up late doomscrolling TikTok and The White Lotus subreddit for season 4 theories. (Natasha Rothwell hive, stand up!) The only problem? Those late nights mean I have dark circles and puffiness in the morning (boo!). While I'm a huge fan of undereye creams, sometimes I get bored and need to switch things up. Enter undereye patches. They're a fast fix for dryness, puffiness, and dark circles—and even help me fake eight hours of sleep. "The skin under the eyes is prone to changes related to aging skin, such as fine lines, and conditions like dryness and discoloration," says dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD. In just 10 to 20 minutes, undereye patches temporarily hydrate the delicate skin and help me look refreshed. Plus, they're super cute and add a fun touch to my selfies, even if they're shared to just my Close Friends circle on Instagram Stories.

Like any other skin care product, eye masks really get their power from their ingredients, some of which are typically hyaluronic acid, vitamin C, niacinamide, and caffeine.

“Eye patches incorporate key ingredients like hyaluronic acid to boost moisture, peptides to firm, ceramides to strengthen the skin barrier, caffeine to help reduce puffiness, and niacinamide to reduce discoloration,” says dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD.

As with any beauty product, there are always a few things to consider before making the investment. Since these masks are mostly advertised for their ability to soothe and hydrate, you'll want to check the hydrating and firming ingredients, and keep your expectations realistic since results are usually temporary. Here's what to look out for.

For starters, look for key ingredients such as aloe, chamomile, cucumber, green tea, glycerin, or hyaluronic acid. You're less likely to come across vitamin C and retinol, but it's a plus if you do. Patches with a cellulose gel material can also prevent them from sliding off your face (a con I often deal with and try to avoid as much as possible).

Not only is the skin under your eyes thinner and more delicate than in other areas of your face, but it’s also where lymphatic fluid drainage occurs, says dermatologist Lauren Penzi, MD. It can also show more blood vessels, and in turn, make dark circles appear more visible, says Dr. Garshick. Most eye masks are created to reduce fine lines, undereye darkness, and wrinkles while giving your skin the boost of moisture it needs. The overall effect of these patches is to revive and hydrate, which is why so many people use them to get a more refreshed look.

Many people complain about looking tired, and eye patches are a nice, quick fix. Still, it's important to be realistic about the kind of results you'll get in just one or two uses. So, you’ll want to zero in on the reason you’re buying patches, says Dr. Camp. For example, you can target puffiness by rocking undereye patches infused with caffeine or green tea while getting ready for work, says Dr. Camp.

As a member of the beauty team at Women’s Health, I’m constantly on the hunt for the best products and spend a lot of my time testing and reviewing the latest drops. I frequently consult skin experts, which is exactly what I did to kick off my selection process here. I consulted five New York-based dermatologists and had them give their recommendations with insight on why these undereye masks are so splurge-worthy. Then, I tested several of their picks and compared them to some of the other undereye masks available in our beauty closet.To narrow down the list even further, I got a few other members of team WH, including Addison Aloian, Lily Wohlner, Brian Underwood, and Danielle Jackson, to get in on the testing process. ICYMI, Wander Beauty basically started the undereye mask trend. This OG mask is made with peptides, amino acids, and hyaluronic acid to improve your skin's texture, tone, and hydration. It's also expert-approved by Dr. Garshick and dermatologist Dendy Engelman, MD. "I love that this mask is made with three different layers that allow the formula to penetrate the skin deeply and prevent it from sliding off the face, so you can multitask while you wear it," says Dr. Engelman.

Wander Beauty patches are as effective as they are Instagrammable. I’ve been a fan of the rose gold and yellow gold patches for five years, and all of my beauty editor friends gush over them. These pretty patches have three unique layers: the surface's foil retains heat and prevents evaporation, the middle grips to prevent slippage, and the base delivers moisturizing glycerin and depuffing calendula extract. For an extra soothing experience, I like to leave mine in the fridge. Cool temperatures help shrink blood vessels under the eyes, so dark circles appear lighter and puffiness minimizes, dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD, said in our guide to undereye skin care.

Patchology is fantastic for targeting lines, says dermatologist Anar Mikailov, MD. He mentions that there's resveratrol, a natural antioxidant found in grapes that helps improve barrier function, and other antioxidants that provide protection against oxidizing agents that can visibly age the skin by causing wrinkles. There’s also antioxidant-rich strawberry extract, which helps brighten dark circles.

After using this patch, I also noticed my undereye area was less puffy and more luminous. My hack is to use these patches while lying down in bed to prevent any slipping.

This undereye mask is basically an expert at reducing puffy, tired-looking eyes thanks to its cooling effects. It also temporarily plumps up my fine lines with hydrating hyaluronic acid.

This option comes with a lot of serum, so it may slip down your face over time. Along with a mix of peptides to help stimulate collagen production, this eye mask contains niacinamide, bakuchiol, caffeine, and vitamin C. Bakuchiol is a great retinol alternative that helps stimulate collagen production, says Dr. Mikailov.

#4988. The 8 Best Slip-On Walking Shoes, According to Our Editors

Looking to get out the door quicker? Don’t let laces slip you up.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

SLIDING INTO A pair of slip-on walking shoes might be the easiest thing you’ll do all day. This footwear was built for speed and convenience, making it an accessory that deserves valuable real estate by your door.

Slip-on walking shoes have a rocky history—older versions had a looser fit, raising the risk of instability and friction, especially with higher mileage. But newer designs use no-tie laces, sock liners, pull tabs, and collapsible heels to create a custom fit that rivals what you’ll get with traditional laces.

These shoes are an obvious choice if you have dexterity issues, but they're also just convenient for everyone looking for an easy pair of walking shoes. Slip-on walking shoes also offer more structure than other laceless shoe designs, which has earned them a fanbase with podiatrists. “They are typically a much better option than flip-flops or slides because they provide more stability and keep the foot properly secured,” says Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois.

Nicole Graf, DPM, founder of Lexington Podiatry and associate professor at the University of Kentucky, also calls slip-on walking shoes a “huge step up” from flip-flops and slides.

Slip-on walking shoes aren’t for everyone. The fit can still throw some people off, and some simply prefer the tighter feel that laces deliver. But if you want travel-friendly shoes you can toss on in a second, these are a solid choice. As people who value quality, supportive footwear, Men’s Health editors have put in plenty of miles in slip-on walking shoes. The below check all the boxes.

The On Cloud 6 is an excellent example of how good a slip-on shoe can be. You can get in and out of this sneaker with no issue thanks to its wide opening, but the shoe’s elastic “speed” laces and sockliner create a snug fit once you’re in. (Those elastic laces can be adjusted to find your perfect fit.)

The sneaker uses Zero-Gravity CloudTec, which is On’s signature lightweight foam with hollow pods below for a cushioned, yet stable, feel underfoot. (Just be aware that those pods are prone to trapping small pebbles and debris.) A built-in flexible plate, called a Speedboard, helps push you forward with each step. This shoe also comes in a waterproof option, if you’re into rainy strolls. With a wide range of color options and an unobnoxious design, you can pair these with just about anything.

It’s tough to find a quality shoe under $100 right now, let alone one from a big brand. But the Adidas Cloudfoam Cuxxion Sock Shoes have some colorways under $50, making them an ideal choice for budget shoppers who don’t want to mess with laces.

This shoe uses Adidas’ signature Cloudfoam technology at the midsole for a plush, cushioned feel. Its Adiwear outsole is durable and grippy enough for most needs, too. But the real standout in this shoe is its elastic sock upper. It molds to your foot to create a surprisingly snug feel, even for narrow feet. The elastic sock collar supports that secure feel, although it may be too tight for people with wider ankles. The engineered knit upper is highly breathable, lowering the odds you’ll end your walk with sweaty feet. We appreciate the oversized pull tabs in front and back, making the process of getting these on and off seamless.

Feet come in all sizes, making it tough to find a slip-on shoe that works for everyone—and putting adjustable features at a premium. The Nike Pegasus 42 EasyOn has a specialized EasyOn lacing and bungee system up top to help you get the level of tightness you want, before locking it into place. (The lock and bungee combination takes some practice to get right at first.)

The shoe has a collapsible heel that springs back into place once you’re in, making the process of getting these on seamless. It’s also crafted with the same ReactX foam and Air Zoom unit as the standard—and popular—Nike Pegasus 42 running shoe, delivering an energetic feel under your feet. Convenient pull tabs at the heel sit flush against the shoe when they’re not in use, adding to the shoe’s overall sleekness.

Read More: Best Walking Shoes for Men Over 50

Stability shoes are designed to guide your foot with each step and prevent too much inward rolling as you go. But choosing a stability shoe usually means sacrificing a high level of cushioning, since a shoe that feels too plush may not be overly supportive. Hoka’s Skyward Laceless manages to create a stable, locked-in feel while still delivering plenty of the brand’s signature cushioning underfoot.

The Skyward Laceless has a stretchy upper that gently hugs your foot, creating a sock-like feel. The ankle and instep are equally snug, which can be a good or bad thing, depending on your foot size and width. This shoe has plenty of foam below for a slightly bouncy feel, but it still corrects your stride as you go. The integrated tongue pull tab is a nice touch, making for easier entry.

The Under Armour SlipSpeed Mega is packed with features you won’t find in most slip-on walking shoes, creating a versatile, unique sneaker. For starters, this shoe converts from a sneaker design to a recovery slipper with the help of a collapsible heel. (Under Armour refers to this as going from “speed mode” to “slip mode.”)

The shoe skips elastic laces or a sockliner upper in favor of Under Armour’s specialized BOA fit system, a 12-point dial that you can turn to adjust the width across the midfoot. The wide base creates a stable feel, while lots of foam cushioning underfoot delivers a plushness you’ll appreciate. A heads-up: This shoe is slightly heavier than others at 11.7 ounces. That’s a difference you may start to feel on long walks.

After a grueling workout, it feels borderline pampering to slide into the right recovery shoe. The Kane Footwear Active Recovery Shoe is armed with features that should make it a fixture in your gym bag.

This slip-on has strong arch support and a slight rocker shape to help ease pressure on the bottom of your feet as you walk. Internal nodes in the footbed help to promote blood flow and circulation down below, while the shoe’s surprisingly secure design helps prevent slipping. The Active Recovery Shoe is water-resistant with an airy design that allows you to take this in and out of the gym shower without ending up with sopping feet. Heel tabs in back make it simple to get in and out.

Merrell is known for its rugged, outdoor footwear and hiking shoes. While the Merrell Jungle Moc isn’t exactly a hiking shoe, it’s a solid option when you want good traction, whether you’re navigating rocky ground or a slippery surface. The Jungle Moc has been a bestseller for years, with its simple slip-on design and high level of cushioning.

Dual side stretch panels and an exaggerated heel tab make it simple to get in and out of these shoes. The suede upper is breathable, but water-resistant to keep you dry in nearly all conditions. The Jungle Moc has a cushioned EVA midsole for stability and comfort, too. While these shoes are easy to get on, the curved heel makes it harder to slide out—just something to be aware of.

Clogs admittedly aren’t the right style for everyone—some offer less support than sneakers and may slip around more than a standard shoe. But the sleek Crocs Dylan Clog is a solid option for people who want a clog style without some of the common issues that come with it.

The Dylan Clog has a deep heel cup to help lock your foot in, lowering the risk it’ll move around as you step. It’s also made from one piece of Croslite (Crocs’ signature material) to prevent wear and tear over time. This shoe looks like leather thanks to its subtle pebbled texture, but it’s water-resistant and dries quickly when wet. The only major downside is that it’s not very breathable in front. If you’re prone to sweaty toes, this may not be the shoe for you.

Not all shoes are created equal, but the best slip-on walking shoes have all of the supportive features you’ll find in standard lace-up walking shoes. “You mostly get what you pay for in these,” says Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California. He suggests taking a pass at dirt-cheap slip-on walking shoes. “The cheaper ones are not going to provide enough support in the long run, even if they might feel good at first,” Graves says. “There should be enough structure to support your arch and the midsole should be firm and not too flimsy.”

Many high-quality slip-on walking shoes provide similar comfort to regular sneakers. Look for elements like a breathable upper, pull tabs to make them easy to get on and off, and a roomy toe box. Structured heel panels and extra padding in this area help to keep your foot secure, even without standard laces.

Traction for slip-on walking shoes will vary depending on the type of shoe you choose. Most will offer decent traction—meaning, enough so you don’t feel like you’re slipping on wet or damp pavement. But a more rugged shoe like the Merrell Jungle Moc has a grippier sole to help provide extra traction over rockier ground.

Yes, slip-on walking shoes can provide arch support. If this is an important quality for you, look for features like contoured footbeds and a stable midsole. You’ll also want a shoe that fits well and stays put once it’s on to ensure your arch support is consistent. “Make sure that you're not getting them too loose just to make it easier to slide on and off—then you'll be sacrificing support,” Graves says.

To find the best men’s slip-on walking shoes, MH editors tested the most recent and popular pairs on the market, evaluating each for support, comfort, and traction. Because these shoes are designed for walking, not just comfort, durability was also a key factor. To round things out, we consulted three podiatrists for their input on how to evaluate a slip-on walking shoe, along with the value of this style. Based on their advice and our experience, we chose these slip-on walking shoes.

#4986. France backs reporting for self-custodied crypto worth 100K euros or more

The amendment would require taxpayers to report holdings worth at least $112,000, but the measure still needs to survive the budget process.

The French National Assembly approved an amendment that would require taxpayers to report self-custodied crypto holdings totaling at least 100,000 euros ($112,000) to tax authorities.

Amendment I-2701 was adopted on Tuesday in a 150–44 vote, with eight abstentions, according to the Assembly’s official voting record. The threshold would be assessed on Dec. 31 of the relevant tax year.

Separately, the Assembly rejected an amendment that would have exempted gains on crypto payments for goods and services from tax if the payments totaled no more than 1,000 euros ($1,120) during the tax year. The proposal was defeated 69–14, according to the Assembly’s transcript.

The reporting requirement forms part of the 2027 Finance Bill and would need to be retained in the final legislation to become law. The Assembly faces a Nov. 17 deadline to complete its first reading of the bill. Senate debate is scheduled to begin Nov. 20, according to its schedule.

The National Assembly postponed Tuesday’s scheduled vote on the budget’s revenue section for the second time as lawmakers continued debating amendments. The vote was originally scheduled for Oct. 20.

The vote’s postponement itself does not introduce a significant change, but the “likely rejection” of the budget’s revenue section could “result in the rejection of the entire bill in the National Assembly, including provisions adopted by way of amendments,” Faustine Fleuret, global head of public affairs at lending protocol Morpho, told Cointelegraph.

On Friday, the Assembly rejected two proposals that would have applied exit taxes to unrealized crypto gains when taxpayers transferred their tax residence abroad.

Lawmakers also approved an amendment on Oct. 16 that would tax gains from converting crypto into stablecoins. The proposal covers stablecoins classified as electronic money tokens under EU rules and would still need to be retained in the final law.

#4984. Muhammad Ali at Home: 10 Photos of the Heavyweight Champion’s Life Outside the Ring

It was a stroke of luck—bad luck—that got Muhammad Ali into the ring for the first time. The Louisville, Kentucky, native was 12 years old when his brand-new bicycle was stolen. The police officer to whom Ali reported the theft happened to own a boxing gym—and became his first coach.

Ten years later, in 1964, Ali, then still known by his birth name, Cassius Clay, became the world heavyweight champion when he defeated reigning titleholder Sonny Liston. The athlete, who earned the nickname “The Greatest,” would go on to win that title two more times, as well as an Olympic gold medal and numerous honors for his civil rights activism and humanitarian work.

There was, of course, another side to the legend: his domestic life. As we gear up for the release of the Prime Video series The Greatest, which explores the prizefighter’s rise to prominence, we’re looking back at photos of Ali in his off-duty hours.

Days after becoming the heavyweight champion, Ali announced his conversion to the Nation of Islam, changed his name, and then relocated to Chicago, where the controversial religion’s headquarters are based. (He later converted to Sunni Islam). In 1967, Ali cited his religious beliefs when he refused to serve in the US Army during the Vietnam War. His boxing license revoked and his championship title stripped, Ali entered a period of exile. He is pictured in his Chicago home the following year, reading a book by Nation of Islam leader Elijah Muhammad. The athlete shared the dwelling with his second wife, Khalilah Camacho-Ali, whom he married at the residence on August 17, 1967. The single-story brick house was in the Avalon Park neighborhood and was a fully furnished gift from the Nation of Islam.

The boxer and his toddler Maryum feeding 10-week-old twins Rasheda and Jamillah in their Philadelphia home.

The couple welcomed a daughter, Maryum, in 1968, and two years later, twins named Rasheda and Jamillah. The newborns are pictured between Ali and Maryum at home in Pennsylvania in this November 1970 photograph. The fighter and his family stayed at the home, in West Philadelphia’s Overbrook Park neighborhood, for about a year. It was later owned by Kobe Bryant’s grandparents.

Ali with fans at his Pennsylvania training camp in August 1974.

Though he soon relocated to New Jersey, Ali would maintain ties to Pennsylvania for decades with his training camp, Fighter’s Heaven. He purchased the Deer Lake property in 1972, the year after the Supreme Court overturned his draft-evasion conviction, allowing him to regain his boxing license. On the land, he custom-built a log gym, a dining hall, several cabins, a mosque, and a courtyard with a large stone fireplace. His training sessions were open to the public; in this August 1974 photo, a group of fans are pictured behind him at the camp. He kept the retreat long after his retirement, selling it in 1997 to martial arts instructor George Dillman. The property is now a tourist destination, complete with a small museum.

Ali at home in Los Angeles before his fight with Larry Holmes.

Ali briefly retired from boxing at age 37 in 1979, but returned the following year to fight Larry Holmes. The boxer poses at his home office in Hancock Park, Los Angeles, in this August 1980 photo, taken about a month before his fight with Holmes.

Ali shoots pool in his Hancock Park house in this 1980 photo.

Ali shows off the game room in his Hancock Park, Los Angeles, home in this 1980 snapshot. Around this period, he started to show early symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, which impacted his athletic ability. He lost the fight to Holmes and went back into retirement.

The boxing champion and his wife Veronica at home in 1982.

In 1981, Ali fought one last time before hanging up his gloves. “I know it’s the end,” he said after losing the fight. “I’m not crazy. After Holmes, I had excuses. I was too light. Didn’t breathe right. No excuses this time. I’m happy. I’m still pretty. I could have a black eye. Broken teeth. Split lips. I think I came out all right for an old man.” Ali stands next to his third wife, Veronica Porché, in front of his Hancock Park dwelling in this photo, taken a few months after his final match.

The Greatest takes a call at home in 1982.

In this photo from the same March 1982 photo shoot, Ali strikes a pose in his opulent Los Angeles living room. The retired boxer had purchased the 14,500-square-foot home in 1979, two years after marrying Porché. The 1916 build, by architect John C. Austin, was an Italian Renaissance mansion complete with seven bedrooms.

The estate featured stained glass window panels designed by Louis Comfort Tiffany (the son of Tiffany & Co. founder Charles Lewis Tiffany) and a stately dining room with intricately carved dark wood and a crystal chandelier, as seen in this October 1985 photo of Ali eating cereal. That year, he and Porché filed for divorce.

Ali outfitted the home with a (packed) trophy room, which he shows off in this 1985 picture. He left the Hancock Park dwelling the following year, when his and Porché’s divorce was finalized. Shortly after, Ali married his fourth wife, Lonnie Williams. As his Parkinson’s disease progressed (he was officially diagnosed in 1984), Williams became Ali’s primary caregiver.

The former fighter has his picture taken by photographer Neil Leifer at home in Arizona’s Paradise Valley.

Ali poses for a photo shoot commemorating his 70th birthday in 2012 at the Arizona home he and Williams shared. That year, he was honored with the Liberty Medal for his humanitarian efforts, which he devoted more time to following his retirement. He was also awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005. Ali died in Arizona in 2016 at 74.

#4982. On Wants You to Feel Your Softest Ride Yet

The Cloudsurfer 3 is built to make everyday runs feel smooth and effortless, even as the miles add up.

Just because you run doesn’t necessarily mean that you’re up on running shoe innovation. In recent years, there have been notable improvements in propulsion and efficiency, thanks to additions like carbon-fiber plates, smart sensors, and midsoles that promise high energy return. What’s more important than these buzzy words is: How do the shoes feel?

After all, you can have footwear designed by rocket scientists, but if you’re uncomfortable with every step, your run will be a slog, no matter the distance. You want your shoe to make the ride feel soft, which is why the On Cloudsurfer 3 stands out over so many others.

On running shoes have always been distinguished by their trademark hollow pods— the “clouds” that are specifically engineered to help create a softer underfoot experience and give the brand its unmistakable look. In the Cloudsurfer 3, On’s CloudTec Phase™ allows those pods to compress in sequence, helping absorb impact and create a smoother transition from heel to toe. This isn’t just another update to On’s running shoe line. With breakthrough Swiss engineering working beneath every step, the Cloudsurfer 3 delivers the brand’s softest ride yet.

An option for everyday and recovery runs as well as longer training sessions, the Cloudsurfer 3 combines CloudTec® Phase with On’s brand-new SurrealTM Superfoam. According to the brand’s internal testing, the pairing provides 15.5 percent deeper compression—and therefore more impact absorption—than the superfoam alone. The result is a softer landing that can help daily miles feel easier on the legs, particularly over long distances.

According to the same internal testing, the Cloudsurfer 3 is also predicted to deliver a 9.9 percent improvement in smooth-ride sensation. That figure reflects the way the reimagined CloudTec® Phase orientation enhances the rolling motion of the foot, helping each step flow more naturally into the next from landing to toe-off.

You’re also getting a newly engineered mesh upper in the Cloudsurfer 3, which provides a secure fit that adapts to your foot while still offering breathability and support. That breathability helps keep heat and moisture from building up, reducing the conditions that can lead to chafing, blisters, and hot spots.

Even the cushioning around the collar and tongue has been updated, so you get a cloud-like feel as soon as you slip them on. It doesn’t hurt that the Cloudsurfer 3 looks cool, too.

Together, these innovations give runners what they want from an everyday shoe: a natural feel, reliable performance, and lasting comfort. The result is a smoother ride, whether you’re going long or heading out for a quick training run.

That softer feel is a big deal, considering a 2025 study found that runners who perceived their shoes as more cushioned had a lower risk of running-related injury. When a shoe feels right, you’re less likely to think about every step—or adjust the way you’re moving to compensate for discomfort. That allows you to settle into your natural stride and focus on the run itself.

Enjoyment is a major factor, too. Wearing a shoe like the Cloudsurfer 3, with its focus on cushioning, responsiveness, and comfort, can be key to unlocking your best run yet—and enjoying yourself along the way. When that happens, even a hard run can feel softer, mile after mile.

Elizabeth Millard is a freelance writer focusing on health, wellness, fitness, and food.

#4981. Influencers Are Doing ‘Olive Oil Shots.’ We Asked 4 Experts If That’s a Good Idea—and They All Basically Said the Same Thing.

The truth about the supposed health practice—revealed.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

SO OLIVE OIL shots are a thing again. Remember in the mid- to late-2010s, when people were knocking back all manner of liquids, including apple cider vinegar, juiced ginger, pulverized turmeric, and extra virgin olive oil? Well, social media influencers have brought back at least the last one, with Bryan Johnson doing “evo” shots and Steven Gundry, MD, recommending a daily dose of the stuff. (Also, both those guys sell their own olive oil. Just saying.)

The supposed benefits of shooting olive range from the more generalized “more energy” to more specific ones, like protecting your cardiovascular system from disease.

Influencers usually back up these claims by citing scientific research on the benefits of adding olive oil to your daily diet. But do the benefits extend to doing shots of olive oil?

“Olive oil is great for heart health and contains beneficial polyphenols, but you don't need to take it as a shot. You get the same benefits by just including it in your meals, and it's generally much more enjoyable that way. But if you want to take it as a shot, there's no harm in that. It's just not superior to including olive oil in your diet in regular ways. You know, with food.”

“I'm a fan of California Olive Ranch 100% California Extra Virgin Olive Oil For Everyday. It's high quality, reasonably affordable (for evoo), and widely available. I use it to saute veggies, roast tubers and veggies, and drizzle on various things.”

“I'm a bigger fan of eating a few shots of olive oil with sauteed veggies or I pour it on my food. But a shot is fine I guess. People like to do it in the longevity scene to invoke ancient Greeks doing shots of ‘liquid gold.’”

“I am an affiliate of the Fresh Pressed Olive Oil Club, which I reallly love. I've not had lots of fancy, fresh olive oils from around the world before and now I have. I like seeing and tasting the diversity. I use a 1-liter glass bottle of EVOO, usually Braggs or Whole Food Organic. I try to go through two to three of these a month for our house of four.”

“I wouldn’t suggest shots of olive oil for any reason. All that’s happening here is that you’re adding a concentrated source of calories and fat to your diet. There are no documented benefits of doing this for the average person, and it can cause weight gain if the oil shots are taken in addition to someone’s current diet. This can ultimately cause health problems.”

“I don’t really have a fave oil. I use brands that have a seal of origin in them to ensure their purity.”

“While olive oil is full of beneficial compounds that may support heart health and longevity, shooting it isn't necessary. Heating olive oil may degrade some beneficial polyphenols, but using it as a salad dressing, sauce, or finishing oil for roasted veggies provides the same benefits, plus enhanced absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and carotenoids.”

“Extra-virgin olive oil can have such a range of flavors. I love San Giuliano Coastal Harvest Olive Oil. It's cold-pressed, which helps preserve more nutrients and polyphenols, and has a really nice, peppery flavor. While I don't take shots of it, I regularly use it in dressings and over veggies.”

Paul Kita is a Deputy Editor at Men's Health, where he has covered food, cooking, nutrition, supplements, grooming, tech, travel, and fatherhood at the brand for more than 15 years. He is also the author of two Men's Health cookbooks, Guy Gourmet and A Man, A Pan, A Plan, and the winner of a James Beard Award.

#4978. This DC Designer’s Nearly 200-Year-Old Virginia Farmhouse Flourishes With Detail and History

In the foothills of Virginia’s Blue Ridge Mountains, just minutes from Shenandoah National Park, the town of Sperryville (population: 350) still feels like a well-kept secret. In recent years, it’s attracted the eye of Washington, DC–based designer Melissa Colgan of Melissa Colgan Interiors, who purchased a weekend home there in 2023.

Though born in the Midwest, the designer and her husband, Daniel Schned, moved to DC in 2016 and spent their early years and weekends exploring the surrounding countryside. “One of the areas we fell in love with is Rappahannock County,” she says of discovering its scenic pastures, rolling hills, and grazing cows. “It feels a world away from DC.”

The staircase is covered in Schumacher’s Caterpillar Leaf print and the stair runner is by Sinclair Till. The cloche is custom by Dan Nakamura.

In the family room, the BDDW sofa is upholstered in a Décors Barbares fabric. The side table is from Covesville Antiques and topped with a lamp by Christopher Spitzmiller. The artwork is by Molly van Amerongen.

The fruitwood dining table from 1stDibs is surrounded with chairs by Lorenzo Castillo and upholstered in a fabric by Schumacher. The 1930s chandelier has custom shades covered in a Decors Barbares fabric. The chairs are by Leah O’Connell (left) and Soane. The artwork is by Joshua Perkin.

In 2020, the couple eloped at The Inn at Little Washington and began looking for a vacation home in the area. Three years later, they found a listing for an 1830s farmhouse and barn, which happened to be the former home and office of the county doctor. “It’s a very special house in Sperryville because it’s where the doctor saw all his patients in the early 1900s,” Colgan says.

What began as an 1830s single-room log cabin evolved to include a barn and second story in the 1890s, followed by another addition in the late 1990s. “A lot of the original details were still there,” Colgan says of the 1,200-square-foot residence. “We just wanted to freshen things up a bit.”

In the family living room, the windows, along with the original chink log siding, date to the 1830s. “I wanted to lean into some of the depth that was already there,” Colgan says of her color palette. “That prompted me into the world of deep reds, ochres, and blues.”

In a cozy corner, a Casamidy chair covered in soft mohair flanks a Swedish Gustavian oak secretary from the 1800s.

Colgan solicited the help of DC architect Alexander Smith of Mortar & Thatch. “The thing we aligned with from the very beginning is we didn't want it to feel like a new renovation,” Smith says. “Maybe we slapped on some paint or got new countertops, but we didn’t want it to seem like we were implanting foreign ideas.”

The biggest task was subdividing the single bedroom upstairs to accommodate Colgan’s growing family. At the time, she was pregnant with her now two-year-old daughter. “We basically took down the walls of the one bedroom, made a middle bedroom for our daughter, then eked every inch we could in order to fit a king bed and built-in closets in our room,” she says. The result is a quaint and colorful two-bedroom blueprint, with dappled light dancing through the street-facing windows.

In the pocket-size half bath, an American Federal mahogany mirror broadens the space, which is wrapped in Iksel Mogul Berry Wallpaper by Schumacher and adorned with an oil painting by Jay Harper.

Incorporating open shelves in the kitchen helped maximize storage while enabling the designer to showcase more of the home’s attractive chink log siding. Farrow & Ball’s Terre de Egypte paint accentuates Colgan’s collections of splatterware mugs and vintage objects, like an early-20th-century painter’s palette.

Today, they spend most of their time in the living room downstairs, with its original chink log siding from the 1830s. “The room is so soulful. You just walk in and take a deep breath,” she says. “The thing that came to mind early on was a little Russian country house or dacha. When we first saw the listing, we were in Switzerland, so that was the original seed for the design.”

Drawing from the warmth and depth of the living room’s original pine floors and log siding, Colgan conjured a rich color palette of ochres, reds, and blues with botanical and floral-patterned fabrics that mirrored the pastoral landscape. “We’re surrounded by mountains and flora and fauna, so I wanted the house to reflect that as well.”

A brisbee curtain in Lake August’s flowering Nasturtium fabric adds light and whimsy to the kitchen’s neutral cabinetry.

The kitchen pendants are by Urban Electric. The walls are painted in Dimity and the cabinets are painted Joa’s White, both by Farrow & Ball. The rug is by Matt Camron.

The furnishings are an array of old, new, and local finds from their 1920s French fruitwood dining table to the early American rocking chair salvaged from Ruckersville Antiques. “We didn’t really have anything for this house because the style is so different from our city home, so we had to start from scratch,” Colgan says. Still, the designer is an avid collector and had some pieces sitting in storage like the BDDW sofa, purchased at auction, that’s now in her living room. Currently, it’s upholstered in Décors Barbares’ lively Roses Tchékhonine print, with winged butterflies flitting across a canvas of cobalt and crimson flowers.

In the primary bedroom, every inch mattered. “We did multiple layouts and wanted to make sure the details, finishes, and everything in there was an appropriate scale so things didn’t feel too big or too small for the space,” says Smith. The walls and his-and-her closets are painted in Farrow & Ball’s Pink Ground and Eating Room Red, with Roman shades done in a Lucrezia fabric by Fortuny. An acrylic and ink work on paper by artist Julie Wolfe, which Colgan gave to her husband for their first wedding anniversary, hangs over the bed.

In the sunlit bathroom, blue and white garden tiles from Marble Systems bloom alongside fittings by Waterworks, D Porthault patterned towels, and an antique French mirror, circa 1785.

Other spaces, like the mudroom and laundry located near the home’s side entrance, were made more welcoming and useful, with cupboards dressed in wholesome, hay-colored gingham skirts. Reconfiguring appliances and adding cabinets and open shelving helped optimize the kitchen’s storage and traffic flow. “We were able to inch out so much in such a small space,” Smith says.

Despite its demure size, the house today is a sensory retreat for the couple. “That first Thanksgiving was a real stress test,” Colgan says. The barn in the back, where the doctor kept his horse for making house calls across the county, was renovated by the previous owner to include a kitchenette, an open living room space, and sleeping quarters. “The barn had pigs in it up until the last owner, and he renovated it,” she says. “I’ve since layered in a lot of fabrics and antiques.”

In their daughter’s room, a late-19th-century faux-bamboo pine and bird’s eye maple bed is made up with D Porthault Pink Coeur’s linens and a one-of-a-kind PROJEKTITYYNY Wisteria baby quilt, stitched with Liberty fabrics. The bookshelf is from Crate & Barrel and the walls and windows are covered in Ottoline’s blue and brown Indian Tulip print.

The walls are covered in Caterpillar Leaf by Schumacher and the slipper chair is custom. The Roman shade is a fabric by Antoinette Poisson.

Off the home’s side entry, a laundry and mudroom papered in Beata Heuman’s Eyelash design is further brightened thanks to the café curtain and cabinet skirts in a jumbo gingham by Beata Heuman, finished with French grosgrain trim.

Ultimately, however, it was the historic farmhouse where Colgan concentrated her creative energy. “A lot of times people come into these old houses and instead of trying to think carefully about how to make modern life function there, they blow out walls and make everything open,” she says. Instead, she champions her home’s nuanced details, including planks of weathered wood that have patinated over time or the way sunlight shimmers off the 19th-century windows, with their panes of wavy glass. “They are very much not energy efficient,” she says, “but they are absolutely beautiful.”

The custom console is painted in Benjamin Moore’s Van Deusen Blue and the walls are covered in Beata Heuman’s Eyelash Spring. The 1960s mirror is from 1stDibs.

On the front porch, a five-piece set by Newell Jacobsen is upholstered in a sky-blue Lisa Fine Madras Performance fabric that complements the painted ceiling, and the neighbor’s vibrant home. “There are some fun houses on our street—the one across the street is yellow,” Colgan says. “I liked the idea of colors out there being a little brighter.”

#4975. The 16 Best Men's Clothing Brands in 2026, According to Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

From the OG classics to newcomer labels you need to know.

AS MEN’S HEALTH EDITORS, we give guys tools they need to level up their lives, and that includes your wardrobe. Enter: The best men's clothing brands for men, a shortlist of labels that deliver on style and function for every vibe and occasion. Whether you’re a seasoned fashion maven or just dipping your toes into the menswear game, having a solid rotation of duds you can rely on is key to looking sharp without overthinking it. More importantly, the right brands make it easy, whether you need office-ready staples, weekend essentials, or something that’ll turn heads on a night out, you can rest assured that you’re getting the same fit every time from the same brand.

Since 2020, our style editors have tested more than 80 clothing brands for men, exploring all kinds of styles including activewear, business casual, sharp tailoring, outerwear layers, and everything in between. To curate the best of the best, we focused on three things: Clothes that are built to last, look sharp, and make you feel unstoppable. Below, the 16 best men's clothing brands that nail craftsmanship, timeless style, and all-around wearability.

Huckberry's in-house label delivers a rugged, workwear-inspired vibe, made with utility and style in mind. Flint & Tinder is essentially for the guy who wants clothes that feel cool and work as hard as he does. The pieces aren’t just about looking good; they can handle all kinds of weather, provide comfort, and won’t fray at the end of a few wears. You get authentic American workwear aesthetics with modern details, meaning every piece can handle everyday wear and the occasional adventure.

In terms of selects, the lineup is super versatile. Expect quality, uniform staples; think robust flannels, durable outerwear (like waxed canvas jackets), sturdy chinos, and comfortable, well-constructed basics. Whether you’re going on a camping trip, chopping down some wood, or grabbing beers with your pals, these designs make for excellent gear in the city, in the wild, and beyond.

If we had to choose one of our favorites from F&T, it would be the Flannel-Lined Waxed Trucker Jacket that looks burly on the outside but feels super toasty on the inside. When the weather breaks, it does a bang-up job at keeping the rain, wind, and cold temps at bay.

Read More: Best Clothing Subscription Boxes for Men

With a roster of products that spans everything from T-shirts and underwear to activewear, Mack Weldon builds a complete wardrobe that’s both high-performing and versatile for your everyday life. In using a variety of innovative fabrics and technologies, the brand offers clothes that look great, feel incredible, and are engineered to withstand your weekly routine (i.e. long work days, rigorous HIIT sessions, all-day errand runs).

If you’re a busy body and constantly on the move, you can find a number of items to support your active lifestyle. In fact, performance features like moisture-wicking and anti-odor protection make it easy to transition from the gym to your daily grind without missing a beat. As for casual outings, Mack Weldon has you covered in that area, too. Whether that means baseball games, coffee dates, or happy hour meet-ups, the clean, minimal designs are a great fit for a polished yet relaxed look, too.

Speaking of which, the Ace Sweatpant is a total winner. Made with micro-brushed French terry, it’s a pair that offers a flattering fit, plenty of breathability, and won’t make you look out of place, no matter where you are.

Read More: Mack Weldon Airknitx Boxer Brief Review

Abercrombie used to be one of those mall-favorites back in the day, but the brand has since revamped its all-American cool–think easygoing duds, with a hint of vintage flair. Its range of versatile, premium-feeling designs are mostly laid-back and look great on guys of all ages. These threads work perfectly in casual environments where you want to look put-together but leave the high maintenance at home. At its core, the brand is all about comfort that doesn’t sacrifice style.

Whether you’re attending a music festival, cruising downtown with friends, or hitting up a weekend bonfire, you can find pieces that transition from day to night, making sure you’re always on point—no matter the occasion. Abercrombie specializes in those casual staples that you need in rotation such as cozy hoodies, sleek vegan leather jackets, perfectly worn-in t-shirts, and several types of denim cuts. When it comes to the latter, the 90s Straight Jean has been a huge hit, offering a wide selection of washes, plenty of stretch, and retro charm.

Bonobos got its start because the founders were fed up with pants that just didn’t cut it. With universal fits at its heart, they set out to build wardrobe essentials that actually work for every guy, no matter his build. Instead of sticking with small, medium, and large sizes, the brand’s assortment of pants features over 12 different waist sizes, plus a range of inseams and fits including athletic, slim taper, and straight. This means you’re guaranteed to find the perfect pair. In tandem with the selection of pants, the shirts come in a series of fits, too.

Aside from killer chinos, the vast inventory consists of golf gear, suits and blazers, swim trunks, and outerwear. In fact, it was the relaxed cut of The Harrington Jacket that resonated with us, which layers easily over all kinds of tops. All things considered, if you need new attire for the beach, the links, the office, or the weekend, it’s all here.

If you've never heard of Buck Mason, think of this LA-based brand as a one-stop-shop for guys who want to look put-together but not pretentious. Instead of chasing trends, the label is set on offering a refined take on everyday essentials, blending American style with modern tailoring and quality craftsmanship. In other words, its expertise lies in paying attention to the details: Taking into account fabric, fit, and function. After all, the brand acquired an American knitting mill to ensure its gear stays authentically made in the USA. As a result, this men’s clothing brand’s designs are about that understated style with classic silhouettes and muted color palettes, mixed with a twist of laid-back California vibes.

Falling in line with those aesthetics is its best-selling, signature Felted Chore Coat—simple at first glance, but crafted with purpose. We love that it's tailored with a slimmer cut through the arms for a sharper silhouette, while the roomier torso leaves space for layering. Plus, the felted merino wool allows you to capitalize on warmth, breathability, and softness without bulk.

In general, Buck Mason’s pieces work in a variety of settings—be it a dinner date, food festival, or Broadway show. Among its collection of garments is high-quality jeans, t-shirts and henleys, button-down shirts and lightweight jackets.

Todd Snyder is known for modernizing classic American menswear with tailored fits, top-of-the-line fabrics, and subtle yet stylish updates. The brand blends timeless silhouettes with contemporary details, often playing with rich textures and unique color palettes. While Todd Snyder is not exactly budget-friendly, the slew of suede jackets, wool coats, and refined suiting will let you channel the best A-listers in the game. In fact, its vintage-inspired sweaters and outerwear have even graced the likes of Chris Evans and Ryan Reynolds.

An undeniable standout is the Italian Suede Snap Dylan Jacket that’s structured enough to look sharp but accommodate easy layering. The trucker-style cut is crafted from buttery-soft calf suede, which not only gives luxury feels but also ages beautifully over time.

Another one of Todd Snyder's biggest strengths is its collaborations, from Timex watches to New Balance sneakers and Champion heritage sweatpants. These partnerships add a level of flair that few brands are able to mimic. Overall, TS expertly delivers high-quality, long-lasting staples that work for guys who want to look put-together without trying too hard.

Everlane is a men's clothing brand that follows its own path. It's really big on creating eco-conscious, classic clothes that will cycle through your ever-evolving wardrobe for years to come. Think authentic denim and minimal organic cotton tees priced so well that you won't have any other option than to stock up on multiple pairs and colorways.

If you're looking to stay cozy through the last stretch of winter, Everlane's got a whole Cashmere Shop filled with ultra-soft sweaters to keep you warm without overheating. The brand’s assortment also makes it easy to transition from the office to happy hour with its monochromatic shirting—from oxford shirts to shackets such as the versatile Heavyweight Overshirt—that has that just-right fit that's neither too slim nor too boxy.

Perhaps best known in the zeitgeist for its finance bro vests, Patagonia is in fact the leading outdoor apparel brand that makes clothes with adventures and extreme climates in mind. It has tons of hiking-inspired basics to anchor a stylish and functional closet. For starters, The Nano Puff Jacket is the gold standard of puffer jackets—light, warm, and endlessly versatile—ideal for street and trail wear. Not to mention, it's a warrior in all kinds of weather, thanks to the windproof and water-repellent exterior.

Its fleece layers are legendary, too. Take the Better Sweater Fleece Jacket, which is cozy, durable, and polished enough to wear just about anywhere. This silhouette is thicker than a standard fleece, but the regular fit allows you to layer effortlessly. In terms of style, you can wear it for weekend hikes or the nearest coffee shop for your daily pick-me-up.

This stalwart label has been in the game for ages and still gets it right—serving up sleek clothing for men, which embodies "quiet luxury" energy, minus the high-roller price tag. When it comes to styling Banana Republic, picture yourself nailing every look—from acing that morning meeting in a crisp dress shirt and tailored chinos, to seamlessly transitioning into dinner at a swanky bistro with a smart blazer.

The brand’s offerings are built for real life, so whether you’re powering through a busy workday, networking at after-hours events, or catching up with friends over drinks on the weekend, there’s something to fit the bill. Banana Republic specializes in dressier, well-cut staples: Sharp button-downs, versatile trousers, structured blazers, and quality knitwear that feels as good as it looks. But make no mistake, Banana Republic also plays with casual attire too. For example, the Ribbed Cotton Henley T-Shirt has that relaxed feel, which is great for those off-duty days when you’re picking up lunch or taking a laid-back stroll in the park.

Alex Mill’s been around for over a decade, carving out a reputation we’d describe as “Normcore classic.” In other words, the brand hits it on the nail when it comes to everyday basics—think slub tees that serve as the ultimate wardrobe workhorses, slightly cropped jeans that pair with any top, and washed chore coats that add dimension to any look. It’s all about minimal fuss, modern sensibility, and letting the pieces become more character-rich with every wear.

These garments really come into their own in spots like creative offices, co-working spaces, or that favorite local cafe—places where you want to look put-together without trying too hard. They’re perfect for laid-back brunches, art gallery openings, or casual dinner dates. Without seeming overdone, these staples can easily elevate your everyday style. Take the Garment Dyed Chore Jacket in Canvas, for instance: It's super low-key—not too in your face, yet still has that unique twist that any artist or designer would appreciate.

The Japanese brand helped redefine what great wardrobe essentials should feel like: clean, well-made, and affordable without ever looking cheap. Its lineup is built around minimal design and great-for-the-price fabrics (think Heattech thermals, a heat-retaining base layer designed to trap warmth without bulk, or Ultra Light Down, Uniqlo’s featherweight yet surprisingly warm down insulation), offering pieces that work across seasons—from crisp tees and chinos to cozy sweaters and functional outerwear that earns its closet space.

What makes Uniqlo a go-to is its ability to effortlessly fit into everyday life. These are clothes you grab on busy workdays, for travel, or just when you want to get dressed without overthinking it. Whether you’re layering thermals under a jacket for winter or reaching for a casual linen in the summer, Uniqlo’s pieces are the building blocks that make everything else in your wardrobe work better.

J.Crew is one of those heritage American labels that you often circle back to because it just gets the classics right. The brand is known for its preppy-meets-laid-back aesthetic, offering staples like blazers, button-downs, chinos, knitwear, and polos that feel polished but never stuffy.These are the kinds of pieces that carry you through a full day from the office to post-work drinks without needing an outfit change. If your style lives somewhere between casual and pulled-together, J.Crew makes it easy to look sharp in a way that feels chill and approachable at the same time.

Cos is the more elevated sibling to H&M—part of the same family, but built around higher-quality fabrics and more refined construction. Rather than chasing trends, Cos invests in premium wool blends, heavyweight cottons, and structured tailoring, which its pieces cost a bit more than its sister brand, but also hold their shape and look polished far longer. You’re paying for better fabric, cleaner finishing, and silhouettes that don’t feel disposable. Its lineup includes sharp wool overcoats, crisp poplin button-downs, substantial merino knits, and tailored trousers with a proper drape—all in shades like black, navy, charcoal, or stone. These clothes can transition from the office to a fancy dinner to speakeasy nightcap situation. Essentially, this is where you go for something a step above fast fashion minus the designer price tag.

Alo may have started as an active brand, but it’s evolved into a full-on lifestyle label that blends workout clothes with fits that you’d wear outside the gym. From moisture-wicking workout tees and sleek tanks to comfortable hoodies and joggers that look good in public, these are the pieces you throw on for a morning session, keep on for errands, travel days, or a casual lunch, and still feel clean.

Tailored cargo trousers, straight-leg Velour pants, and track pants with clean hems and minimal branding can pass at the office, while the carpenter-style bottoms and relaxed cargos feel polished enough for dinner plans. Up top, Alo’s bombers, pullover sweatshirts, and shackets are structured, not slouchy or logo-heavy, making them easy substitutes for a crewneck, knit, or light jacket.

If your uniform leans athletic but put-together, without looking like you just walked out of a sweat-drenched Barry’s class, Alo makes it easy to never feel under- or overdressed. One note: most of its clothing runs big, so be sure to size down for a closer fit, unless you prefer a looser cut.

Madewell established its reputation on solid denim, and that foundation still shows, but over the years the brand has evolved beyond jeans. Over the past few years, it’s quietly strengthened its menswear roster, offering easy essentials like soft tees, cozy knits, overshirts, and brushed flannels that layer cleanly without bunching. The overall vibe at Madewell is relaxed but put-together. These clothes are made for weekends, casual dinners, and low-key nights at a bar or speakeasy. They feel broken-in from day one but still read sharp. If your uniform starts with great denim and goes from there, Madewell is an excellent place to begin.

Few brands have done more to define American prep than Tommy Hilfiger. From rugby shirts and flag sweaters to chinos, polos, and lightweight outerwear, the label consistently delivers timeless staples that feel both classic and current. What keeps Tommy relevant, though, is its knack for evolving the formula through smart collaborations and fresh takes on heritage style. Recent partnerships, including its ongoing work with the U.S. SailGP Team, prove the brand still knows how to make prep feel cool for a new generation.

A polished but relaxed approach to office dressing that’s also suitable for after-work drinks—think chinos, dress shirts, knit polos, and unstructured blazers. Brands such as Bonobos, Alex Mill, and Banana Republic have this kind of style down pat.

If you have plans to attend a black-tie event, gala, wedding, or simply want to look extra sharp, you’ve got to suit up. In this case, you’ll turn to structured blazers, tailored trousers, dress shirts, and dress shoes in classic colors like navy, gray, and black. Brands such as Bonobos, Todd Snyder, Banana Republic, and Buck Mason have suiting on lock.

From lightweight jackets to heavy-duty coats, outerwear is all about function and style. This includes bombers, leather jackets, shackets, parkas, and puffers perfect for transitional weather or full-on winter. Brands such as Flint and Tinder, Patagonia, and Alex Mill will have you geared up.

Clothing designed for movement but stylish enough for everyday wear. Think workout shirts, joggers, sweat-wicking polos, gym shorts, and sneakers that work for both gym sessions and casual outings. Brands like Alo and Patagonia offer a solid collection of these duds.

Easygoing staples like jeans, hoodies, henleys, sneakers, and flannels—perfect for relaxed weekends, brunch, or laid-back office days. Brands such as Abercrombie, J.Crew, Everlane, and Uniqlo deliver in this category.

When shopping for the best clothing brands for men, fit is everything. It dictates not only how comfortable you feel but also how your outfit communicates your personal style. Generally, men’s garments are broken down into four broad categories: Relaxed, Tailored, Classic, and Slim. You don’t have to stick to just one, but each serves a different aesthetic and function—let’s break it down.

Relaxed-fit clothing is all about comfort. It’s cut with extra room through the chest, waist, and legs, allowing for a looser, more laid-back silhouette. This is ideal if you’re looking for casual wear, streetwear, and workwear-inspired looks. Think boxy tees, oversized hoodies, wide-leg trousers, and unstructured outerwear. Patagonia tends to lean into this fit as its fleece jackets, outerwear, and casual basics are built for movement and outdoor adventure. Alex Mill focuses on casual staples with slightly relaxed, vintage-inspired cuts.

A tailored fit offers a balance between structure and comfort. It follows the body’s shape without clinging too tightly, creating a refined yet wearable look. This is your go-to fit for business casual, smart casual, and elevated everyday wear. Think tapered chinos, slightly structured blazers, and slim-but-not-skinny button-downs.

Slim fits are designed for a clean, modern silhouette. These clothes contour the body without excessive looseness, making them ideal for dressier looks, contemporary minimalism, or even athleisure. Key pieces include slim-fit jeans, fitted turtlenecks, and sharply cut blazers.

Classic fit is the middle ground between relaxed and tailored, giving you room to move without excess fabric. This is the fit you’ll find in traditional menswear, from business suits to heritage denim. It’s not baggy, but it’s also not hugging your body either.

Not all clothes are created equal, and neither are price tags. Some items are worth dropping some serious cash on, while others can be a rip-off. The key is knowing when to invest and when to save because a well-thought-out wardrobe isn’t about spending the most, it’s about getting the most value out of what you buy.

This is your fast-fashion and essentials tier—solid for trying new styles or grabbing wardrobe basics without overthinking. But here’s the catch: Cheap can often mean short-lived. For instance, a $10 tee from a fast-fashion retailer may look good today but will likely warp, fade, or pill after a few washes. That’s fine for trends like an oversized striped tee you might wear for a season, but when it comes to daily staples, spending a little more pays off. You’d be better off spending $58 on an Alex Mill slub tee that lasts for years and is worn 50-plus times, which equals less than $2 per wear.

This is where cost meets quality. You’re getting better fabrics, stronger construction, and brands that care about longevity. Think nicer denim, well-cut chinos, and quality knitwear—things you’ll actually wear often, so the investment makes sense.

This is where justifiable spending comes into play. A $500 Buck Mason suede jacket? Pricey up front, but wear it 50 times per season for five years, and suddenly, it’s $2 per wear—less than a daily coffee. The same goes for boots—drop $300+ on a well-made pair, and you won’t have to replace them for a decade. In this price range, you find premium outerwear, leather goods, boots, and everyday pieces.

At this level, you’re paying for craftsmanship, exclusivity, and long-term investment. A $1,300 leather jacket from Todd Snyder isn’t for everyone, but if you’re buying into history, durability, and premium construction, it’ll outlive you. Same with a properly tailored suit—if you wear it for major life events over decades, it’s an investment, not an expense.
