#4948. 3 Steps to De-Catastrophize Your Anxious Thoughts

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

People with anxiety often come to therapy complaining of a specific and extreme form of worrying. They ask questions like:

If your mind also plays a reel of worst-case scenarios every time your anxiety rises, you might be engaging in catastrophizing. Catastrophic thinking is distorted perception and cognition.

Typically, when a person catastrophizes, they blow things out of proportion and feel irrationally threatened by current, past, or imaginary situations. If you tend to catastrophize, here are three steps to de-escalate your thought processes.

Catastrophizing can quickly lead you down a dark thought spiral. The best thing to do: Immediately bring yourself back to the present.

Research published in Acta Psychologica suggests that mindfulness, both in the moment and as a personality trait, shows great promise as a combatant to anxiety and catastrophizing. Training and practicing mindfulness can give your emotion regulation faculties a much-needed boost.

Another practice that can help someone who struggles with catastrophizing is breathwork. Research shows that deep breathing — or diaphragmatic breathing — relieves anxiety by lowering heart rate and blood pressure. Focusing on your breath grounds you in the present and therefore acts as a buffer between you and your catastrophic thoughts.

Small worries accumulate and turn into catastrophic thinking. Research explains that setting aside and scheduling a block of time solely for worrying is a simple but effective stress-management technique.

If you have anxious or catastrophic thoughts during an important moment, defer them to your ‘worry time’ and focus on the present moment. It can also help you become aware of and address your anxieties.

Since catastrophizing is a cognitive distortion or, simply put, a malfunctioning thought process, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is recommended most often when it comes to addressing catastrophic thinking.

Research shows CBT is effective against catastrophizing; it is based on awareness. Under CBT, the person struggling with catastrophizing is made aware of the dysfunction in emotion regulation and thought processes and is given exercises tailored to dismantle irrational thinking.

Often, the best antidote to catastrophic thinking is to talk to someone who can offer an objective perspective, like a therapist or counselor.

As with other distorted thought processes, catastrophizing flourishes in isolation. The first thing anyone should do when they can’t control their own disturbing thoughts is to say them out loud, preferably to a loved one or a medical professional.

#4946. Tesla FSD ‘subscriptions’ hit 1.74M, counted the way Musk’s pay package wants

Tesla says it now has 1.74 million active “Full Self-Driving” subscriptions, up 67% from a year ago. A footnote in its Q3 2026 shareholder letter explains how it gets there: the metric follows “our 2025 CEO Performance Award” and “includes both upfront payment and monthly subscriptions.”

Here’s what Tesla has reported under that definition:

Tesla stopped selling FSD as a one-time purchase on February 14, 2026. New customers can only get it as a subscription, at $99 a month in the US. But everyone who paid upfront before that, at prices that reached $15,000, stays in the count as long as the car is active. The only exclusion is free trials.

We flagged this in April when Tesla reported 1.28 million. Six months later, Tesla still doesn’t say how many of the 1.74 million actually pay every month.

The same approach shows up elsewhere in the letter. Tesla’s “cumulative deliveries” figure, now 10.2 million, also counts “any unsupervised Robotaxis placed into commercial operation,” again to match the pay package, which has a 20 million vehicle milestone.

Tesla also says more than 75% of new deliveries in North America included FSD subscriptions in Q3, “a nearly twenty percentage point sequential increase.” It says it believes “FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available.”

That’s a big number, and Tesla doesn’t define it. The letter doesn’t say whether it counts subscriptions started at delivery with an introductory offer, or how many of those buyers are still paying after a few months. The active-subscription metric excludes free trials, but Tesla doesn’t say the same about the attach rate.

Musk’s 2025 award has 12 tranches. Each requires a market cap milestone and one operational milestone. The operational list includes 20 million vehicles delivered, 10 million active FSD subscriptions, 1 million Optimus robots, 1 million robotaxis in commercial operation, and adjusted EBITDA targets. As of June 30, Tesla considered only one of them probable: 20 million deliveries.

Tesla added 260,000 net FSD subscriptions in Q3, its best quarter yet. At that pace, it would take about eight years to reach 10 million. At the pace of the last 12 months, about 700,000 a year, it would take closer to 12. The award runs until 2035.

Counting people who bought FSD outright isn’t wrong on its own. Those cars do have the software. The problem is calling them “subscriptions” and presenting the total as proof of momentum, when the definition was written for Musk’s pay package and not for investors trying to understand the business.

The metrics that are far off in Musk's 2025 comp plan don't matter because if there is a change of control (i.e., SpaceX buys Tesla), all the comp plan metrics vest and count as achieved, and good old Elon gets paid. And you wonder why he wants this merger?

This is now Tesla’s headline software metric. The board wrote the definition, Musk’s compensation depends on it, and the company won’t say how many people pay $99 a month. Tesla obviously knows that number.

The attach rate is the more interesting claim, if it holds up. A 75% take rate on a $99-a-month product would be a real business. So show us the retention: how many North American buyers who started a subscription in Q2 are still paying today?

#4945. Wall Squats, Planks Once a Week May Help Lower Your Blood Pressure

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Isometric exercises, even if done only occasionally, could help improve blood pressure, according to a new study.

Researchers report that study participants who did these types of exercises once or twice a week saw reductions in blood pressure over a short period.

They added that participants who engaged in isometric exercises three times a week maintained improvements in blood pressure over a longer period.

The researchers said that previous studies had indicated that isometric exercise training reduces blood pressure more than other forms of exercise and even some drug treatments.

However, they said previous research had not established how often isometric exercise training needs to be performed to maintain these health benefits.

Isometric exercises involve a person holding a pose for a few minutes at a time. Examples include wall squats and floor planks.

The researchers said their study provides important information for people who don’t have time to exercise daily.

The researchers wrote that the study “offers evidence that lower frequency [isometric exercise training] can help maintain short-term [blood pressure] reductions, providing a pragmatic option for individuals with limited time or adherence challenges.”

They published their findings on September 29 in BMJ Open Sport and Exercise Medicine.

Experts not involved in the research said it provides helpful guidance for people who want to improve their blood pressure.

“The main takeaway is that you don’t need to exercise every day — or even several times a week — to experience significant blood pressure benefits from isometric exercise,” said Michael Fredericson, MD, a professor of orthopaedic surgery at Stanford Health Care.

“We already knew that performing isometric training for even just a few weeks can lower blood pressure,” added Amanda Paluch, PhD, an associate professor of kinesiology at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and chair of the American Heart Association’s Physical Activity Committee. “This study adds to the research by looking at how much training is needed to maintain those gains.”

“It is encouraging to see measurable improvements in blood pressure with a relatively brief and infrequent exercise routine,” said Jennifer Wong, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of Non-Invasive Cardiology at MemorialCare Heart and Vascular Institute at Orange Coast Medical Center in California. “These findings suggest that even small, consistent efforts can make a meaningful difference.”

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that nearly half of adults in the United States have high blood pressure. That’s about 120 million people.

The condition, also known as hypertension, increases the risk of heart disease and stroke.

High blood pressure occurs when the force of blood pushing through blood vessels is consistently too high.

Blood pressure readings consist of two numbers. One is the systolic pressure (top number), which measures pressure when your heart beats. The second is diastolic pressure (the bottom number), which measures the pressure between beats.

Treatment usually involves medications such as beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors, as well as lifestyle factors such as a healthy diet and exercise.

In their study, the researchers aimed to determine how much isometric exercise was needed to lower and maintain blood pressure.

The researchers recruited 100 adults with an average age of 37. Subjects included male and female participants with normal-to-high-normal systolic blood pressure (120–140 mm Hg) who engaged in less than 150 minutes per week of moderate physical activity.

The participants also had no injuries or illnesses, were not taking and had not previously taken blood pressure medication, were not smokers, and did not consume more than 14 units of alcohol per week.

The participants were divided into five groups. One group served as a control and did no isometric exercise, while the other four groups followed the same four-week home-based lower-body isometric training program.

The regimen consisted of four sessions of isometric wall squat exercise, separated by two minutes of seated rest, performed three times a week.

During the next four weeks, the participants were split into four training schedules.

One group continued to exercise three times a week. A second group exercised twice a week, while a third group exercised once a week. The remaining group stopped the exercises entirely.

Blood pressure, heart rate, and other cardiac measurements were taken at the start of the study and after four weeks and eight weeks.

The researchers reported that the four groups who completed the initial four-week exercise routine showed significant reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure compared to the control group.

Over the next four weeks, the researchers found no statistically significant difference in diastolic blood pressure among the groups.

However, the researchers reported that participants who continued isometric exercise training three times a week achieved the greatest reduction in systolic blood pressure compared with baseline. That group also maintained improvements in other cardiac measures.

The group that had stopped doing isometric exercises after the initial four-week period showed a reversal of their blood pressure improvements.

The researchers wrote that the study “demonstrates that while lower frequency [isometric exercise training] may be sufficient to maintain [blood pressure] reductions over the short term, higher frequencies are required to preserve these benefits and the associated vascular and cardiac autonomic adaptations.”

The researchers noted that the eight-week study period was limited and that further research is needed. They also acknowledged that the participants were from a relatively small cross-section of people.

There are several ways isometric exercises may help lower blood pressure.

“Repeat isometric exercises (contracting a muscle and holding a position) seem to change how the blood vessels regulate pressure between workouts,” said Kevin Shah, MD, a cardiologist and program director of Heart Failure Outreach at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Blood pressure comes down to how hard the heart pumps and how much resistance the blood meets in the vessels,” added Paluch.

“Research suggests isometric training works mainly on that second part. It helps your blood vessels relax and open up, so blood flows through more easily.”

“Isometric exercise seems to promote cardiovascular adaptations that can lower blood pressure,” explained Fredericson. “Over time, this training can enhance the cardiovascular system’s ability to regulate blood pressure.”

Experts interviewed by Healthline say that the wall squats used in the study are one of the most beneficial isometric exercises.

They also recommend static leg extensions, handgrip exercises, planks, and exercises that involve sustained muscle contraction.

“Start slowly, with manageable goals,” Wong said. “Even one or two short sessions per week can be a starting point,” she said. “Begin with brief holds, allow adequate rest between sets and sessions, and gradually build up as strength and comfort improve. The goal is to establish a routine one can maintain consistently.”

Paluch recommended starting small and keeping it simple. She says 10 to 20 minutes per session is sufficient.

She suggested four 2-minute holds of a wall sit or handgrip squeeze with 2 minutes of rest between each hold. Those can be done two to three days a week.

“The message is that consistency matters,” she said. “If you’re able to maintain three times a week, that appears to be the best way to maintain the gain, but it’s not an all-or-nothing situation.”

“You don’t have to maintain the initial pace forever to get something out of the training, especially when life gets in the way and adherence or time becomes a challenge,” Paluch added. “Even getting in one day a week is better than nothing.”

For those just getting started with exercise, Shah recommended starting with a short walk before adding isometric exercise.

“A 10-minute walk on most days is a manageable first step,” Shah said. “Gradually increase the length of walks and then add strength training. Consistency matters more than an exhaustive routine that is not sustainable. Remember: Progress and not perfection.”

Fredericson advised starting slowly and building from there.

“For someone completely inactive, even 5 to 10 minutes of movement per day is a meaningful starting point,” he said. “Walking is an excellent option because it requires little to no equipment or preparation. From there, they can incorporate strength training two or three days a week.”

#4944. Why You Shouldn’t Take Anything Personally

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Don’t take anything personally. Easier said than done. This represents the second agreement in the bestselling book The Four Agreements written by Don Miguel Ruiz (1997). In it, he astutely states, "Even when a situation seems so personal, even if others insult you directly, it has nothing to do with you. What they say, what they do, and the opinions they give are according to the agreements they have in their own minds."

Despite this, we find ourselves allowing someone's criticism, disapproval, or lack of responsiveness to determine how we feel about ourselves. Our mood and confidence can instantly shift because of a perceived disapproving tone or sensing that we’re the cause of someone’s irritation or frustration. We may react irrationally, impulsively, and intensely based on someone’s reactions, and our perceptions and interpretations.

Taking things personally is often an automatic psychological response shaped by our insecurities, attachment experiences, learned beliefs, and fundamental desire and need to belong. Research suggests that perceived rejection can activate our sympathetic nervous system, helping explain why interpersonal slights can feel disproportionately painful (Eisenberger et al., 2003).

1. You do not like everyone; therefore, you cannot expect that everyone will like you.

Consider how many people you have encountered whom you did not particularly connect or resonate with. Sometimes we have negative feelings that get evoked solely by someone’s presence or mannerism, even if there isn’t any rational justification for it.

Our personal preferences are influenced by many factors such as another’s personality, values, expectations, etc. When we’re not readily accepted, or outwardly rejected, we assume and interpret it as evidence of our inadequacy or lack of worthiness.

Our brain’s tendency is to seek external approval and acceptance and gauge it as a valid measure of our worth. We’re taught this early on in our development and societal standards reinforce it. We frame it as: “If they think I have value, then I must. If they think I do not, then I must not.”

We do not learn that someone else’s preference or opinion is just that, and that our standards and opinion about ourselves matter most. You can reframe and consider that someone's preference for you doesn't determine your value, and you can be an incredible person, despite not being someone’s preferred person.

2. You cannot read minds. Your triggers, perceptions, judgments, and assumptions are all yours.

We frequently confuse our thoughts, feelings, and interpretations as absolute facts. If someone mistakenly doesn’t acknowledge us, we conclude that they don’t care about us and we’re not important enough to them. We also sometimes fail to own and take accountability for our own triggers and often get defensive, deflect, and blame to avoid facing our own fears and vulnerabilities.

In relationships, mind reading, personalization, catastrophizing, and other cognitive distortions can skew reality and be counterproductive and harmful (Beck, 2020). The inaccuracy is understandable given that our mind constructs explanations based on our past experiences, expectations, and emotional states.

To balance out your thinking, you can ask yourself: "What do I actually know, and what am I assuming? How else can I see this?" This is approaching the circumstance and person with overarching openness, curiosity, and expansiveness.

3. Criticism, aggression, and other harsh responses may reflect someone else's internal struggles.

Individuals can externalize their shame, frustration, insecurity, or unresolved emotional pain through hostility, defensiveness, or criticism. Psychodynamic theory describes projection as a defense mechanism through which individuals attribute aspects of their internal experience to others (Bailey & Pico 2023).

For example, a highly insecure person may be especially critical toward others. To distinguish whether a projection is being enacted, you can consider their delivery, intensity, or emotional reaction.

4. Negative energy is to be observed, not absorbed.

Imagine someone is speaking to you impatiently and with irritability. Within seconds, your chest tightens, your heart rate accelerates, your thoughts spiral, and you feel compelled to relent to protect yourself or actively defend yourself. Their emotional state has comingled and become yours.

Research on emotional contagion suggests that people can influence one another's emotional experiences, sometimes without conscious awareness (Wang, 2024). Self-awareness, self-regulation, and self-compassion don't require emotional absorption.

You can connect with and offer empathy for someone else’s reaction and experiences without absorbing and taking on their negative energy. It requires thoughtfully and mindfully deciphering what is theirs and what is yours, and how you choose to react to it.

5. Someone's negative mood is not automatically about you

You may encounter distance, irritability enacted by a harsh tone or body language. Your immediate thought might be, "What did I do?" We often personalize others’ behavior, as connected to something we said or did, without evidence to support it.

Their mood can be reflective of their disappointment, fatigue, hormones, stress, or concerns that can be entirely unrelated to you. Before jumping to conclusions, approach with curiosity and consider asking, "I wonder if something’s going on for you. Is everything okay?" You can choose to approach with compassion and be attuned to someone's emotions without automatically assuming you're responsible for them.

Rejection can be particularly painful because belonging is a fundamental psychological need. Experiencing rejection can contribute to negative self-confidence, social anxiety, and the ability to sustain healthy trusting friendships and intimate relationships.

When someone rejects us, we often transform a specific experience into a more global conclusion. We make inferences such as “They didn’t choose me" becomes "I'm not good enough." Even though intellectually we know that rejection can reflect differing needs, incompatibility, timing, or circumstances beyond what we can control, we tend to personalize and generalize it.

You can remind yourself that your worth isn't determined by whether someone recognizes, attunes to, appreciates, or chooses you. You can’t avoid rejection, but you can strengthen your self-respect and self-compassion based on how you respond to it.

7. People's reactions provide you with vital information

You can learn a lot from observing others’ reactions. It can give you a glimpse of their expectations, perspective, judgments, and emotional state. Emotional maturity involves vulnerability in noticing and acknowledging each person’s contribution, taking accountability, and repairing and healing when appropriate.

In order to accomplish this, you can identify if there is a difference of opinion, a divergent way of seeing circumstances, or an altered way of behaving based on differing core values. The goal is to evaluate, validate and reach mutual understanding so that future interactions can be healthier and more satisfying.

8. Proactively protect your emotional energy

We can spend hours self-doubting, replaying conversations, anticipating rejection, questioning ourselves, or trying to change someone else's opinion of us. This rumination or perseveration spirals into thoughts about the thoughts, feelings about the feelings, thoughts about the feelings, and feelings about the thoughts. The emotional cost is exhaustion, exasperation, and typically extends beyond the original interaction.

Learning to notice, acknowledge, and interrupt your thoughts allows you to redirect your attention, even though your mind wants desperately to problem-solve. You could more readily focus on what you can directly influence, such as your interpretations, boundaries, responses, and choices.

The greatest emotional freedom comes when you no longer require other people to behave differently to feel secure within yourself. You recognize that you have choices regarding the way you respond.

You can recognize that you can be impacted by someone’s behavior without it defining you or automatically driving your behavior.

It can be challenging to notice parts of yourself that you would rather avoid or rid yourself of. Your activation, which can manifest itself as aggression, distancing, or in other ways, is about you. No one triggers you; you get triggered. Recognizing that can change not only how you experience others, but how you experience yourself.

Bailey, R., & Pico, J. (2023). Defense mechanisms. In StatPearls. Saint Petersburg, FL: StatPearls Publishing. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559106/.

Beck, J. S. (2020). Cognitive behavior therapy: Basics and beyond (3rd ed.). NY: Guilford Press.

Eisenberger, N. I., Lieberman, M. D., & Williams, K. D. (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion. Science, 302(5643), 290–292. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1089134.

Ruiz, D. M. (1997). The four agreements: A practical guide to personal freedom. San Rafael, CA: Amber-Allen Publishing.

Wang, D., Liu, C., & Chen, W. (2024). The role of self-representation in emotional contagion. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 18, Article 1361368. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2024.1361368.

#4942. Tesla energy revenue drops 16% as it refunds customers over tariffs

Tesla’s energy business deployed more batteries in Q3 2026 but brought in less money. Energy generation and storage revenue fell 16% year-over-year to $2.88 billion, even though storage deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh.

Tesla’s shareholder letter blames the drop “partially” on “tariff-related customer refunds.” It doesn’t say how much it refunded, to which customers, or why it was accounted for as reduced revenue.

Here’s how the segment has moved over the last five quarters, based on Tesla’s reported results:

Gross margin bounced back to 33.1% from 20.4% in Q2. But energy gross profit still fell to $954 million from $1.07 billion a year ago, and Tesla listed “lower Energy Generation and Storage gross profit” among the reasons its operating income fell 56%.

Year-to-date, Tesla has deployed 36 GWh, up 11% from 32.5 GWh over the same period of 2025. Energy revenue is down 6% to $8.43 billion. Deployments also came in well short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected for Q3.

This isn’t the first time tariffs have shown up in the energy segment this year. In Q1, Tesla listed “energy one-time benefits related to tariffs” among the drivers of its profit improvement, and energy gross margin hit 39.5%. We questioned those levers at the time, and Tesla never put a dollar figure on the energy portion.

Now money is flowing the other way. Tesla doesn’t explain the refunds, but the most likely reading is that some storage customers paid tariff-related charges that Tesla no longer owed after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February. That’s a guess, though, and the letter leaves investors to make it.

The rest of the energy news in the letter is about getting tariffs out of the supply chain. Megafactory Texas started production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai. Tesla also shipped its first Megapacks built entirely with its own LFP cells from Nevada, where it has 7 GWh of cell capacity in early ramp.

Tesla says storage demand is at its “highest-ever order rate and backlog,” driven by data centers that need power faster than the grid can deliver it. One of those customers is Musk’s own: xAI, now part of SpaceX, bought another $269 million of Megapacks this year, after $430 million of purchases from Tesla in 2025.

Props to Tesla for refunding its customers on the same day that GM is enriching its board with corporate stock buybacks, to the tune of tens of billions.

Energy was supposed to be the steady part of Tesla while the car business stalled. This year it’s been anything but steady: a 39.5% margin in Q1, 20.4% in Q2, 33.1% in Q3, and revenue down even as deployments rise. A lot of that noise is tariffs, and Tesla keeps describing them without quantifying them.

Now, if Tesla is really reimbursing customers for tariffs, it’s a good thing. Many companies getting tariffs refund are pocketing them.So kudos to Tesla.

With that said, the company’s own CEO is responsible for getting elected the clown who installed those illegal tariffs in the first place. So…

#4941. How to End the Year with Purpose

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

As the year winds down, we can find ourselves consumed with the busyness of the holiday season, in the thick of responsibility at work and school, and perhaps wondering if we are just spinning our wheels, glancing back to see where the time has gone.

For productivity expert and author Tiago Forte, the Annual Life Review has become an anchor in his yearly rhythm, providing clarity and direction for a life lived with intention. Grab a journal and a pen, a copy of Forte’s latest book, Life in Perspective: The Art and Power of the Annual Life Review, and make deep self-reflection a gift you give to yourself each year.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Life in Perspective.

Tiago Forte: I've been a content creator, coach, teacher, and author for the last 13 years, focused on helping people become more productive with technology. I decided to write this book because I realized over those years that being productive is not helpful if you don't have a clear sense of where you're going and why.

Modern technology is an incredibly powerful force for getting what you want, but you have to know what you truly want in the first place; otherwise it will just fill your time with distraction and noise. My personal answer to this need for deeper intention has been a practice called the Annual Life Review, which I've followed every year for the last 17 years, and this book is my attempt to make it available to others who feel the same need for clarity and balance in our rapidly changing world.

Q: How has practicing an annual life review impacted your own life? In today’s fast-paced world where many of us are seeking answers online, what is the value of looking within for the validation, direction, and inspiration we need?

Tiago Forte: There are endless sources of external information that we're flooded with every day, all year long: podcasts and videos we consume, the advice of gurus and media personalities, and the digital feeds that seek to dominate our attention on every platform.

The annual life review is about turning down the volume on all those external sources and tuning in to internal ones instead – our inner voice, our intuition, our desires, our dreams. No one else can tell us what is right for us, in our unique life circumstances, or what we need to feel fulfilled and joyful. The only source for those kinds of answers lies inside.

The benefit of finding those answers, which I've experienced again and again, is a sense of deep calm, peace, certainty, and self-confidence that I know where my life and career are headed.

Q: What is the method that you disseminate in this book, and how can readers apply it to their own reflective practice?

Tiago Forte: When I first started conducting annual reviews, there was no method or framework to help me structure them. So my process was haphazard and filled with mistakes and wrong turns. Later on, when I learned that many others also practiced year-end reviews of some kind, there was still no definitive book or method to follow.

Annual Review Course (ARC) is the one I developed over the years, first for myself, and later for the students in my course. It takes you on a learning journey from the past, through the present, and finally to the future, where all the insights and realizations you gleaned from the past and present can inform your future plans.

Q: What role might reading and journaling play in this process of annual life review? How have reading and writing helped you to grow, personally?

Tiago Forte: Reading and journaling play a crucial role in the annual review, alongside many of the most proven practices that many people are already familiar with, like meditation, reflection in nature, visualization, and goal-setting.

What the annual life review does is place all those practices into a framework so they build and compound on each other. This leads to an experience that is more than the sum of its parts – a crescendo of insight and meaning that no single one can produce on its own.

Q: How do you hope Life in Perspective changes readers’ lives for the better?

Tiago Forte: I hope it gives them a counterbalance to the fear, uncertainty, chaos, and mental fragmentation that modern life often creates in our lives. A special time and place that they know they can set aside once per year, or anytime they want to return to themselves, and reliably reach a state of balance and clarity. I hope it introduces them to a wider global community of reviewers, from whom they can learn and be inspired. I hope it becomes a cornerstone of their self-reflection and provides a foundation of intention for years to come.

#4940. Low-Energy Diet Plus Structured Exercise Reverses Early Onset Diabetes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study has found that a combination of a low-energy diet and structured exercise reversed early onset type 2 diabetes in about half of participants.

The research focuses on adults under 45 years old who developed type 2 diabetes early in life. The authors presented their findings at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting, held September 28 to October 2. The study was published on October 1 in The Lancet Regional Health Americas.

Type 2 diabetes is a condition in which the body becomes less able to respond to insulin or has difficulty producing it, leading to elevated blood sugar and low energy. If untreated or not properly managed, it can lead to serious complications such as vision problems, kidney disease, and nerve damage.

These findings offer hope for better treatment options for people with this condition, which the authors say is known for causing faster health decline when compared to later-onset diabetes.

The study was conducted at three centers in England and Canada, linked with the University of Leicester, McGill University, and the University of Alberta.

Researchers selected adults ages 18 to 45 who had early onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin therapy.

A total of 96 participants were randomly divided into two groups: one received usual care, and the other took part in a program combining a low-energy diet with supervised and independent exercise.

The intervention group followed a strict diet of 800-900 calories per day, consisting of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrates, and 20% fat. Participants were encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids daily and were given a fiber-based laxative if needed.

For the first two weeks, the diet was entirely based on meal replacements (Optifast). From week 3 to week 12, the same calorie limit was maintained, with greater food variety, including one meal per day made from regular foods such as protein sources, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

The exercise program involved supervised aerobic and resistance training twice a week and one session of independent exercise per week during the first 12 weeks. After this, from weeks 13 to 24, participants followed a weight-maintenance diet and exercised independently.

Participants stopped all glucose– and blood pressure-lowering medications at the start of the diet unless they had a specific kidney condition called albuminuria (high levels of a protein called albumin in the urine).

The main goal of the study was to determine how many participants achieved remission of their diabetes after 24 weeks. Remission was defined as having a blood sugar level below the diabetes threshold (measured by glycated hemoglobin or HbA1c less than 6.5%) and not taking any diabetes medication for at least 12 weeks.

The study also examined secondary outcomes such as fitness levels, body composition, and heart health.

After 24 weeks, 54% of participants in the diet and exercise group achieved remission, compared with only 4% in the usual care group.

They also lost weight. The diet and exercise group lost an average of 8.4 kilograms (about 18.5 pounds), while the usual care group lost only 1.2 kilograms (about 2.6 pounds).

After adjusting for various factors, the diet-and-exercise group lost about 7.5 kilograms more than the control group.

Additionally, most of this weight loss was fat, with about 6.7 kilograms of fat lost at 24 weeks, which the researchers note is important for improving diabetes.

According to the researchers, the intervention helped preserve muscle mass, which is usually lost during weight loss. This is significant because maintaining muscle is important for long-term health, strength, and metabolism.

They further highlighted that early onset type 2 diabetes can cause serious health problems at a young age.

However, their study shows that a combined approach of diet and exercise can not only help people lose weight and improve health but can also lead to real remission of diabetes, without needing medication.

This is important because early onset type 2 diabetes usually worsens quickly and is harder to manage than diabetes that starts later in life.

The researchers additionally believe their approach could be especially helpful for younger adults who may be planning to have a child, as managing diabetes early is critical for health during and after pregnancy.

The study’s success in a multi-ethnic population also adds to its significance, showing the program could work for diverse groups.

The researchers noted that most people in the diet-and-exercise group experienced side effects early in the program, including constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue. However, these were mostly mild and resolved over time.

Avery Zenker, a registered dietitian and medical writer, explained the importance of this work. “We have evidence that type 2 diabetes doesn’t have to be an inevitably progressive disease,” Zenker told Healthline.

“This can give hope for people with diabetes and help empower them to make impactful lifestyle changes.”

Zenker, who was not involved in the study, added that type 2 diabetes remission is not only possible but more likely in younger people who tend to have a shorter disease duration and a less complicated health history.

Jennifer Pallian, BSc, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess, who wasn’t involved in the research, said that you can put these findings into action right now.

First, you can start a lower-calorie diet. “A reasonable target used in the research was to reduce daily calorie intake by about 500–750 calories, with the goal of losing at least 5% of starting body weight,” she told Healthline.

Zenker noted there are other factors to consider besides the number of calories. “There’s a big difference between a low calorie diet that’s predominantly whole foods compared to one that’s mostly ultra-processed and nutrient-poor,” she said.

“It’s important to consider other recommendations like whole foods, high fiber, and reduced intake of ultra-processed foods.”

Along with making dietary changes, Pallian advised working toward getting at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week. “It also helps to make the plan measurable,” she said. “Set specific nutrition and activity goals, keep track of what and how much you eat, and record your physical activity too.”

Pallian suggested taking note of situations where it’s harder to stay on track so you can spot patterns and make adjustments.

Zenker further noted the importance of starting small and not feeling as if going to the gym is the only way to get exercise.

“Some simple ways one might start to increase daily activity could include adding a short body weight routine in the morning, taking a short walk after a meal, or dancing to music at home,” she said. “Even activities like yard work or cleaning the house can count as physical activity.”

Finally, Pallian advised regular visits with a healthcare professional to monitor blood sugar and blood pressure. These values may improve with weight loss, which may require your doctor to adjust your medication regimen.

#4939. Race Day Roundtable: Speed Stories From Runners Who Raced in On’s Cloudboom Strike 2

Three athletes competing at three different distances share their experiences—and satisfying finishes.

Running “fast” is objectively subjective. What’s fast for you could be slow for another runner and impossible for someone else. Fast can even mean something different for individual runners depending on factors like where they are in a training cycle, if they’re coming back from an injury, or the distance they’re running.

Some runners equate fast with a specific pace-per-mile. Brooklyn-based fashion designer Florence Canonoy, for example, said it’s about seeing her paces drop on her tracking app month after month. “I just run to feel good, and then I look at my watch and it’s like 8:15 [per mile], and I’m like, ‘oh, I’m getting fast,’” she told Runner’s World.

For others, like Mollie Kaplan from Florida, running fast has nothing to do with the time on her watch. “When I’m feeling confident and happy, I feel like that’s when I produce my fastest times—when I’m not putting as much pressure on myself,” she said.

And for Long Islander Chris Chung, fast is a feeling: “When I’m doing interval workouts, that’s what fast feels like to me,” he said. “It’s feeling the wind in your face, in your hair, and just feeling like you’re floating.”

Regardless of how you define it, most runners would agree that their footwear plays a role in just how fast they feel on a particular day, especially race day. Below, Canonoy, Kaplan, and Chung share what they each learned pursuing personal goals in different races—all while wearing the On Cloudboom Strike 2.

Mollie: My first marathon in New York City in 2024 was my fastest. I’ve been wanting to PR since then. But going into Chicago, we had a yellow warning [weather alert] with less than ideal conditions. So I was a little frustrated because after training all summer in the heat, I was really excited to finally do a cooler marathon and was definitely prepared to PR. But I took the pressure off myself the last two weeks before the race. My goal was not to look at my watch. I just wanted to go based on feeling and not to freak myself out.

Chris: This was my first half marathon back from an injury, a stress fracture in my femur. I hadn’t run 13.1 miles in a year, so I was like, ‘I’m just going to let it come to me and see how I feel. Let me just keep it below 1:50.’

Florence: I was taking my last couple races easy, but this was the one where I actually felt really good. So I was like, ‘Okay, let me push for it.’ It was one of my first races where I really took it seriously.

Mollie: I felt pretty strong from the start and I knew that it was going to be a good day for me. I can usually tell from the first mile. And the Cloudboom Strike 2, they kind of give you speed without trying. So they propel you forward a little bit, which is really great.

Chris: I started at the front and got caught up in the wave of people going out quickly. Within the first quarter mile, I was running PR pace at 6:20s and thinking, ‘I’m definitely not holding this because I haven’t trained like this at all.’ So I pulled myself back. I knew there were some hills on the course, so I just kept it effort-based. The Cloudboom Strike 2 maintained its responsiveness even when slowing down a little bit. I really liked how the rocker didn’t feel too aggressive, so it didn’t feel like I had to stay up on my toes the entire race. But at the same time, the roll-off felt really smooth and helped me maintain my cadence fairly well. The upper was comfortable and didn’t feel overly tight. It had some leeway in it and it felt light and breathable.

Florence: At the beginning, I felt really good, so I started running really fast and the Cloudboom Strike 2 had really good return. Mollie: I saw my mom, my sister, and my boyfriend four times throughout the course, and every time I saw them, I had a boost of energy right after. Mile 20 was a turning point for me because I was like, ‘I’m still feeling so good I could speed up at this point,’ which I’ve never felt before in a marathon. And then when I finally looked at my watch at mile 24, I knew I had two miles to go and was super close to PR. That’s when I started picking it up, and it was just such a great feeling.

Chris: There’s a section of the race where you run along the seawall in Vancouver; you’re literally running alongside the ocean. Chris: Other racing shoes can be really firm and aggressive. With this shoe, I feel like that little extra cushion really felt good for where my fitness was. It’s just a very overwhelming feeling as you’re crossing the finish line.

But when I saw my time, I kind of stopped a little bit because I was so excited and so happy. I’ll definitely be wearing Cloudboom Strike 2s again, and I would definitely recommend them to anyone who’s in the market for a new pair of shoes to race in.

I see the finish line right there, so might as well sprint it.’ So that’s what I did. It felt amazing. Everybody was cheering.

Enjoy the journey. Celebrate the little wins, especially in your training cycle.

Florence: This race taught me the importance of relying on feeling and not paying too much attention to my watch. When I look at my watch a lot, I tend to run a bit slower. But when I just focus on myself, whatever’s playing in my earphones, and just feeling good and just doing it, I run faster. We have our goals, but rely on how you feel. I think the number one thing is just enjoy it.

#4938. The Surprising Ways Professional Dancers Overcome Performance Anxiety—and How to Do It Yourself

These science-backed strategies will help you enter a calmer state.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As the audience settles in their seats and the orchestra begins tuning its instruments, Isabella Boylston, 40, is hit with a sense of panic backstage. Even after 20 years of performing in front of audiences, the American Ballet Theatre principal dancer isn’t immune to performance anxiety. “I feel like a tiny furnace of adrenaline is burning inside of me, my brain is working overtime going through steps and scenarios, and I also feel like I get less circulation to my fingers and toes,” she says.

Whether you’re giving a presentation during a meeting, training for a race, or even getting ready for a date, performance anxiety is extremely common. In fact, 63 percent of the general population reports experiencing anxiety around public speaking. “Performance anxiety can show up in any sort of activity that involves being evaluated or where there is some expectation of the level you’re trying to perform at,” says sport and counseling psychologist Natalie Léger, PsyD. Worry and doubt about the outcome are “extremely normal,” she says. But despite how commonplace anxiety is around performance, it can be hard to manage, and even harder to talk about.

Dancers are no strangers to performing under high-stress situations—and oftentimes, performing through less-than-ideal circumstances such as injury, illness, or minimal rehearsal time. That’s especially true right now, as professional ballerinas gear up for one of their busiest seasons of the year, when they perform The Nutcracker for the holidays. That’s why we turned to some of the pros for their best tips to help regain control over nerves. Here’s what they recommend.

“The first step in being able to tackle anxiety is awareness,” says American Ballet Theatre director of repertoire Nancy Raffa, who helps teach the dancers choreography and mental health practices, and holds a degree in psychology. “Anxiety is a built-up fear towards an outcome that hasn’t happened yet, so instead of criticizing yourself that there’s something wrong with you, ask yourself what it is that you’re anxious about to start shifting the thought process.” Then, give yourself grace and know that how you feel is totally valid.

It's in these moments that Léger suggests introducing some short affirmations, reminding yourself that you’re capable and prepared. You can also try instructional self-talk, which helps shift your attention to the present by giving yourself a small assignment to focus on like holding your shoulders back and your head high. “Our emotion center of the brain is really activated within moments like this, and so if you give yourself instruction, that starts to bring oxygen to the part of the brain that’s more related to decision-making and thinking logically,” she says.

You can’t always predict when anxiety will creep in, but having a well-structured routine can give you a sense of security ahead of that anxiety-inducing activity, says Léger. Jasmine Perry, 31, a corps de ballet dancer with Miami City Ballet, focuses on the root of her anxiety, which is the fear that fatigue will interfere with her performance ability. “So, I focus on what makes me feel strong,” she says. Perry prioritizes getting at least seven hours of sleep, eating balanced meals, and making sure that anything she needs for performance day is ready to go the night before.

Sleep CheckInsufficient sleep can make anxiety worse. If you struggle to go to sleep the night(s) before a big talk or performance, develop a routine around sleep. That may look like “staying away from the screens in the hour leading up to sleep, not working out too close to going to sleep, ensuring that your bed is not a place that you’re reading or watching TV,” Léger says.

A growing amount of research points to a correlation between increased social media use and anxiety. So, consider assessing your social media habits to take stock of where your “energy is being pulled or supported,” says Léger. “For example, feeling checked out while doomscrolling when trying to go to sleep is highly unlikely to support optimal performance, while watching a video of a chef make a recipe you’re interested in trying after training can feel like it’s supporting your creative mind, which can be helpful for performance.”

Start by limiting your screen time around your sleep schedule, both before you go to bed at night and when you wake up in the morning, Léger says. Training yourself to resist reaching for your phone as soon as you wake up helps to put you in touch with the present moment, which is the goal ahead of a performance.

During the busiest seasons, Boylston often completely deletes her social media apps. “It helps me feel more focused and there’s less temptation to self-sabotage and compare myself with others,” she says. Can’t commit to a full social media detox? Perry recommends using an app like Opal to limit your use, or you can use the app time limit setting on your phone to set up timers for specific apps.

The night before or in the hours leading up to a stressful task, Perry finds a quiet, calm environment and takes a few minutes to herself. “I try to visualize the thing that I have to do, and in that image in my mind, implement the things I need to consider the next time that I do it,” she shares. “That way, I’ve had time to think, and process, and let it all settle in, so I’m able to allow those things to happen more naturally, versus physically trying to go over everything in the moment in a panic.”

The key to an effective visualization practice is to make the scene you’re envisioning feel as real as possible, says Léger. Ahead of a presentation, that might mean picturing the room you’ll be speaking in, as well as your audience, or even trying on the outfit you plan to wear. “All of these elements, felt through your own eyes, can lead to the brain firing the same neurons it would in a real-life performance, just at a lesser intensity,” she explains. This practice can also boost confidence by making the task feel more familiar.

Breathing from your diaphragm signals a relaxation response in the body and brings the heart rate back down. “If you think about it, if you were actually under threat, you would never slow down to take a deep breath, you would just act quickly,” says Léger. “Through deep breathing, you’re starting to introduce to your nervous system, ‘I’m okay, I’m safe.’”

Try alternate nostril breathing, says Raffa. Inhale through your left nostril as you hold the right side closed, then switch to exhale through the right nostril as you hold the left side closed (and alternate as you repeat the exercise). Or try deep belly breaths: “Put one hand on your chest and one hand on your lower abdomen and do five to 10 deep breaths where you inhale and let the belly expand out, then exhale and let the belly go back in,” she says. If it helps, breathe with a rhythm by doing three counts in, three counts out.

In the hours (and even days) leading up to a stressful task, it can be hard to stop yourself from obsessing over the unknown. That’s when it’s time to change focus and soothe your brain. “I try to do something that’s totally unconnected to what I have to do that evening, whether it’s reading a book or getting outside and looking at nature,” says New York City principal dancer Emma Von Enck, 29. She also has her own playlist of classical music that calms her down—almost like white noise—before she gets ready for a show.

If you feel like your anxiety is more severe or interfering with your day-to-day life, Léger recommends getting in touch with a mental health professional. But leaning on your family, close friends, or a trusted colleague is also key. “When you talk with peers and articulate what your experience might be, a lot of people are going to see how so much of this is just a normal part of the human experience,” she adds. Normalizing performance anxiety and knowing that you’re not alone goes a long way in helping to ease some of the burden.

It may also be comforting to read up on performance anxiety. Boylston recommends The Inner Game of Tennis by W. Timothy Gallwey, which helped her learn how to stay present and not fixate on the outcome of a situation. Or, try Peak Performance by Brad Stulberg and Steve Magness, which examines the practices of top performers across the arts, sports, and business. Von Enck credits it with helping her to hone her own pre-performance routine.

At some point, though, do your best to let go of control. “In anything where you’re trying to excel, you want to control every element, but you have to be flexible in seeing it as a challenge when something isn’t going perfectly,” Von Enck says. And know that it might take some time to master the art of performance anxiety. “Getting to a place where you can quiet the mind is a process,” says Raffa. “It’s just like dancing; to master the technique, you need to repeat, repeat, repeat.”

Meet the experts: Natalie Léger, PsyD, is a sport and counseling psychologist, mental performance consultant, and the owner of The Collective Edge, a sports and counseling psychology private practice in Washington, D.C. Isabella Boylston is a principal dancer with American Ballet Theatre in New York City. Nancy Raffa is the American Ballet Theatre director of repertoire who helps teach the dancers choreography and mental health practices, and holds a degree in psychology. Emma Von Enck is a principal dancer with New York City Ballet. Jasmine Perry is a corps de ballet dancer with Miami City Ballet.

#4937. Early Medical Pain Can Produce a Lasting Memory

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Several years ago, I worked with a woman who experienced trauma on the first day of her life. She was born with Rh incompatibility, a potentially deadly condition that occurs when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby and her immune system attacks the baby's red blood cells. This woman required a blood transfusion in which all of the blood in her body was drained and was replaced with transfused blood. This medical procedure saved her life, but she is experiencing lasting psychological adverse effects from the trauma associated with this procedure.

As a medical student, I remember watching an infant with his arms and legs strapped down to a board in order for the doctor to perform a circumcision. As the baby cried and screamed, the doctor performing the procedure said that the young boy would not remember this procedure years later. No anesthesia was used. Was the doctor correct? I have wondered about this for more than 40 years, and I can tell you that my research into epigenetic memory has taught me that he was probably wrong.

As a father, I took my 2-year-old daughter to a routine pediatrician's appointment for a vaccination. She cried after the shot, but otherwise seemed OK. The doctor told us she would probably have a sore leg the next day, but Tylenol would take care of it. Well, the next day, our daughter wouldn't walk on her sore leg. She cried and cried, despite our efforts to manage her pain with Tylenol and Ibuprofen. Well, years later, our daughter grew up to be one of the most courageous women I know. She climbed every 14,000-foot mountain in Colorado—all 58 of them! But she has had to deal with a lifelong fear of needles. If she has blood drawn, she has to lie down because she is likely to pass out if she sees the needle. For years, I have wondered: Is her fear of needles related to that early vaccination?

For much of the 20th century, physicians believed that newborns didn’t feel pain. Infants commonly underwent surgery with little or no anesthesia. That belief began to change in 1987, when a review published in The New England Journal of Medicine showed that newborns can experience pain, and they can also experience powerful stress responses due to the pain.

This raises the question: Can pain experienced early in life create a memory that persists for years? Research involving epigenetic memory suggests it is possible.

Epigenetics refers to chemical modifications that alter how genes are expressed without changing the DNA sequence. These modifications help cells “remember” what has previously happened.

In 2004, a study in Nature Neuroscience showed that rat pups receiving little maternal care developed epigenetic modifications to a gene in the hippocampus that left them with exaggerated stress responses as adults. Five years later, another study found similar changes in the brains of suicide victims who had been abused as children. These studies suggested that early trauma can be remembered by modifications to our cells’ DNA.

Strong evidence in humans linking medical procedures to epigenetic change comes from studies involving premature infants. These babies may undergo about 10 painful procedures per day, including heel lances, needle sticks, intubation, and suctioning.

An Italian study found that very preterm infants exposed to more skin-breaking procedures showed increased changes to the serotonin transporter gene between birth and discharge. Serotonin helps regulate mood, anxiety, and pain. A follow-up study linked these changes to greater negative emotionality at 3 months of age.

These changes may persist. Researchers in Canada found that at age 7, children born very preterm had greater epigenetic changes than full-term peers. Neonatal pain predicted that epigenetic changes were associated with more behavior problems later in life. This same group later connected greater neonatal procedural pain to physical changes in the brains of these children at the age of 8.

Healthy, full-term infants are not immune to these trauma-induced changes. Newborn circumcision is one of the most common surgical procedures performed in the United States, and historically it was often done without anesthesia.

In a 1995 study, researchers noticed that circumcised boys cried longer and showed more pain behavior during vaccinations at 4 to 6 months of age than uncircumcised boys. Their prospective 1997 study confirmed it. Circumcised infants reacted more strongly to routine vaccination months later than those who had received a topical anesthetic before circumcision.

In other words, a single painful event in the first days of life appeared to change the infant’s pain system, and pain relief partly prevented it. Whether epigenetic changes underlie this effect has not been directly tested, but the pattern of lasting sensitization from early pain fits closely with the previously described findings.

Toddlers and school-age children remember procedures as well. A review found that a minority of children develop posttraumatic stress symptoms after surgery, and 12 to 31 percent of children undergoing cardiac surgery develop posttraumatic stress disorder. Medical fear in childhood can also shape how people approach health care as adults.

The evidence is preliminary that these changes are due to epigenetic memory. But it is encouraging to note that epigenetic changes appear to be potentially reversible, and maternal sensitivity can reduce these effects in full-term infants.

Necessary procedures should not be avoided because of fear. But the evidence argues that we should be taking infant and child pain seriously. Strategies for reducing the effects of painful and other traumatic procedures include providing anesthesia for circumcision and analgesia for other painful procedures, offering skin-to-skin contact, or breastfeeding during needle sticks, avoiding unnecessary procedures, and preparing older children for what to expect.

The infant may not remember the procedure. But their body may.

#4936. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: Is Worrying About Sleep Keeping Us Awake?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

As a busy, sleep-deprived, middle-aged father of two young kids, including an irrepressible 8 year old ball of energy who is, without fail, up and ready to take on the world at 6 o’clock every morning (usually with a steady stream of questions about dinosaurs, the natural world and the origins of the universe in his back pocket), do I really need another set of headlines informing me that not only am I falling short in getting the requisite 40 winks a night but I’m also at risk of 83 diseases into the bargain?

Another day, another headline-grabbing sleep study lands, this time linking a greater amount of sleep – specifically sleep of the rapid eye movement (REM) variety, also known as dream sleep – to a lower risk of dozens of diseases.

The recent study published in PLOS Medicine found that REM sleep is linked to a lower risk of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis (MS). As an added bonus, the study also found that a higher amount of deep sleep was associated with a lower risk of seven health conditions, including depression and type 2 diabetes.

So far, so alarming for a self-confessed “bad sleeper”.

Yet also fairly unsurprising. The accepted science, combined with anecdotal experience, has long told us that the right amount of good quality sleep corresponds directly with improved short and long-term health outcomes, both mental and physical. Evidence suggests that 7-9 hours of sleep per night is typically the sweet spot for a healthier life. Where this particular study differs from those that have come before is that scientists used wrist trackers to gather much more detailed information over a multi-year timeline about participants’ sleep stages, including irregular sleep patterns and variations in sleep duration. The findings were drawn from real-world data from more than 95,000 participants in the UK Biobank database.

Now, as the aforementioned and self-proclaimed VBP (very busy person – if you know, you know), who works long hours across UK and US timezones for the day job whilst serving as a sub-par encyclopedia for the real boss (the aforementioned 8 year old) outside of work, the general demands and pressures of daily life are more than sufficient to make consistently good sleep something that is all too often out of reach.

I know this to be true because the wearable I use reminds me of the fact with cold, hard data on a daily, if not hourly, basis. One of the first things my wife and I do each morning (after fending off existential questions from a third grader) is hawkishly plug into our Oura app to trade sleep scores and discuss what did or didn’t contribute to our invariably bad or, very rarely, good night’s sleep. Deep sleep, REM sleep, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, latency, even sleep debt – a laundry list of data points that we pore over in a futile attempt to make our sleep consistency optimal whilst living a life that doesn’t readily allow for it. Scientists have even given this phenomenon a name – Orthosomnia – where the anxiety of analyzing and perfecting sleep scores actually disrupts rest and intensifies poor sleep, and in the most extreme cases, insomnia.

It turns out we’re not alone. Results of a Gallup poll from 2024 – with the rather on-the-nose headline “Americans sleeping less, more stressed” – showed Americans report averaging 6.5 hours of sleep per night, comfortably below the recommended baseline of 7+ hours. Perhaps more tellingly, in a survey from 2024, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that nearly 70% of Americans report losing sleep due to anxiety.

Which brings me back to my original point. Anxiety-induced stress makes for the perfect bedfellow (pun intended) for a bad night’s sleep. The kind of anxiety-induced stress that can be both caused and amplified by obsessing over wearables data and a steady torrent of sleep-related content that aims to scaremonger rather than inform.

In fairness to the UK Biobank study, it is unequivocally important and unique research steeped in actionable real-world data and peer-reviewed medical science. And yet we live in a world increasingly awash with AI-generated content, sporting sensationalist headlines and powered by algorithms designed with an inherent imbalance to engage rather than empower. In that environment, gold-standard scientific work like this is all too often reduced to the lowest common denominator.

If you’ll indulge a minor tooting of our own horn here, this is precisely the inverse of how the team of wonderfully talented editorial misfits at Healthline Media thinks about and creates health information. We take research-backed science and our embedded clinical rigor and apply it to every aspect of our work. But we never lose sight of the fact that behind every study, there’s someone lying awake in the early hours running the math on their own risk factors, and that what they need in that moment is recognition that we are all at different stages on that journey, and a helping hand along the path to better health.

Life isn’t linear, sleep isn’t linear, and health is certainly not linear. Some nights I’ll get my seven hours. Plenty of others I won’t. And that is ok. Because either way, my alarm clock has a favorite dinosaur and a nonnegotiable 6 a.m. start time, and no peer-reviewed study or scary headline is going to change that. So I’ll take the data and the empathy, leave the anxiety, and see you all again at dawn.

If there’s something keeping you awake at night, or you just want to learn more about the wonderful world of sleep, we have a wealth of science-backed information at our dedicated Sleep Health hub. There you can also find Healthline’s Better Sleep Challenge – a three-week series designed to help you sleep better, feel more rested, and wake up ready to thrive each day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4935. Nail Discoloration Can Be a Mystery. Dermatologists Are Here to Solve It.

Research is uncovering all sorts of new causes—and solutions. Here’s your ultimate guide to both.

NAIL DISCOLORATION AND yellowing isn’t exactly the easiest thing to talk about—and, turns out, pinpointing the cause of it isn’t any easier. With a fairly wide range of visual cues to consider, board-certified dermatologist Dana Stern, MD, explains that ‘discoloration’ is a descriptive catch-all for a nail that has “some kind of color variation from what is considered the normal nail appearance. It’s associated with many different nail issues.”

That makes it particularly difficult to treat. After all, you’ve got to know what’s behind your issue before you can tackle it appropriately. What we can tell you for sure: Whether you’re currently experiencing some unwanted color in your nails or are just curious about future indicators, Dr. Stern says that nail discoloration is an under-discussed topic.

Meet the experts: Dana Stern, MD, is a board-certified dermatologist in New York City. Jennifer Hanway is a board-certified holistic nutritionist.

Well, no longer. Ahead, we break down the specifics on nail discoloration, how to treat and prevent it, and a recently discovered connection between nail discoloration and GLP-1 use.

The spectrum of colors that fall under the umbrella term of nail discoloration are plentiful. “It could be a wide variety of colors including brown, black, white, green, red, purple, and yellow,” says Dr. Stern. Below are common associations with each discoloration shade.

The answer: it depends. It’s actually quite common to have discoloration but it’s hard to nail down (pun intended) the rate of occurrence because it’s a symptom of underlying conditions and not considered a disease within itself.

Nail changes and discoloration frequently occur due to age, normal changes in growth rate, and yellowing are extremely common in older adults. Fungal and bacterial infections, causing greenish nails make up a large percentage of nail discoloration or abnormalities.

Despite overall prevalence and with no single culprit at times, it’s important to understand that nail discoloration can be an indicator of your overall health. “Your nails can reflect aspects of your nutritional status, but they don’t tell you exactly what you’re missing,” explains Jennifer Hanway, a board-certified holistic nutritionist. Though she says that certain changes in nail color have been associated with specific deficiencies, “none is diagnostic on its own,” making it difficult at times to pinpoint the cause and treat it. Dr. Stern mirrors that sentiment, saying that since there is such a wide variety of scenarios for discoloration, it’s important to see a dermatologist.

Hanway says that in some cases, vitamin and mineral deficiencies can cause discoloration. “Vitamin B12 can sometimes cause nail pigmentation; iron-deficiency anemia can cause pale nail beds, and in some cases, a condition known as koilonychia, which is when the nail becomes centrally concave.” Other deficiencies, such as zinc, can affect overall nail growth and appearance.

Though your first step should be to speak to your doctor, it’s also important to take clear photos of your nails for reference and to keep notes. Make reference to which nails are affected, when the changes started, and whether you recently changed your diet, lost weight, started taking supplements, or have begun a new medication. “Speak to your doctor about whether testing for nutritional deficiencies or other factors may be appropriate,” says Hanway.

Depending on your symptoms, medical history, and diet, Hanway says that you may need full bloodwork to test for ferritin, vitamin B12, or other targeted tests.

Dr. Stern says that you can prevent white patches or keratin granulations by using a base coat when you have your nails done or by avoiding prolonged polish wear. If you’re someone who has their nails done regularly, Dr. Stern recommends seeing an experienced nail tech to avoid any chance of encountering discoloration. “Pseudomonas tend to occur in moist spaces on the nail, classically in a lifted acrylic or other type of enhancement, which is why having them done by a professional nail tech can lessen the chances of this occurring.

If you hurt a fingernail where significant blood accumulates under the nail, your dermatologist can evacuate the blood by drilling a small hole in the nail can help to remove the pigment, while also helping to save the nail from falling off.

In terms of nutrition, Hanway says that adequate protein and overall nutrient intake matter. “Nails are made primarily of keratin, a structural protein, so getting enough dietary protein supports overall nail health.” Protein options include eggs, fish, greek yogurt, and nutrient dense foods such as red meat, shellfish, which provide you with iron and zinc. “Supplements should be targeted rather than taken on a hunch, and should ideally be with your healthcare professional’s guidance,” she says.

A multivitamin may help to fill the nutritional gaps when food intake is limited, but it won’t exactly replace a balanced diet or guarantee any nail changes won’t occur. Hanway cautions against taking biotin supplements, even though they are often marketed for stronger nails. “The evidence of benefit in people without a deficiency is limited,” she says. Higher doses of biotin can also interfere with certain laboratory tests, potentially producing misleading results, so be sure to let your healthcare professional know if you are taking it before having bloodwork.

If you’re one of the millions of American women on a GLP-1 medication, know that a recent study suggests there’s a relationship between nail discoloration and these drugs (although it’s not entirely clear on the connection or causality). The 2026 European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology study reported that nail discoloration occurred in 46 percent of GLP-1 users, compared with 17 percent of adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes who had never taken these medications. To add insult to discoloration, nail detachment was also reported by 39 percent of GLP-1 users, compared with 9 percent of the comparison group. Though these are noticeable differences, it’s safe to conclude that there may be an association, but it does not prove that the medication caused these changes.

Dr. Stern points out that the full study was not released to the public, and did not report that about half of the GLP-1 users had nail problems prior to treatment. “This would mean that this study population had a high rate of nail disorders prior to treatment and therefore these nail issues were unrelated to GLP-1 therapy,” she explains. “When the investigators looked at nail changes that began after starting GLP-1, the previously reported associations disappeared entirely. This is a situation where it does not seem that association is equal to causation, but it would be great to have access to the whole study.” Until then, these findings should be considered preliminarily until fully evaluated through peer review.
