#4934. I’m a Run Coach. Here’s Why a Marathon Doesn't Have to Be Your Ultimate Running Goal

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

This time of year, after most fall marathons have ended and our feeds have seen weeks of people crossing finish lines at some of the biggest in the world in Berlin, Chicago, and New York, it’s really hard to avoid feeling like you should run a marathon. I personally have posted countless videos of myself on the internet saying, “I’m never doing this again,” and even I’m tempted to go back on my word every November.

To be fair, I love the marathon. I’ve run 12 of them. I’ve run them very, very fast. And I’ve run them very, very slow. My first one changed my life. It gave me the courage to move to New York City and try to figure out what to do after graduating college. Six months later, I became one of the first running influencers, and I’ve spent the 12 years since building a global community, Badass Lady Gang, to help thousands of women belong and redefine their relationship with strength, power, and what it means to be a runner.

But I also feel complicated feelings about the marathon. As a running coach, I’ve watched the same conversation happen online for over a decade. Somewhere along the way, newer runners are told, or quietly absorb, that the marathon is the ultimate finish line. Which makes sense, right? Our brains love order and hierarchy. When you think about what it means to progress in running, it feels logical: going faster and farther are straightforward ways to show you’ve improved. But that’s not how it works. The marathon isn’t the objective ultimate goal. Or always the most fun one. And, it’s definitely not something that every runner needs to chase.

Every year I watch too many runners struggle through the training not because they lack commitment or drive, but because they’re chasing a goal they didn’t fully want or that their life can’t accommodate right now. And honestly, it’s just a really hard distance to master! A fellow coach and pillar in the community, Peter Bromka, put it best: “The marathon owes you nothing.” I hate that he’s right. You spend months killing yourself (metaphorically) for one huge goal, and then anything can happen on the day. It’s too hot. You get hurt despite doing everything right. You have an off day and watch your goals fly out the window.

We’re in the largest running boom the sport has ever seen, and I think it’s largely because we’re lonely. One in five Americans said they always or often felt lonely or socially isolated in a 2018 study by the Kaiser Family Foundation. And the stakes are real: the U.S. Surgeon General has warned that loneliness carries health risks comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day. Running is one of the few activities that genuinely makes a dent in the loneliness epidemic because pretty much anyone can be a runner (even though it is easier and more accessible for some more than others). You can be fast, slow, old, young—if you’re lacing up your sneakers and moving, you’re a runner. Come marathon season, we also hear stories of the incredible adaptive athletes who cross finish lines with a range of disabilities, too.

Basically, there’s a reason run clubs are hot right now. They give people a way to put their phones down and find a community. The more you show up, the more you see people of all shapes, sizes, ages, fitness levels, and backgrounds crushing distances you thought weren’t possible for someone like you. Before you know it, you’ve signed up for your first half marathon and everyone is asking when you’ll run a marathon. Once you get on that path, it’s hard to stop.

Loneliness isn’t the only thing fueling the boom. We’ve also lost the sense that we control our livelihoods, our schedules, our futures. A marathon is something you choose. It’s one place where you get to call the shots: you set the goal, decide how to train, and define what success looks like, even when curveballs come. It gives you back agency in a world that feels uncontrollable. And in an age when we produce our lives online, it looks great on a feed. It’s badass to train for a marathon, especially when you feel like you have nothing else exciting to share.

So yeah, it’s not just a feeling that everyone’s running a marathon lately. It’s real. Over 1.1 million people applied to London. Chicago saw a 12.2 percent jump in participation from 2023. New York jumped 15.1 percent in the same time period. Races sell out in hours. Getting a bib is almost as hard as finishing 26.2 miles. That’s not an accident.

I work in this industry, and I can tell you a lot of money is spent each year making you feel like you should run a marathon. Last year, New York Road Runners, the nonprofit behind the New York City Marathon, spent $3.8 million on advertising and promotion. And much of that content is built around one image: a runner crossing the finish line, arms overhead, tears in their eyes, sharing how they became the person they always dreamed of being. It works. It makes you believe transformation is possible, and it is. But the marathon industry has weaponized our deep desires to belong, to achieve, to become, and forced us on 26.2-mile slogs across our respective cities.

The result: This overwhelming pressure that everyone needs to get out there and run a marathon—and an exponentially growing number of sign-ups. Never in a million years did I think we’d get to a place where getting into a marathon was almost as hard as running it. But here we are.

I spent a decade being paid by the biggest brands in the world to promote the marathon. I built my business on being vulnerable online and sharing my own transformation through running. So believe me when I say: Not everyone needs to run a marathon.

Before I tell you why you don’t need to run a marathon, let me explain why I first decided to run one. It was never something I envisioned for myself. In my mind, “real” runners ran marathons. (Kooks, if I’m being honest.) Then, I graduated from college with a theater degree and had to start paying off my student loans. My community scattered. And I couldn’t run from the grief I’d suppressed after losing my brother my freshman year of college in a tragic accident.

On Thanksgiving morning in 2012, I started actually running from my problems. Running was brutal and wonderful in a way that left no room for my feelings. It demanded every ounce of attention just to keep putting one foot in front of the other or fall over and pray for a quick end.

I know. Dramatic. But I was the person who made the jokes about only running from the cops. Or a bear. I missed over 70 days of school my senior year ditching PE to avoid running. But desperate times! Running really did feel like a lifeline.

Running gave me structure and something to feel excited about. Becoming a runner gave me something to work toward and confidence when friends and family asked me what my plans were now that I graduated from college. Instead of saying, “I don’t know if I’ll ever work a day in my life doing the thing I love most,” I could say, “I’m training to run a marathon” and feel pride and purpose. They would look at me gobsmacked and impressed. “YOU! Running a marathon? WOAH!” Yeah, I’d think to myself beaming with pride. ME.

I went from couch to marathon in seven months. The running magazines I turned to for advice told me I shouldn’t do what I was doing. “You should run for at least a year,” “Going from couch to marathon shows you don’t respect the distance.” (Those were actual pieces of advice in articles I remember reading when I was training for my first marathon.) But I wasn’t running for a time goal. I felt like I was running for my life. I had to do it.

Training was horrible in the most fulfilling way. This was 2013 and learning to run was very different from what it is now. There were blogs written by former high school or collegiate runners or message boards with the type of runners who told you you didn’t belong if you loved to hate running like I did or ran slow. I didn’t know what I was doing. I made every single mistake you could possibly make training for and then running a marathon.

The biggest? I wasn’t ready. I grabbed a free plan from an app, ramped up my mileage way too fast, and got hurt almost immediately. I ran in shoes a size and a half too small. I didn’t know how to take energy gels (and ran the race with an absurd number of them sandwiched between my two sports bras). I wore nipple guards made for men, terrified my nipples would chafe.

And despite all the mistakes and missteps, running my first marathon saved my life. When I crossed that finish line, I immediately had this sense of if I could do that, there really isn’t anything I can’t figure out how to do.

I’ll never forget watching my first New York City Marathon from the sidelines the year I moved here. We were near the finish, at Columbus Circle, and I knew immediately that I had to run it the next year. I felt so proud to be one of the crazy people who had run a marathon, and so connected to what the runners were going through. There’s nothing like belonging to a group that has shared something so grueling and rewarding. And so, one marathon turned into two and before I knew it, I was a person who ran marathons for fun.

Coaching changed everything. I’ve watched a mom of three in her 40s break two and a half hours in the half marathon after years of believing she’d never be fast enough. I’ve watched countless women who’d been convinced they couldn’t be runners, because of what they endured in PE class, finally feel strong in their bodies while training to run a fast mile. I’ve watched women facing everything from depression to addiction pick up running as a tool and use it to get through the hardest stretch of their lives. And I realized the same joy, transformation, and belonging happen at every distance. There is no hierarchy.

But, it’s more than that. Oftentimes, when we talk about the marathon, we don’t grapple enough with the reasons it may be easier for some. Back in my 20s, the marathon was genuinely easier. Everything is easier in our 20s, even if it doesn’t feel like it at the time. We have bodies that recover much quicker, time that’s actually our own, and energy that feels endless.

I had all of that when I ran my first marathon at 24. I was braver, more naive (a gift!) and had no idea how to sit still in discomfort. I thought movement was the quickest way through, so I threw myself fully into crossing finish lines. (Funny enough, taking a break from marathons taught me what it means to sit in the hurt and actually do the work to heal.) That doesn’t mean that once you hit 30 or 40, your hopes of running a marathon are out the window, but it does mean that as you get older, you should be kinder to yourself if things feel hard or don’t look as shiny as they may seem online.

Which brings me to something we don’t say enough: a lot of the runners we look up to or love following on social media—the ones who are making us feel like we have to be a part of this—are often younger, and what we see is a story they’re producing. When you’re feeling inspired by a creator, or measuring your own training, chip times, or total races against theirs, remember who and what you’re comparing yourself to. This may be someone whose whole job is to run and work out, who has access to endless training and recovery resources, and who isn’t sharing the full story about their highs and lows. Social media literacy matters. Without it, we’re measuring ourselves against a bar that wasn’t built with us in mind.

When runners come to me and are deciding whether to throw their name into a marathon lottery or sign up, here’s what I tell them.

Not pressured. Not because you think it’s the logical next step. Compelled. That pull that screams, “I have to try this,” or “This matters to me more than anything else in the world.”

Marathon training is long and it beats you down, both physically and mentally. As a coach, my job is to help my runners uncover what’s really driving them: their real why. Because your why is the only thing that gets you out the door when you’re tired, sore, and regretting your entire decision. It’s the north star that keeps you lacing up on vacation, when your kid is sick, on a lunch break, before a wedding, on an 89-degree day, when every part of you is done. Without it, you’re just suffering for the sake of suffering.

It really is an unpaid (and expensive) part-time job. It requires hours of running and strength training every week—for months. It requires flexibility in your schedule and will leave you feeling exhausted, hangry, and spread thin for at least 16 to 20 weeks, depending on what your running looked like before you actually started marathon training.

And don’t even get me started on timing. You’re either training in the dead of winter where it’s freezing, dark, and icy when you wake up and get off work or in the summer when you’re juggling summer vacations and brutal heat.

How do you feel about running 15 miles around the Grand Canyon or in Italy? Is that doable? What about the weddings on your travel schedule? What do your weekends look like for the next four to five months? If you sign up for a marathon, they look like a whole bunch of staying in, waking up early to run double-digit miles, and obsessing over the forecast for this weekend’s long run.

Moms. Caretakers. People with busy, unpredictable lives.

I spend half my coaching time talking athletes off the ledge when life throws wrenches in their training and they feel like they’re failing. You end up traveling relentlessly for work and aren’t comfortable running in the dark in a city you don’t know. Or you hate the treadmill and have to do most of your training on one. Your kids get back-to-back-to-back sicknesses and you spend four weeks not able to run because you’re fighting off what they had. A parent ends up in the hospital. A partner gets a diagnosis no one saw coming. Extreme weather, which is becoming a new normal for many of us, makes training complicated or even inaccessible. The list goes on and on. Anything can and will happen during marathon training.

The question isn’t, “How bad do you want it?” That’s not how life works. No excuses? Tell that to a parent who doesn’t have reliable help. It's whether you have the time—real, uninterrupted time—to train the way you envision and the wiggle room to adjust to any and all of the above scenarios.

It’s about so much more than everyone posting their curated, perfect peak weeks.

Influencers know what to say to speak to whatever insecurities or fears you’re feeling. Or what to say to get just enough engagement, or outrage, to get our numbers higher. Running a marathon is big business and most of your favorite influencers are making a lot of money sharing their stories. Sometimes, it honestly feels like exploitation. Which is gross. But I wish more people understood that no one is sharing their actual lives.

The second you start filming yourself, whether you’re aware of it or not, you’re producing. You’re making choices that will resonate or earn engagement. So whether someone is sharing the highlight reel or highlighting everything that’s going wrong, remember that you will never know what’s actually happening.

Keep that in mind if you catch yourself comparing your undertrained or ordinary reality to someone else's seemingly perfect one. And keep it in mind when you relate to someone who says their training has been a train wreck too. I can tell you firsthand that making running interesting and entertaining is very, very hard.

If you struggle with perfectionism, marathon training may feel like you’re riding the struggle bus. But if you can train, show up imperfectly, and work with your perfectionism, look at social media with a grain of salt, and feel proud of what you could do, then you're in for an incredible ride.

I’m here to remind you that not everyone needs to run a marathon to transform their life, find belonging, or to have a great time being a part of something spectacular. I say this as someone who loves, reveres, and had her life changed because of the marathon: It really is just a distance. Real change doesn’t come from running 26.2 miles. It comes from specificity and intention and showing up for yourself, whatever that distance is.

There are so many other goals you can pursue with running that will give you the same result. Have you ever gone all in on a 5K? Or a 10K? Spent 16 weeks working to see how fast you can run a mile? Run the perimeter of your town with a group of friends? Can you train for a half marathon with a friend who has never done it before and be their cheerleader every step of the way? These aren’t less impressive goals. They’re your goals. And they hit just as hard.

Goals are empty without meaning. The marathon is a spectacle that feels like the ultimate test. But taking on the biggest, most difficult challenge in a sport isn't the only place where magic lives. You can find that same feeling in other distances, other challenges, and other ways of pushing yourself. The real work starts when you ask yourself one honest question: "Why does this goal matter to me?"

The marathon is an incredible accomplishment. But there is no hierarchy when it comes to distances and goals. It’s not a ladder. Just because you run a half doesn’t mean that you should run a marathon next. And, you can spend your whole life running and never even think of attempting a marathon.

You get to decide what fills your cup, what challenges you, and how you spend your time and energy. Only you have the power to choose what changes you.

So the next time FOMO creeps in and you feel like you’re missing out if you don’t run a marathon, remember this: You already have everything you need to change your life. You don't need 26.2 miles. You just need to show up for yourself.

Can you run a marathon? Yes. Should you? That’s entirely up to you.

#4933. Is Love for Dogs Always "A Many Splendored Thing?"

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

I know I'm not alone to have experienced people say something like, "I love my dog" and then observe countless different sorts of human-dog relationships that can change in the blink of an eye. I'm not saying that the people who claim they love their dog don't, but in many cases when they tell me that and I see how they mistreat their canine companion I can only say, "I glad they don't love me."

I've always wanted to know more about the variegated nature of human-dog relationships and was pleased to learn of Melina Jacques' recent book What It Really Means To Love Dogs: A Cultural And Ethical Exploration in which she discusses "a set of contradictions that are widely experienced but rarely named. Certain forms of intrusion become routine, while those expected to accommodate them are often left without a clear way to articulate what is happening."

Marc Bekoff: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

Melina Jacques: One of the book’s central arguments is that dogs have become powerful cultural symbols associated with goodness, compassion, love, loyalty, and virtue. A significant portion of the book explores how this symbolic status emerged and why it is so vigorously defended.

The book examines how this symbolic status influences public attitudes toward dogs and can discourage critical discussion of issues that would be readily and openly addressed in other contexts. It explores the consequences of dog ownership for human communities, including attacks, chronic noise, neighbourhood conflict, relationship breakdown, and the diversion of resources and attention away from other priorities. For example, dog attacks in the United States result in reconstructive surgery approximately every 19 minutes, with children disproportionately represented among the victims. Yet discussions of dog attacks are often redirected toward individual circumstances or responsible ownership rather than examining broader questions about the normalization of dog ownership and public safety.

Persistent barking can have consequences far beyond sleep deprivation. Repeated exposure to unwanted, unpredictable noise can activate the body’s physiological stress-response systems, involving stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline. Over time, chronic noise exposure can contribute to sustained psychological distress and adverse cardiovascular and metabolic health effects, effectively making people’s own homes sources of chronic environmental stress.

Conflicts over dogs' behaviour and the prioritization of dogs' needs can also contribute to tension and relationship breakdown. These are not simply isolated inconveniences but consequences of a cultural environment in which the presence and interests of dogs are often treated as beyond question. Municipalities also devote resources to animal shelters and responding to complaints and attacks.

I also examine the ecological impacts of dogs, including predation, disease transmission, disturbance of wildlife, nutrient pollution, and threats to vulnerable species. Research discussed in the book implicates dogs in 11 vertebrate extinctions and identifies nearly 200 species worldwide that are threatened by their impacts.

These impacts extend beyond direct predation. The scent of dog urine, for example, can alter wildlife behaviour, causing wild animals to avoid otherwise suitable and valuable habitat. Dog waste also introduces nutrients into the environment, contributing to nutrient pollution and affecting surrounding ecosystems. Dogs can also introduce infectious diseases and parasites into wildlife populations. Free-ranging dogs, in particular, can act as reservoirs or sources of transmission for pathogens, such as parvovirus or canine distemper, that affect wild carnivores and other susceptible species, sometimes placing additional pressure on already vulnerable populations.

Hybridization presents another ecological concern. Domestic dogs can interbreed with wild canids, including grey wolves and golden jackals, introducing domestic-dog genes into wild populations and potentially compromising their genetic integrity.

Another major theme concerns dogs themselves. Although dogs are widely regarded as among the most loved animals on Earth, I question whether many aspects of modern dog ownership truly serve their interests. For example, breeding dogs to satisfy human preferences for particular physical characteristics can produce animals with serious inherited health problems, raising questions about whether commercial interests and aesthetic preferences are being prioritized over dogs’ physical well-being and quality of life.

Similarly, behaviours that may reflect frustration or unmet needs arising from unsuitable living conditions are increasingly being managed with psychotropic medications. Rather than addressing the underlying circumstances contributing to dogs’ distress, we may simply be medicating behaviours that humans find inconvenient or undesirable.

The book also explores the economic and psychological forces that sustain dog culture, including the role of the pet industry, social incentives, identity, and moral self-image. The pet industry, for example, has developed an enormous commercial ecosystem around dog ownership, encompassing food, accessories, grooming, training, veterinary services, insurance, and other products and services. These commercial interests benefit from the normalization and expansion of dog ownership.

At the psychological level, dog ownership can also become intertwined with personal identity and moral self-image. People may regard owning or adopting a dog as evidence of their compassion and kindness, making criticism of dog-related practices feel like a personal attack rather than an opportunity to examine the consequences of those practices. The book explores how these economic interests and cultural beliefs reinforce one another, helping to sustain a culture that is rarely subjected to critical scrutiny.

At its broadest level, the book asks a simple question: What does it actually mean to love a dog? My conclusion is that caring responsibly for animals requires us to look beyond sentiment and think honestly about the consequences of the relationships we create with animals.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

MJ: Many books explore dogs through the lenses of behaviour, cognition, welfare, history, or companionship. My book differs in that it places these topics within a larger examination of dog culture itself and the consequences that arise from it.

Rather than treating dogs solely as animals, I examine them as cultural symbols and explore how that symbolic status shapes public attitudes, social norms, and policy decisions. The book also investigates an institution that is rarely subjected to critical scrutiny: pet ownership itself.

Drawing on multiple disciplines, it investigates why dogs occupy such a unique place in human society and what consequences follow from that distinction.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about what it really means to love a dog they will give their companion canine a better and more fulfilled life, a win-win for all?

MJ: Yes, although perhaps not in exactly that way. If readers come away with a deeper understanding of dogs and a greater willingness to think critically about their needs, many dogs could benefit. One of the book’s central themes is that genuine concern for dogs requires us to ask whether the lives we create for them are truly compatible with their interests.

At the same time, I hope readers expand their circle of concern beyond individual dogs to include human communities, wildlife, ecosystems, and other animals affected by our relationship with dogs. If the book encourages people to reflect more deeply on those questions, I would consider that a positive outcome.

Dog researcher Dr. Clive Wynne calls Jacques' book "a provocative corrective" and dog expert and bioethicist Dr. Jessica Pierce captures the essence of Jacques' book as follows:

"Dog lovers who care deeply about the well-being of dogs, and about our place in a shared social and ecological world, should read this book. Melina Jacques raises challenging questions that are too often ignored, asking us to examine both the burdens that contemporary dog-keeping can place on other people and communities, the impacts our practices can have on broader ecosystems, and the costs they can impose on dogs themselves. Thoughtful, provocative, and deeply humane, this is a book that deserves to be read with an open mind."

Dr. Jonathan Balcombe, ethologist, and author of What a Fish Knows and Beyond Tooth and Claw writes: "Melina Jacques has written a thought-provoking and highly controversial examination of our relationship with dogs. Her thesis challenges deeply entrenched assumptions about what it means to live with and care for dogs, and she makes a compelling case for reconsidering many of those assumptions. Jacques knows she is swimming against a powerful current, yet she goes forward determined and undaunted. I admire that. This is a worthwhile and provocative contribution to the literature on our relationship with other animals, and one that deserves a wide readership."

#4932. FDA Issues Class II Blood Pressure Medication Recall, Over 13,000 Bottles Affected

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Some people taking a common blood pressure medication may have pills that don’t dissolve the way they should.More than 13,500 bottles of 25 mg chlorthalidone tablets are under a nationwide recall after failing lab tests, according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).Inventia Healthcare Limited voluntarily recalled the tablets on September 3, 2026, according to the FDA’s enforcement report.

The report lists the reason for the recall as “Failed Dissolution Specifications.” That means the tablets failed a test that measures how the medicine is released from the pill, according to the FDA.“Chlorthalidone is a diuretic, or ‘water pill,’ commonly used to treat high blood pressure and reduce excess fluid retention in the body,” Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, told Healthline.This is the second time this year Inventia has recalled its 25 mg chlorthalidone tablets.

The first recall was initiated on June 5 and covered 11,460 bottles. Both were for the same reason: failed dissolution specifications, according to FDA enforcement reports.

Together, the June and September recalls cover 25,027 bottles.

The FDA classified both recalls as Class II.

The two recalls cover three batches of the chlorthalidone tablets, USP, 25 mg, according to the FDA enforcement reports. All three expire in April 2027.

The 25 mg tablets are light yellow, round and flat, with “103” stamped on one side and nothing on the other, according to the drug label.

Recall initiated on September 3, 2026; 13,567 bottles affected.

Recall initiated on June 5, 2026; 11,460 bottles affected.

Patients whose supply is part of the recall “should contact their pharmacy to discuss obtaining a replacement and ask whether they should continue taking the medication in the meantime,” Chen said.

For Class II recalls, people can generally keep taking the medicine unless the recalling company gives other instructions, according to the FDA.

In some cases, stopping a medication may be more harmful than continuing to take the recalled medicine, the agency said.

If you’re concerned that your medication has been recalled, here’s what you can do:

A Class II recall means using the drug may cause temporary health problems, but the chance of serious harm is unlikely, according to the FDA.

“The voluntary recalls cited are classified as Class II, at the retail level,” an FDA Spokesperson told Healthline.

A retail-level recall means the company is “removing the product from retail stores and pharmacy shelves,” Ileana Elder, a branch chief in the FDA’s Office of Compliance, said in an FDA podcast. When a recall doesn’t extend to consumers, stopping a medication unnecessarily can be more harmful, and patients should contact their pharmacy with questions, Elder said.Healthline reached out to the companies for more information about the September recall, but had not heard back by the time of publication. The FDA referred further questions to the companies

However, based on a preliminary assessment of the batches recalled in June, Rising Pharma Holdings, a distributor of one of the recalled lots, stated that “no impact on patient health and safety is anticipated.”

“If a medication does not dissolve at the expected rate, it may not be absorbed by the body as intended,” Chen said. “This can reduce the amount of medication that reaches the bloodstream and potentially decrease its effectiveness.”

In a dissolution test, a lab places a tablet in a controlled liquid medium to determine whether and how quickly the active ingredient is released, according to FDA guidance on dissolution testing.

A failed result means the batch didn’t meet the release standard set for that product, according to FDA guidance on drug quality standards.Manufacturers propose and justify these standards, and regulators approve them as part of drug approval, according to the same guidance.

In the United States, the official standards stay the same from the time a drug is released until it expires, the guidance said.The September FDA enforcement report doesn’t say how the recalled tablets failed. A notice from Rising Pharma Holdings about the June recall provides more details.

Rising found two problems at the 18-month mark of ongoing quality testing of its 25 mg tablets, the company said in a notice posted by the California State Board of Pharmacy:

According to the drug label, chlorthalidone treats:

The label recommends that most people with high blood pressure start with one 25 mg dose per day. That’s the strength involved in both 2026 recalls.

#4931. It’s finally here: Porsche puts wireless charging into production [UPDATE]

Buried in a press release titled, “Even more colours and even greater convenience for the Cayenne Electric” was news that Porsche, for the first time, would be offering electrically wireless inductive charging on its impressively powerful Cayenne Electric SUV.

In a new explainer video released today, Porsche explains how its engineers developed inductive charging for the Cayenne Electric, from the transfer of power across an air gap to detecting foreign objects, guiding the car into position, and testing the system in real-world conditions without microwaving the family pet.

You can click the “play” button, at top, and read the original press release that came out a few weeks ago, below. Enjoy!

With the launch of Porsche Wireless Charging in its latest Cayenne Electric SUV, Porsche is introducing a particularly convenient form of EV charging that makes living with its most powerful car EVER even simpler than before: instead of connecting a cable, Cayenne drivers just have to park their portly P-car over a strategically placed pad, and the charging process then begins automatically.

The Porsche Wireless Charging system pairs a charging pad on the underside of the Cayenne with a ground pad installed in the customer’s parking space. Porsche calls the latter “weatherproof” for outdoor installation, and claims a charging rate of up to 11 kW and with an efficiency of about 90% for easy overnight charging.

Integrated safety mechanisms like motion sensors and cat foreign object detection are baked in to avoid microwaving the cat ensure safe operation, designed to stop the charging process automatically if, “a living creature comes close to the vehicle or the ground pad or if a metallic object lies on the latter and heats up.”

Porsche Wireless Charging is being rolled out globally in stages, and is available to order now in Germany and other European markets.

So this system was designed and engineered by a company in Germany and there is a Society of Automotive Engineers standard for both the pad and the receiver in the car. This could be showing up in other vehicles too.

If you’re not there, feel free to use wireless charging to your advantage and negotiate a crazy deal for yourself on a new Cayenne that’s on the lot today – or just watch the wireless charging explainer video, below, and let us know what you think of Porsche’s new plug-less plug-in in the comments section at the bottom of the page.

#4930. It Just Got Easier to Get Peptides in the US. Here's What Could Come Next.

Spoiler: More access doesn’t necessarily mean more safety.

ON WEDNESDAY, THE U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced a new policy that makes six experimental peptides more readily available. According to a document released by the HHS, the government will not penalize specialized pharmacies for making and supplying these popular substances to patients with a prescription. The peptides: BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500.

This does not mean these particular peptides have been approved for use by the FDA. In fact, none of them have gone through the rigorous human testing required for FDA drug approval. And the new policy is not intended to be permanent. Instead, it allows temporary access as the FDA decides on a longer-term plan for the six peptides. It also includes the caveat that compounders report “serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded,” according to the document.

This topic has been red-hot since July, when the FDA held an advisory committee meeting to consider whether to add these peptides to a list of substances that U.S. compounding pharmacies are allowed to manufacture and supply. These substances are already widely used and obtained on the gray market. If people are going to use them, advocates have argued, it would be safest if those substances came from licensed pharmacies and are used with physician oversight.

Critics, on the other hand—including FDA scientists—are concerned that the government may be opening the floodgates to under-studied and potentially harmful drugs. These substances, they note, have not been fully vetted for safety and effectiveness. And some of these peptides are already being promoted and sold on the basis of scientific claims that experts say are unsupported or questionable.

Here's what could come next, if you're thinking about taking one of these six compounded peptides.

Some parts of the current conversation played out at last month’s PepMed conference in Washington, D.C. A sign pointing guests to the registration table featured a stylized gold peptide overlaid on the white dome of the U.S. Capitol. PepMed’s organizer, the American Academy of Peptide Medicine (AAPM), founded just last year, has already become a major voice in this debate.

In advance of the FDA’s July meeting, AAPM submitted hundreds of pages to a crowded public docket, including information about each of the seven peptides then under review. Several of its advisory board members spoke during the meeting’s public comment sessions. And the group appears to have the ear of the administration. PepMed speakers included the assistant secretary for health, Admiral Brian Christine, and a host of prominent MAHA figures.

The September event opened with an on-the-record media hour, featuring a dozen speakers, including physicians and owners and CEOs of compounding pharmacies and telehealth companies. A recurring theme was the danger of the gray market, where peptide quality can be difficult or impossible to verify and consumers often make treatment decisions without medical oversight—“this is not a victory for patient safety,” said Ricardo Rossello, PhD, a U.S. congressional delegate for Puerto Rico and AAPM advisory board member who co-founded Beijing Prosperous Biopharm, a medical research company.

Many of the speakers also lamented the failure of the U.S. health care system to fully meet the needs of patients, and some of the day’s speakers, including Alex Tatem, MD, an Indiana-based urologist and men’s health specialist with a large YouTube following, presented experimental peptides as part of the solution. “Our established medical system is very much a sick care model,” said Tatem, who serves on the AAPM’s medical advisory board. It’s important to help patients in a health crisis, he told me in an interview. But people want to be proactive about disease prevention. In his view, the peptides under FDA’s consideration can play a role by expanding “the toolkit that’s available to providers.”

At the FDA’s July advisory committee meeting, the agency’s scientists advised against allowing broad access to these peptides, in part because they have not been fully vetted for safety and effectiveness in the kind of long-term, rigorously designed human studies typically required for drug approval.Even at the conference, some doctors acknowledged the evidence gaps. Abud Bakri, MD, works in California as a physician who specializes in caring for hospitalized patients. He also runs a separate medical practice focused on preventive and longevity medicine, and he serves on the Enhanced Games Independent Medical Commission. His interest in peptides has been long-standing enough to predate his medical career.

Bakri, now 33, has been a powerlifter since he was 17. He explained that he has a genetic condition that may increase his risk for ligament injuries. He first used BPC-157 almost a decade ago, and believes the peptide helped him recover faster, though he acknowledges that this is hard to prove definitively, given the absence of well-designed human studies.

If just a fraction of the rat and Petri dish research holds up in humans, BPC-157 could be an incredibly helpful drug in the ICU, he told me at the conference, during an interview at an outdoor dining area. But ideally, he says, its effectiveness should be proven before it’s used in this setting and potential side effects should be better understood. “If I’m going to have an honest conversation with a patient,” he said, “I need to be able to fully elucidate the risk, which I can’t for some of these compounds.”

After the conference, I spoke by Zoom with Thomas Kremen, MD, a physician at UCLA Health who works for several athletic teams, including the Los Angeles Chargers and Lakers. Kremen and his colleagues recently reviewed the evidence behind six popular experimental peptides. He and his co-authors seemed unimpressed. “It’s probably not a strong stance to be recommending these things,” he told me.

Would it be accurate for physicians to tell their patients that a peptide like BPC-157 heals tissue?

“Maybe if they're talking about a rat in some study,” he said. “But I think if you're making a claim, you better be able to cite the literature that supports that.”

Right now, not only is there a dearth of high-quality clinical evidence that peptides work and are safe, unsupported claims are being made about these compounds.

For instance, among the documents that AAPM submitted to the FDA’s public docket was a white paper claiming that two experimental peptides—epitalon and BPC-157—are endogenous, indicating they are naturally produced by the body. Similar descriptions can be found on websites for telehealth companies and online peptide vendors suggesting their products are synthetic versions of naturally derived peptides.

Epitalon is a lab-made peptide based on an extract that researchers in the Soviet Union obtained from cattle brains. Terry Roberts, PhD, a researcher who studies epitalon at Brunel University of London, said it’s unclear whether humans produce this peptide. As far as he’s aware, no studies have explicitly described its presence in humans.

And BPC-157? The peptide was discovered in gastric juice, said Vince Luca, PhD, a researcher at the Moffitt Cancer Center in Florida. Yet 35 years after its discovery, nobody has found a gene that encodes for it—it could have come from a microbe or from food. It’s not impossible that the body produces BPC-157, said Luca, but he thinks it’s unlikely. He also says that health care professionals “should know enough not to tell [people] that it's an endogenous peptide” when it is very unlikely to be one. And regardless, he continued, “there are plenty of endogenous peptides that, injected at high concentrations, would have a really negative effect on the body.” In other words, being endogenous alone doesn’t mean it’s safe.

(The American Academy of Peptide Medicine’s press team did not respond to queries asking how the group determined that BPC-157 and epitalon are endogenous.)

“My prediction is that those who are already using the gray market will continue to do so,” said Ryan Beattie, director of business development at Adaptog Research & Life Sciences, a UK-based company that sells experimental peptides. “So I think in the initial term, people will use compounding pharmacies in the US. What I then predict will happen is people will then get used to it, get more aware of it—and then switch to the gray market because of the cost.”

He may be right. For this story, we spoke with two peptide users who had been living with chronic pain, and after trying physical therapy as well as other treatment approaches, turned to the Wolverine stack, a combination of BPC-157 and TB-500. Both said they felt the peptides helped them—and neither was sure they’d switch to compounded versions, which are more expensive than the gray market and aren’t covered by insurance. One of them, Charles A., asked, “What are the hoops and what are the costs going to be?”

A third person, who asked to be referred to as James—the name he uses in online communities—tried an oral version of BPC-157 four years ago and said he hasn’t been the same since then. Shortly after taking the experimental compound, he felt anxiety followed by sensory and emotional numbness that still hasn’t gone away. He also developed an autoimmune condition. Online, he found others with some similar experiences. When he looked carefully at the published research, he concluded that it didn’t match the online hype. “I felt very foolish afterwards.”

Some scientists are continuing to investigate these peptides. At Moffitt, Luca is currently studying BPC-157 and he’s keeping an open mind.

Over the next few months, he and his colleagues plan to run a variety of very basic experiments in which they add the peptide to human cells and see how those cells respond. The results could provide additional insight into what, precisely, this molecule is doing in the body—and they may help explain why users have reported everything from striking benefits to lasting harm.

Perhaps one day, BPC-157 will prove to be an effective drug, said Luca. But for now, his advice is to wait on using it and other experimental peptides: “I just worry that people are a little too cavalier in how these are handled.”

Sara Talpos is a Michigan-based journalist covering biomedical research and public health. She’s written for publications including STAT, Science, and Undark, where she’s a contributing editor.

#4928. Tesla pushes unsupervised FSD to Q2 2027, and only inside Robotaxi zones

Tesla now says unsupervised “Full Self-Driving” in customer-owned cars will arrive in Q2 2027. It’s the latest date on a promise Elon Musk has been making to FSD buyers for the better part of a decade.

But there’s a catch. On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call today, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy described it as owners adding their own vehicles to Tesla’s managed Robotaxi fleet, not owners getting a car that drives them anywhere they want to go.

“When can we anticipate FSD unsupervised in customer cars?” was one of the top retail shareholder questions submitted for the call, backed by about 1.1 million shares, as we noted in our Tesla Q3 2026 earnings preview.

Elluswamy’s answer was Q2 2027. And the way he framed it, step one isn’t a software update that lets you climb into the back of your Model Y and sleep while it drives you to your destination – what Elon Musk sold to customers since 2016. It’s Tesla letting owners put their cars into its own Robotaxi network, where Tesla runs the operation.

So an owner’s car would only drive itself unsupervised where Tesla’s Robotaxi already operates.

Tesla’s Robotaxi service runs in six US metros right now, and most of the service areas cover small slices of those cities. When Tesla mapped its Miami Robotaxi zone, it covered mostly West Miami and a strip toward Doral and Sweetwater. Orlando and Tampa launched in July with similarly small geofences.

Inside those zones, the service sticks to low-speed routes, largely stays off highways, and avoids the harder parts of town. In the Bay Area, it isn’t unsupervised at all. California rules still require a safety driver in every car because Tesla doesn’t want to release data to the California DMV, which it has to do beyond a level 2 autonomous system.

The fleet is small too. Tesla says Robotaxi reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of Q3, a month after Cybercab joined the Austin fleet, according to Tesla’s Q3 2026 results. Third-party tracking this spring showed the number of fully driverless Teslas on the road in the dozens, nowhere near the hundreds of thousands Musk had talked about. Waymo, meanwhile, was already in both Orlando and Tampa before Tesla showed up, and it has over 3 million miles.

That’s not what Tesla sold. For years, the pitch to FSD buyers was a car that would eventually drive itself anywhere through a software update.

Musk told investors in July 2025 that unsupervised FSD would be available “for unsupervised personal use by the end of this year in certain geographies.” A year earlier, he said he’d be “surprised” if Tesla didn’t have unsupervised self-driving the following year. And HW3 owners who bought FSD have already been told their computers can’t run unsupervised FSD at all, with no clear upgrade plan.

Now the target is Q2 2027, and the product is narrower: your car joins Tesla’s fleet, in Tesla’s zones, on Tesla’s terms.

I'll take a Tesla FSD promise seriously when they start making progress in the California DMV process towards being approved for autonomous driving. Right now, they along with 23 other companies have the DMV permit to do testing with a driver. 5 companies, but not including Tesla, have the permit to do driverless testing. 3 companies have the permit for driverless deployment. Waymo for all speeds and conditions. Mercedes for daytime highways with speed under 40 mph (ie can handle being autonomous in a traffic jam). Nuro with speeds under 35 mph.

It took Waymo 10 months to progress from driverless testing to driverless deployment. Thus, it would be extremely optimistic to hope that Tesla will have the California DMV permit for driverless deployment by Q2 2027. I note that providing a California taxi service is important enough for Tesla for them to be operating that service with human drivers.

If you can believe it. Believing a Tesla FSD timeline is a fool’s errand at this point, and I don’t see any reason to treat Q2 2027 differently from every other date Tesla has given since 2019.

But even if it happens on time, look at what’s actually being promised. This moves the goalpost from “your car drives you anywhere while you sleep” to “your car can work as a Robotaxi inside a small geofence that Tesla controls.” No highway road trips. No driving you home from the airport across town. No unsupervised commute unless you happen to live and work inside one of the zones.

It’s the goalpost moving of all goalpost moving.If one thing was clear from the call, Tesla has no idea when it will actually happen. They are just guessing. Ashok again reiterated that safety is the bottleneck, which is why Tesla limits itself to low-speed roads and harder environments. He guesses that those safety issues will be fixed by next year, but he doesn’t know.

#4926. Cutting Back on Ultra-Processed Foods May Help Ease Depression Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emerging research has linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) with an increased risk of depression. Now, a small study published September 23 in JAMA Psychiatrysuggests that reducing UPF intake may help ease depression symptoms.

There is no universally accepted definition of UPFs. However, a widely used classification system known as NOVA defines them as industrial formulations made primarily from substances extracted or derived from foods, often with additives not typically used in home cooking. Examples include soft drinks, packaged snacks, candy, sausages, hot dogs, and pastries.

Previous research has linked UPFs to an increased risk of depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and other mental health conditions. In the new study, participants reduced their UPF intake by more than 85% and had significantly lower depression scores across three standard measures while following the low-UPF diet.

This small study included 20 participants who:

The participants also had to agree not to change medications, therapy, exercise, or sleep during the study.

Of the 20 participants enrolled in the study, 19 completed it. The average age was 44. Participants followed both their usual diet and a low-UPF diet during separate phases of the study, with the order randomly assigned.

Participants generally found the low-UPF diet acceptable and manageable. They also had lower depression and anxiety scores during the low-UPF diet phase compared with their usual diet.

On one commonly used depression measure, the PHQ-9, average scores declined from 8.68 during the usual diet phase to 5.53 during the low-UPF phase.

The study had several limitations, including its small sample size, reliance on self-reported dietary data, and uncertainty about which aspects of reducing UPFs may have contributed to the changes in symptoms.

The researchers also said that larger studies are needed to determine whether reducing UPF intake can improve depression symptoms.

Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study, agreed, noting that more research is needed to understand whether reducing UPFs directly improves depression symptoms or whether other aspects of the overall diet may be contributing to the observed benefit.

Dara Houp, PsyD, a licensed clinical psychologist with Pathways Psychological Services in NYC, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it’s important to distinguish ultra-processed foods from processed foods more broadly.

Routhenstein agreed that the distinction is important. “Processing is not inherently negative. Many nutritious foods are processed in some way.”

“I would not encourage people to simply label a food as ‘processed’ or ‘unprocessed’ and make decisions based on that label alone. I prefer to look at the overall dietary pattern, the nutritional value of the food, and what role that food plays in the diet. A packaged food can still provide meaningful nutrients and be part of an overall nutritious eating pattern,” she said.

There are various proposed mechanisms for how UPFs may affect mood.

For example, UPFs are often low in fiber, vitamins, and minerals, which can play important roles in brain health.

Houp noted that some ingredients found in UPFs, including artificial sweeteners such as aspartame, may affect the gut microbiome.

“Our gut is a primary location for producing neurotransmitters, responsible for manufacturing the vast majority – upward of 90% – of our body’s serotonin. When the gut microbiome is disrupted, it directly interferes with healthy neurotransmitter production,” she said.

Houp added that diets high in UPFs may be lower in antioxidant-rich foods, such as fruits and vegetables, which could contribute to oxidative stress. Research suggests that people with depression may have lower antioxidant levels and higher markers of oxidative damage.

Routhenstein also noted that researchers are investigating how UPF consumption may influence inflammation, metabolic health, and the gut-brain axis, all of which may have implications for mood.

Reducing your UPF intake can start with small, sustainable changes.

Routhenstein suggested starting by looking at the foods you eat most often rather than trying to overhaul your kitchen.

“Identify one or two foods that are frequent sources of UPFs and consider what you could realistically replace them with. For example, you might swap a daily sugary drink for water or sparkling water, or choose fruit, nuts, yogurt, or another minimally processed option in place of a packaged snack,” she said.

Other ways you can help reduce UPFs include:

Routhenstein added that you don’t have to eliminate convenience from your diet. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, canned fish, oats, plain yogurt, tofu, and other minimally processed foods can make healthy eating much more practical.

“The goal is not to eat a perfectly unprocessed diet. It is to gradually shift the overall pattern toward more nutrient-dense foods that provide fiber, protein, healthy fats, vitamins, and minerals,” she said.

#4925. Hard Times and the Practice of Staying Engaged

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Dedicated to Wendell Berry and The Berry Center, whose work continues to inspire care for the land, for community, and for the life we share.

In Standing by Words, Wendell Berry writes, “The impeded stream is the one that sings” (Berry, 1983). I keep returning to this line. Picture a stream running over a smooth, open bed. The water moves easily and makes almost no sound. Put stones in its path, and the water has to find its way around and over them, and that’s when we hear it. The resistance gives the stream its voice.

Berry’s image speaks to the way we live. He sees uncertainty, resistance, and inspiration as essential companions on any meaningful journey. Inspiration opens up possibility. When life becomes hard, our first instinct is usually to want the difficulty gone. We want certainty back. We want the stones out of the stream. Berry offers another way to see it: The moments of not knowing are where wisdom, creativity, and purpose take shape. The challenge is to stay engaged with what baffles and resists us long enough for it to shape us.

Staying engaged needs something to guide us, something to keep us practising, and something to renew us when we’re tired. In therapy, I talk about these as the three M’s of intentional living: a Motto, a Mantra, and a Muse. Each one answers one of Berry’s companions. A motto gives us direction when we’re uncertain. A mantra keeps us steady as we work through resistance. A muse inspires us and reminds us what’s possible.

The three M’s are personal, and the words people choose depend on what they’re facing. The following sections show how a motto, a mantra, and a muse take shape amid self-doubt, a strained relationship, and grief. These are struggles people commonly bring to therapy.

When we can’t see what lies ahead, we lose our bearings. A motto is a statement of principle that restores them, giving us a direction to walk in even as uncertainty remains.

For someone living with self-doubt, “My voice is worth hearing” affirms self-worth. When boundaries are strained, “I protect my peace” honours the right to inner calm. In grief, “I carry love forward” acknowledges the loss while embracing the love that remains. A good motto is short enough to remember and strong enough to stand up to doubt.

Where the motto gives direction, the mantra sustains the practice. We meet resistance in the present moment, in the conversation we’re dreading or the morning that feels too heavy to begin. A mantra is the phrase we bring into those moments and repeat when we most need steadiness.

“I trust my own voice today” helps someone with self-doubt speak up. “I honour my limits with kindness” affirms self-respect without hostility. “I carry their love in my heart” becomes a daily act of remembrance. Each repetition strengthens conviction, and over time the mantra becomes part of the inner language that steadies us. This is the impeded stream finding its way, one stone at a time.

A muse is our source of inspiration. It’s often found in a memory, a ritual, or a symbol: a teacher who encouraged us, a practice that restores balance, a place that brings rest.

In self-doubt, a muse might be the memory of being supported. When strengthening boundaries, it might be a place, real or remembered, that offers safety. In grief, a family ritual, a piece of music or a well-worn object can become a bridge between what was and what continues.

The words that steady us rarely emerge fully formed but slowly surface through reflection, often by noticing what we already value and naming it. The questions below are some I’ve found helpful in therapy for drawing out a motto, a mantra, and a muse. Each answer is personal, reflecting something of our experience and what rings true for us.

A statement of principle that guides and steadies us through uncertainty.

The motto questions open a reflective space about values, principles, and direction:

Mantra: Strengthening the practice of living

A phrase repeated in the present moment to cultivate steadiness and self-trust.

The mantra questions help people experiment with language that soothes, empowers, and motivates:

Muse: Reconnecting with inspiration and possibility

A source of renewal that stirs imagination and reminds us of what gives life meaning.

The muse questions explore the deeper wells of memory, imagination, and inspiration that sustain growth:

People I see in therapy often describe this work as grounding, clarifying, and connecting, because it links inner reflection with outward action.

We all go through seasons when our confidence dips, when relationships test us, or when we feel the weight of grief. Berry’s insight is that these are the seasons when our lives take their deepest form. A motto, a mantra, and a muse help us move through them with intention. They keep us engaged with what unsettles and resists us, so we can learn what those difficulties have to teach. Like Berry’s stream, we find our voice by meeting what stands in our way.

Berry, W. (1983). Standing by Words. North Point Press.

Tesla said today it will sell Cybercab to consumers by the end of this year, raising questions of what end users would do with a vehicle with no steering wheel and no self-driving software.

During Tesla’s Q3 conference call today, a question was asked about when Tesla will deliver unsupervised FSD to customer cars.

That question was answered slightly differently than usual. Instead of the standard “end of next year” that we’ve heard every year for a decade, Tesla changed the answer to: “middle of next year.” In other words, Q2 2027.

So, alright, that’s when Tesla says its cars will be able to drive themselves with nobody paying any attention. Great. It would be quite a big step from their current level 2 system to a level 4 or 5 system, which are the only categories that could be deemed as “unsupervised” as level 3 still includes a driver in the driver’s seat who needs to be ready to take control at any time.

But then, in the same question, Tesla made another prediction. VP of Engineering Lars Moravy said that Cybercab will be in customer hands by the end of this year – which means within the next two months. Here’s the answer:

In short we’re trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year in 2026, obviously we’re producing a lot in Texas but all of those are going to our own internal Robotaxi fleet, and as Tesla grows we’ll mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers and Cybercab will be the first. And so as we start small this year and we learn about all the things Ashok mentioned about delivery and ownership and fleet management and autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we’ll continue to scale that.

Musk then added on to the answer, highlighting that Cybercabs would mostly be Tesla-owned transport-as-a-service vehicles, which somewhat contradicts Tesla’s call for Cybercab fleet buyers which it put out the same day as its Cybercab launch event.

But did you notice anything? Moravy said that Cybercabs would be in customer hands – that is, not Tesla’s hands – by the end of 2026. And Ashok, in his answer which we reported on here, said unsupervised FSD would be in customer hands in Q2 2027 (if that’s to be believed).

This would leave a half-year where these Cybercabs, which are intended to come with no steering wheel or pedals, are completely inoperable. You couldn’t even push them into your driveway, because you’d have no steering wheel to help you do so.

Unless, of course, these Cybercabs get delivered with steering wheels – which most of the ones in the wild have these days anyway. And if they did, then why not just call it a Model 2 and sell it to people for $25k, like you should have done in the first place?

Either that, or the vehicles will be limited to the same areas that Cybercabs are already limited to. Despite Musk predicting that Robotaxis would cover half the US population by the end of last year, it is currently available only in small portions of 6 cities in 2 states.

The entire fleet of autonomous cabs in Austin, the most built out market by far, is estimated at 300 cars, including Model Y units. So where are the thousands of Cybercabs that are pouring off the line? And isn't that pretty poor planning, to have an assembly line dedicated to production that runs in the tens per week demand?

If Tesla gives customers access to the same software it uses (which it has promised for a long time), then presumably they could operate Cybercabs in the same areas. But Tesla said, in the same call, that it won’t give people access to that software, even in the areas where it’s already operating, until Q2 2027.

So, per Tesla’s statements today, it plans six months of selling a car that is usable by precisely nobody, to do precisely nothing.

Either that, or all the timelines are made up. But Tesla would never do that, would they?

#4923. ‘I Got Rhabdomyolysis From a Kettlebell Workout Even Though I’m an Experienced Exerciser’

There’s a difference between pushing yourself and overdoing it.

I could tell something was off one morning during the summer of 2020 when I went to the bathroom and saw what appeared to be grainy bourbon swirling around in my toilet bowl. (Sorry if I’ve forever ruined your fave whiskey for ya!) Startling, oh yes. Thinking back, I had been nursing achy hamstrings following a kettlebell workout a few days prior. And since my pee certainly hinted that something wasn’t working right internally, I suspected the two were connected.

Until that workout, I hadn’t picked up a kettlebell in months. It had been my primary form of exercise for six years—I even got certified to teach it—but I was starting to burn out, so I swapped in a less intense Pilates practice. Now I was ready to ease back into the swing of things (key word: ease).

I began with a 30-pounder and did one-minute intervals of swings, squats, and presses, eventually moving up to 45 pounds. I’d worked with that weight before—but again, it had been awhile. I left the gym hobbling (oh, my hammies!) but otherwise fine.

The soreness lingered but wasn’t bad enough for me to cancel Saturday Pilates. A stretch might be good, I told myself. But I woke up the next day to my unfortunate bathroom sitch.

I was vaguely aware of the condition known as rhabdomyolysis, in which injured muscle tissue breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream, potentially damaging the kidneys. But I figured there was no way my 25-minute kettlebell sesh could have been intense enough to cause that level of harm. Yet I found myself Googling “that thing when you work out too hard” (who can remember the word rhabdomyolysis?). One of the first symptoms I came across: dark, brownish-colored urine.

After some initial testing at urgent care, I was referred to the ER, where doctors measured my creatine kinase (CK)—an enzyme found in your muscles that, when elevated, may indicate damage. I learned just how injured I was: A healthy adult’s CK level falls between 22 and 198 U/L (units per liter); mine was a whopping 90,000 U/L.

When I was told I would have to be admitted for at least a day, it was a strange pill to swallow. I wasn’t suffering from any other symptoms, like dehydration, nausea, or faintness. Yet I spent the night in the hospital spooning an IV bag to flush my kidneys fast enough to avoid damage. (Renal failure can be one of the more serious side effects of rhabdo.)

I was told to take six weeks off from exercising. When I did venture to my first hardcore class (boxing), I sneaked a peek at my pee for days afterward, just to make sure everything seemed A-OK. Fast-forward a year later, and I’m healthy as ever.

I get it: You feel a sense of pride when you fight through the so-sore feels. But you’ll come back stronger if you take a day off when…

Sweat on Sunday and still achy by Wed? Cue to cool it.

If you’ve played tennis forever but feel zapped during a longer or hotter practice, it might be your bod asking for a break.

Let’s say you have been training for a race and can’t run as fast as you did last week, but your regimen is the same. Build more recovery time into your plan.

FYI, exercise-induced rhabdo isn’t terribly common—about 12,000 cases are diagnosed annually in the U.S., according to a study in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. But Todd Cutler, MD, an internist at NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center, says nurses in his ER noticed an uptick in rhabdo cases that coincided with the recent rise in popularity of high-intensity cycling classes.

It’s not typically an exercise newbie who gets injured, either; it’s often a healthy, relatively fit person who pushes themselves to extremes the first time they try a new workout (or when they return after an absence). It makes sense, given my experience. “If you weren’t fit in the first place, you wouldn’t have been able to do the exercise,” says Dr. Cutler. In other words, my underlying health allowed me to reach the point of overexertion.

There’s a fine line between pushing yourself (which nets you gains) and going overboard (which leads to injury). The tipping point is different for everyone, which is why it’s key to be in tune with your body. (Hamstrings feel as if they’re under a blowtorch? Put down the weight!) If you’re trying something new or going back to working out after a hiatus, ease into it, advises Lauren Borowski, MD, a sports medicine specialist at NYU Langone Center for Women’s Sports Health.

My new mantra: Match workouts to current ability (no matter your past experience). And…rest days are clutch. Take them. The kettlebell will still be there tomorrow.

#4922. Even As a Wicker Man, Alexander Skarsgård’s Got Game. This Scent Will Give You Some Too.

The actor is the face of Valentino’s newest fragrance, Vendetta.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF ANYONE CAN MAKE RATTAN hot, it’s Alexander Skarsgård. The actor’s latest film project, about a craftsman who creates a wicker husband (Skarsgård) for a lonely woman (played by Olivia Colman), has been an unlikely hit since its release in theaters last week. But basket weave isn’t the only material Skarsgård’s rocking—he’s been killing it on the red carpet lately, too.

There was the gold Saint Laurent suit earlier this month at the BFI London Film Festival, the sick Chopova Lowena skirt to promote Wicker at the Los Angeles premiere last week, and the head-to-toe Valentino outfit he wore at the house’s show during Paris Fashion Week. It seems there’s nothing Alexander Skarsgård can’t infuse with his unique brand of Swedish swag.

Shop the new Valentino Vendetta fragrance.

So, it should come as no surprise when Valentino tapped the 50-year-old star as one of the faces of its brand-new fragrance pillar, Vendetta (alongside Dakota Johnson for the women’s version). Unlike Valentino’s most famous scent family, Born in Roma, which features a spiked pyramid design, Vendetta’s bottle pays homage to the brand’s classic V motif, with a rich, sensual juice created by master perfumer Marie Salamagne.

You’ll get the sensuality from the campaign imagery, photographed by iconic duo Inez & Vinoodh, and the epic accompanying video, directed by French filmmaker Romain Gavras, but what about the fragrance itself?

“It has a boldness and a kind of self-assertive quality to it,” Skarsgård tells me when I ask him to describe the scent. “It’s not quite as heavy as I thought it would be. That first note of ginger has a lightness to it and then it evolves into those richer, deeper notes that last longer.”

For his part, Skarsgård says he’s a signature scent kind of guy—a far cry from the scentmaxxing approach of today’s TikTokers, who douse themselves in enough cologne to create their own noxious atmosphere.

“I’m a proponent of finding your fragrance and sticking with it,” he says. “You become associated with that smell, it becomes part of who you are.”

That’s not to say he hasn’t had his share of missteps. Born in Stockholm, Skarsgård began acting at a young age—his first film role came when he was just seven—but quit as a teenager to join the Swedish navy and, eventually, attend university. Along the way, he learned some valuable fragrance lessons, as most guys do. “I think when I was a teenager, I overdid it a lot,” he says. “You want to marry your scents, so it’s a combination of the fragrance and your own natural scent.”

A woody-spicy addition to the Valentino fragrance family, Vendetta is the first new scent pillar from the brand since its blockbuster Born in Roma.

It’s quite an evolution for a lad who equates childhood with the unmistakable aroma of sausage. When I ask Skarsgård about his first connection to fragrance—that unmistakably transformative power of scent—it’s the sausage factory that faced his front door.

“To this day, it really brings me back, and they’re fond memories,” he says. “Whenever I smell sausage, I’m an eight-year-old again. I’m getting ready for school, seeing my buddies, thinking about this girl I had a crush on. It strikes a chord.”

Of course, processed meat isn’t a key part of the olfactive experience of Vendetta Uomo. It opens with a sharp note of sparkling ginger with the typical brightness of a top note. From there, a warm, rich cinnamon liquor accord envelops the nose and gives way to earthy, grounding patchouli and woods. It’s at turns inviting and accessible while still drawing you in with something seductive and unique.

It’s sex in a spritz, the idea being that you too can have the appeal of a 6'4" Norse god. Ironically, Skarsgård’s everyday life couldn’t be more different from what he says most people see when he’s walking the red carpet or strutting his stuff on screen.

“When I’m not working, I’m trying to spend as little time as possible thinking about [my skincare and sartorial choices],” he says. “It’s all about comfort. I’ve been on a shoot for four months and I’ve been wearing the same shorts and flip-flops for months.”

But isn’t that part of the appeal of a fragrance—the ability to be a different person, someone out of your ordinary? Sure, you could be wearing a pair of sweats and a hat, but with a spray of Vendetta, you’re suddenly wearing a leopard-print overcoat on top of it.

It’s a good look. Just ask Alexander Skarsgård.

#4921. Rio Tinto eyes a giant hot-brick battery to cut fossil fuel use

Rio Tinto wants to put Australia’s cheap midday electricity to work at its Yarwun alumina refinery – by storing it in hot bricks and using that heat battery to make steam after the sun sets.

The global mining giant and California-based Rondo Energy have started engineering and design work on a huge heat battery near Gladstone, Queensland. Rondo calls it Australia’s largest planned thermal energy storage project and says it would be a first for the alumina industry.

Alumina is a hard white powder made of aluminum and oxygen that’s used to make aluminum metal, sandpaper, and strong ceramics. Globally, aluminum sector refining accounts for roughly 175 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually.

It’s still at the study stage, but the potential payoff is substantial. Rio Tinto estimates the battery could supply around 5% of Yarwun’s steam needs and cut the refinery’s direct emissions by about 67,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide annually. It would replace some of the coal and natural gas used to generate steam.

Rondo’s heat battery uses electricity to heat refractory bricks, which can withstand high temperatures. The bricks hold that energy as heat, which is then used to produce steam for the refinery’s existing steam network.

That matters because industrial heat demand doesn’t stop when solar production drops. Rondo’s heat battery charges during hours when electricity is cheap and plentiful, then delivers heat continuously so factories can keep running.

The proposed Yarwun system would have 360 megawatt-hours (MWh) of thermal storage and deliver up to 30 megawatts MW of heat. The Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) lists its electrical charging capacity at 78 MW, allowing it to take in electricity faster than it releases the stored energy as heat.

For the refinery, another attraction is that the battery would feed into equipment it already uses. The study will assess whether that integration can deliver reliable high-pressure steam at a cost that makes sense.

“This project shows how Australia’s abundant energy can become a competitive advantage for industry,” said Dr. Kira Rundel, Rondo’s head of Australia. “Heat batteries allow manufacturers to use low-cost electricity to produce the reliable, round-the-clock heat their operations need.”

ARENA is providing an initial A$3.6 million for the engineering and design study. If the project moves ahead, the agency will provide up to A$38 million for deployment. There’s also a further A$33.3 million in contingency support.

Rio Tinto will match ARENA’s A$3.6 million study contribution. The company says its total investment over the project’s life is expected to exceed ARENA’s funding if deployment goes ahead.

“Reducing emissions from alumina refining is complex, particularly when it comes to generating the high-pressure steam needed for our operations,” said Rio Tinto Pacific Operations managing director Armando Torres.

“This study will help us determine whether thermal energy storage can provide a technically and economically viable alternative to fossil fuels for part of Yarwun’s steam requirements.”

The feasibility study is expected to take about 12 months.
