#4847. Michael Strahan Shares the Words That Helped His Daughter Through Brain Cancer Treatment

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Michael Strahan appeared in commercials for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, delivering a message he never imagined would become so personal: “No parent should have to hear that their child has cancer.”

But in 2023, the beloved TV host and former NFL player faced that reality when his daughter, Isabella, was diagnosed with brain cancer at 19 years old.

“[That] line that I used to deliver, usually at the end of the commercial…here I am actually filling that line in my life in real time,” Strahan told Healthline.

Strahan believes his longtime connection with St. Jude was more than a coincidence. After years of advocating for families affected by childhood cancer, he found himself on the other side of that experience.

“When I needed that family…they were there for me,” he said. “I’m just appreciative, and I think things come back to you; give out good, good comes back.”

In October 2023, Isabella began experiencing vomiting, headaches, and balance issues during her freshman year at the University of Southern California (USC). Tests revealed that she had medulloblastoma, a fast-growing cancerous brain tumor located in the cerebellum. She underwent emergency brain surgery, radiation therapy, and four rounds of chemotherapy.

While medulloblastoma typically occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 9, it can also affect young adults like Isabella.

“[The] biology in adolescents and young adults can differ meaningfully from pediatric cases, requiring specialized expertise at centers of excellence for this disease,” Arnab Chakravarti, MD, director of the Brain Tumor Program at The Ohio State University, told Healthline.

Medulloblastoma is sometimes confused with glioblastoma, the most common type of malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Glioblastoma is particularly aggressive, with a median overall survival of just 15 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%.

However, Chakravarti explained that medulloblastoma has a significantly higher cure rate than glioblastoma.

“[This is] a point of genuine hope that deserves to be communicated clearly,” he said.

Radiation therapy is a cornerstone of medulloblastoma treatment. Isabella received proton therapy, which uses precisely targeted radiation to treat tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

“For medulloblastoma, this physical precision is transformative,” Chakravarti said. “Proton craniospinal irradiation dramatically reduces [collateral] exposure — preserving cochlear function and hearing, reducing cardiovascular risk, protecting the thyroid, and most critically, sparing developing brain tissue in ways that translate into measurably better neurocognitive outcomes years after treatment.”

He added that multiple prospective studies have shown that children and young adults treated with proton craniospinal irradiation experience less cognitive decline and better quality of life compared to those treated with conventional radiation.

Today, Isabella is back at USC, embracing the everyday routines she once had to put on hold.

“I am back at USC, so…it’s been great, in the midst of exams, so it’s a little stressful, but I actually [am] inviting the stress in because at one point I didn’t have exams, so I’m happy to be back,” Isabella told Healthline.

Along with attending classes, Isabella is enjoying activities such as working out and cooking. She continues to undergo MRI scans of her head and spine every three months, but said that after another year, the scans will become less frequent, occurring every six months.

“But really…I don’t have a lot of doctor’s appointments,” she said.

“It feels like a brand-new life, but it’s a good one. And that’s wonderful,” Isabella said.

Isabella said her family’s support played an important role in helping her through cancer treatment. Spending so much time together in the hospital brought them closer as they watched movies and played cards and board games to pass the time.

“[It] really, really bonds you to people, and just having my dad and my whole family there was something that [you] can’t beat,” she told Healthline.

Michael said that despite the difficult circumstances, he cherishes the time he spent with his daughter. Before her diagnosis, Isabella was a typical teenager who spent much of her time at school or with friends.

“They say you spend the most time with your kid for the first few years of their life, and then once school starts, you don’t get a chance to spend as much time as you would like with them,” he said.

While Michael said he and Isabella already had a close relationship, her diagnosis brought the family even closer and helped them reflect on what mattered most.

“[What] was really important was family, and relationships, and the love that you have for each other, and the support you have to give each other,” he said. “I think that our relationship now is better than ever.”

Today, Michael makes an effort to visit Isabella at USC whenever he’s in Los Angeles during the NFL season.

“Some weekends she [has time for me]. Some she doesn’t,” he said. “But just to have that relationship with your child, where they want to hang out with you, is a good feeling, and that’s the relationship that we have.”

Michael and Isabella are sharing their story to raise awareness about brain cancer and offer hope to other families facing similar challenges.

They recently participated in a fireside chat in New York City hosted by Real Chemistry and SMAC, where they discussed their family’s experience navigating Isabella’s diagnosis, mental health, caregiving, and the impact of sharing their story.

Throughout her treatment, Isabella also documented her experience through a series of YouTube vlogs and the ABC primetime documentary, “Life Interrupted: Isabella Strahan’s Fight to Beat Cancer.”

For Michael, helping others is a value he learned from his parents. He recalled how his father used his transportation business in Germany to support people in need after retiring from the military.

“[He] would take donations, and use his money and his trucks, and drive stuff to Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, and drop it off there at local churches and the shelters for people, who he had no connection with,” said Michael. “So for me, I think I do what I feel is on my heart and what’s important to me.”

For parents caring for children with cancer, Michael emphasized that it’s OK to feel overwhelmed or emotional. He encouraged them to show their children love and support while helping them maintain hope for the future.

“I think positivity is the main thing because it was so tough on her at the time when she was [saying], ‘I can’t do it. I can’t do this. I can’t do that,’” said Michael.

Michael said he made a conscious effort to replace words like “can’t” and “if” with “when” while encouraging Isabella during treatment.

“Anytime she got down on herself, I’d say, ‘when you go back to college, when you do this, when you do that,’” said Michael. “And I just think the positive attitude and the love that you can give and the confidence that you can display towards your loved one [or] your child who’s going through something like this is the only thing you can do because you’re at the mercy of medicine.”

Now in her senior year at USC, Isabella is looking ahead to life after graduation.

“[There’s] a lot of interesting opportunities and things that I want to pursue,” she said.

Michael has no doubt she will find her way.

“She’s so talented, and this experience, in my opinion, has opened up my eyes to more talent that she has that I didn’t realize…the talent to connect people, and be in front of a crowd. I always thought she’d be nervous because I get nervous, but she’s better than me,” he said.

#4846. A Former College Athlete’s Battle With Depression

He spent years trying to power through his depression, cycling through several traditional oral antidepressants, before finding a medication that worked for him.

JEREMIAH FELT GLUED to his couch, too sad and unmotivated to move. He was supposed to be getting ready for his wedding—a day when he expected to feel more confident than ever. Instead, his groomsmen had to come to his apartment and help him get there. A former college athlete, Jeremiah was still a big guy, and it took all of them to lift him from the couch and carry him out the door.

It’s not what you think. Jeremiah had absolutely no doubts about marrying the love of his life. He was in the throes of a depressive episode, one of many he had experienced dating back several years. For Jeremiah, becoming a husband meant becoming a provider and protector. But on the day he was supposed to step into that role, he was the one who needed help—and he felt ashamed.

The wedding-day episode was just one part of a much longer struggle. Jeremiah’s symptoms first appeared in college and worsened after graduation. When he entered the workforce, his symptoms worsened and he became exhausted and increasingly apathetic—to the point of neglecting his hygiene. Eventually, he became too depressed to get out of bed in the morning and lost his first job.

In 2012, Jeremiah was officially diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD), a mental health condition that can have a significant impact on daily life and make it difficult to find motivation or energy for self-care. Over the next nine years, persistent symptoms made it difficult for him to maintain employment, and he eventually went on disability.

DEPRESSION IN MEN often hides in plain sight. In 2021, 6.2 percent of U.S. adult men and 10.3 percent of U.S. adult women experienced a major depressive episode, according to the National Institute of Mental Health.

Those numbers tell us how common depression is, but not what it looks like. Men and women can experience many of the same symptoms, including sadness, hopelessness, fatigue, changes in sleep, and loss of interest in favorite activities. However, depression often shows up differently in men. Feeling sad or emotional isn’t always the main symptom. For many men, symptoms can show up as headaches, digestive problems, tiredness, irritability, or long-term pain. Feeling isolated or seeking distractions to avoid dealing with feelings or relationships can also be signs.

According to Craig Chepke, MD, DFAPA, a psychiatrist and medical director based in Huntersville, North Carolina, men may have a hard time talking about their feelings and asking for help, making diagnosis and treatment difficult. “Depression in men is often missed or misread, including by men and others close to them, because it doesn’t always look like what people expect depression to look like,” he explains. “Instead of sadness, it may show up as irritability, anger, withdrawal, or self-medication. Sometimes it takes an ultimatum from someone who cares about them just to get them into the office. Depression is a medical condition, not a character flaw, but I hear men with depression say variations of the same thing over and over: ‘If I was just stronger, I’d be able to handle this on my own.’”

Jeremiah agrees. “You feel like less of a man, like you should be able to just power through somehow, or snap out of it,” he says. “But you can’t. You don’t. Depression affects your confidence in every aspect of your life. It becomes a dehumanizing experience.”

BEYOND HIS OWN self-doubt, Jeremiah had a hard time finding healthcare providers who would take his symptoms seriously. He dealt with therapists who minimized his struggles. One provider even attributed his symptoms to restless legs syndrome.

At times, Jeremiah felt that some doctors viewed depression as a “woman’s disease,” subtly calling his masculinity into question. Being a Black man added another layer as he navigated a healthcare system that didn’t always understand his experience.

He experienced more difficulty when he opened up to loved ones. “Being a man is lonely in general. There are very few men you can talk to beneath the surface level about things even though you call each other friends. I shared my struggle with MDD with my two closest friends, and it kind of freaked them out,” he says. “We didn’t talk much after that for about a year.” He received a similar reaction from cousins and extended family members, who weren’t sure what to say or whether to treat him differently. Things improved once they saw that his personality hadn’t fundamentally changed.

Jeremiah’s marriage, however, became a turning point. His wife, a clinical therapist, was uniquely positioned to recognize his condition. Starting around 2016, she began noticing subtle changes, how he would pick up and lose interest in activities and hobbies, and how Jeremiah would withdraw into himself around the house. It was then that she encouraged him to seek professional help. But asking for help was only the beginning. Finding a treatment that adequately addressed his symptoms would take years.

IN 2021, JEREMIAH was diagnosed with treatment-resistant depression (TRD), which affects about 30 percent of people with MDD. TRD is generally defined as MDD that has not resolved after trying at least two traditional oral antidepressants. “By the time someone checks off medication after medication on an intake form, they’ve usually lost something more valuable than time,” Dr. Chepke says of people living with TRD. “They’ve lost hope that anything can get better.”

Jeremiah knew his feelings were real. “TRD is a bully and it will hit you in the face from the moment you wake up,” he says. “Your best days are not behind you. You’re just going through something that a lot of men go through and just aren't able to admit it. You’re working to hold onto the life you want to live, not just your health, but your lifestyle, who you want to be, and the type of man you want to become or already are.”

For a while, Jeremiah kept trying new medications and started losing hope when they didn’t work. But with help from his wife and doctor, he found a different path.

LOOKING BACK, WHAT mattered most to Jeremiah was his wife’s consistent support through the process. In the early years of treatment, she helped him remember appointments and his medication schedules that kept him moving forward when motivation was scarce. Jeremiah’s doctor recommended he try SPRAVATO® (esketamine), an FDA-approved nasal spray for adults with TRD, used alone or with an oral antidepressant.

It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective for use in preventing suicide or in reducing suicidal thoughts or actions. SPRAVATO® is not for use in place of hospitalization if your healthcare provider determines that hospitalization is needed, even if improvement is experienced after the first dose of SPRAVATO®. SPRAVATO® is not for use as a medicine to prevent or relieve pain (anesthetic). It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe or effective as an anesthetic medicine. It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective in children. (Please see additional Important Safety Information including Boxed WARNINGS, limitations of use, and a list of side effects below. Click here to learn more.)

SPRAVATO is only available through a restricted distribution program called the SPRAVATO Risk Evaluation & Mitigation Strategy (REMS). SPRAVATO can only be administered at a certified healthcare setting, and patients self-administer the pre-filled nasal device at a REMS-certified treatment center under direct clinical supervision and are monitored for at least two hours after taking SPRAVATO. SPRAVATO may have serious side effects such as sedation, dissociation, and respiratory depression, and the risk of abuse and misuse.

SPRAVATO represents a different treatment approach for TRD. Unlike traditional antidepressants that work on serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, SPRAVATO acts on glutamate, a chemical messenger in the brain that is thought to regulate depression. The role of glutamate in depression and the exact way SPRAVATO works are unknown.

As his depressive symptoms improved, Jeremiah began to engage more with others. He also joined a support group for Black men navigating these challenges. Hearing other people’s stories reminds him that he’s not alone. Today, he works as an IT and cybersecurity instructor in Chicago, speaks at industry conferences, and builds robots in his spare time.

Jeremiah’s experience is his own, and treatment decisions are personal. “There’s no one treatment that’s right for everybody,” Dr. Chepke says. In his practice, Dr. Chepke has witnessed reductions in certain patients’ depressive symptoms when incorporating SPRAVATO into their treatment. While not all of his patients may benefit, seeing some move from repeatedly cycling through different treatments to an option studied specifically for TRD has helped shape how he approaches care for this population.

If you haven’t found relief from your depressive symptoms, talk with your doctor about the options that may be appropriate for you—and most importantly, know that there is hope.

Jeremiah and Dr. Chepke were compensated for their time participating in this article.

#4845. The Loneliness Trap

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

With unyielding inflation, economic uncertainty, and geopolitical friction sending collective anxiety levels higher and higher, many of us now consider genuine contentment an unaffordable luxury. Yet many decades of history serve as reminders that even amidst tremendous upheaval, human joy has never depended on what you can buy or external calm.

In this challenging environment, most of us want what we’ve always wanted: to be genuinely happy. Yet we are not willing to do what it takes to become happy.

A study from almost a century ago of the residents of the Northern English town of Bolton shows us the severe effects of not carving out time for our loved ones, a decision that most of us make every day. In the year my father was born, just over 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) to the east in Hungary, 1938—and then again in 2014—the residents of Bolton were asked what made them happy.

The most common ingredients of happiness among responses spanning 78 years were economic security and personal relationships, which were often tied together. Little mention was made of external events.

Joseph Roberts, a miner, despite answering the survey in 1938 when the threat of Hitler loomed large—the Nazi leader had already occupied Austria and parts of what was then Czechoslovakia—shared that what made him happy was returning from a day of hard work and spending time with his family.

“I see my kiddies and wife I am happy,” shared the miner. “When I am washed and romp with my kiddies, and when it is weekend and I tip up my humble wage and share with my wife in doling it out and we find we can manage another week we are happy. I am in regular work although it is hard and dangerous but I am happy because I have a contented mind.”

I am guessing you would agree that happiness is a seed you must grow in your life. Yet what most people do not understand is that you can’t grow your happiness alone; you can only do so with the help of others.

Since you cannot grow your happiness alone, it must also be true that happiness is a seed that grows in the gardens of others. How does this work?

We all seek happiness yet find it elusive. The reason is that most of us do not realize that one of the best ways to experience happiness is to help others experience it.

Plato understood this well. “Caring for the happiness of others,” observed the Greek philosopher over 2,500 years ago, “we find our own.”

Research also bears this out. Not only do people feel even more appreciated, happy, and connected to us than we expect them to when we give to them, but we also counterintuitively often benefit, as psychologists Sonja Lyubomirsky and Harry Reis note in their book How to Feel Loved, even more than they do.

I was reminded of this truth last month, when I spent nine days in a small town in rural Kenya where I had lived and worked as a Peace Corps volunteer 35 years earlier. Facilitating a pro bono leadership conference for rural primary and secondary school leaders and supporting five Kenyan women educators in teaching a women’s empowerment program for single mothers in one of Kenya’s most impoverished regions, I was struck by how happy I felt connecting with the people around me.

Returning to my comparatively more hermetic life of writing, researching, and teaching in Rome has been a jolt to my system; yet the memories remain and bring peace. In the end, I am like everyone else I’ve ever met in the world: traveling on an eternal search for connection and meaning.

Following the Italian way of expressing love, when you tell the other person “Ti voglio bene” (which means “I wish for your happiness”), you offer them the seed of happiness to plant in their own garden. You give them your support to grow in the way they desire, toward their own goals and values, or “to become,” as the former president of the American Psychological Association and the father of client-centered therapy, Carl Rogers, once wrote.

If the seed flourishes and becomes the flower of happiness, the other person may or may not bring you this flower one day. Sound risky? It may be; yet it’s the only way you will ever have the experience of seeing this flower in full bloom.

In other words, interconnectedness is the only path that will enable you to experience and sustain happiness throughout your life.

“Sounds good, Mr. Idealistic Author,” you may be thinking. “But how do I make daily decisions that will bring this interconnectedness into my life?”

If you want a more interconnected life, you will first have to ask yourself some tough questions about your daily decisions, right down to whether you should spend your time today ordering another gadget on Amazon or going hiking with a friend. Let’s consider this choice.

What do you think will bring you more happiness—an Amazon delivery or going on a hike with a friend? A study by Amit Kumar of the University of Texas has found that once you have a base level of financial resources, experiences rather than objects are the drivers of happiness.

Why? Experiences (“doing” something such as going to a meditation retreat or on a bicycle ride or to a restaurant or a concert) are more often shared, while objects (“owning” something such as a new shirt or book) are most often enjoyed alone.

In the end, the love we’ve shared with others is all we take with us. “All that we love deeply,” Helen Keller sagely observed, “becomes a part of us.” This is why experiences, which facilitate the sharing of love, produce much more long-term happiness than objects.

How, then, can you usher more happiness back into your life? Prioritize doing activities you enjoy in person with people you care about rather than buying objects to enjoy by your lonesome.

Just as you pursue objects to purchase and yet Prime shipping does not drop happiness at your doorstep, you also pursue social information about the people in your social network. As I write in my book Screened In, this search—like buying objects—does not bring the social connection that is the purveyor of genuine happiness into your life.

In sum, then, stop texting and call, go out with, see, visit, meet—in short, spend time with other, values-congruent people as often as you can.

In other words: Just. Connect. In person. In real time.

Spend time with the people you love, or could love if you were to get to know them better. Then happiness will cease to be a distant stranger and will become a part of your life again.

#4844. What Rest-Pause Training Can Do for Your Workout

A simple practice lets you push past failure—without lowering the weight.

TRY AS YOU might, you can’t pump out reps forever when you’re working toward building bigger muscles. Eventually, you‘ll be too fatigued to complete another rep with good form, a point referred to as “technical failure.” Pushing beyond your last good rep can lead to sloppy lifting mechanics, which can compromise your results or, worse increase your risk of injury. If you find yourself stuck lifting the same weight for the same reps, it may be time to get creative with how you push past that iron hurdle.

One way to head off the siren song of ego lifting is by implementing a planned rest-pause set. It’s an intense lifting technique that requires focus and intention, and as effective as it can be, it shouldn’t be done for every set or even every exercise.

By briefly resting after reaching failure, you can squeeze out a few more quality reps using the same weight. A few extra reps might not seem like a big deal, but they can add up over time, giving your muscles an extra dose of the tension that drives growth.

To do a rest-pause set, you’ll take an exercise to the point where you can’t complete another rep with good form. You’ll then rest for five to 15 seconds—in one MH workout plan, fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. recommends taking “three deep breaths” for a pause—then squeeze out a few more reps (expect to be able to do two to four) using the same weight. You can repeat this process, though one additional round of reps is a good starting point.

If you rest longer than 20 seconds, Alexander Rothstein, an exercise physiologist and program coordinator of exercise science at the New York Institute of Technology, says you’re starting to approach a standard rest interval. "If you give yourself that brief moment to… recover, and then you continue the set, you haven't flushed away all of the waste products, and you haven't fully recovered your energy stores, but you are still capable of doing a few more high-quality reps,” he explains.

The purpose of a rest-pause set is to push your muscle to complete a few more hard (but high-quality) reps. If you’re aiming to build muscle, it’s those hard reps near the end of a set that are key; a rest-pause set allows you to sneak in a few more of those reps. While lifters of any experience level can perform rest-pause sets, they’re especially useful for advanced lifters who’ve already cashed in their newbie gains and find it increasingly difficult to progress their lifts and add muscle.

Say you’re doing the dumbbell bench press, an exercise on which you’ve been stuck using the same 50-pound dumbbells for sets of 8 to 10 reps for over a month. You get to that 10th rep and, once again, can’t muster another. Instead of calling it this time, you’ll sit up, rest the dumbbells on your thighs for 15 seconds, and then bust out another two reps. Congrats. You just eked out more worthwhile reps, which, over time, should help you progress.

“But isn’t that cheating?” you ask. No—and even if it were, there are times when cheating pays off for muscle gains. And research suggests that traditional sets and rest-pause sets can produce similar gains in strength and muscle. One small study had 18 experienced lifters perform six weeks of traditional sets or rest-pause training with the same relative load. One group completed three sets of six reps; the other did one set to failure and then as many rest-pause sets as necessary to hit 18 reps. Both groups achieved similar strength gains, but the rest-pause group experienced greater increases in thigh muscle thickness and leg-press muscular endurance.

As for how to start using them, pick one exercise per workout—ideally, a move you’re struggling to progress—and do the final set of that exercise as a rest-pause set. This often works best with the final exercise in your workout. The rest-pause protocol can be downright exhausting, and using them too early may compromise your ability to hit your typical reps and weights during subsequent sets.

One note: You can perform rest-pause sets with just about any exercise, but there are two places where they’re especially beneficial. Weight machines are the safest, letting you easily push to fatigue, then take your brief “rest”. Exercises that offer support for stabilizing muscles (think: chest-supported rows) also work well. And many single-joint free-weight exercises, like dumbbell curls are good options. If you’re going to attempt a rest-pause set with the bench press or back squat, have a good spotter on hand.

There’s more than one way to increase the volume of a single set, and these methods are often referred to as intensity techniques. Below, we’ll briefly compare the three most popular ones to rest-pause sets.

A drop set is when you reach failure on a lift, then immediately reduce the load (often by 10 to 20 percent) and try to squeeze out a few more reps. In many ways, it’s similar to a rest-pause set, but because you’re lightening the weight, you’ll find it easier to maintain good form.

“Personally, I just like the volume approach of drop sets,” Rothstein says. "When you do drop sets, obviously the load is being reduced, so it's not as potentially strength beneficial as it might be to just do rest-pauses and still lift heavy loads."

A cluster set is when you break up a traditional straight set into a series of mini sets, or clusters, with short rest periods between each. They're a popular training method among strength athletes, such as powerlifters and weightlifters, who want to accumulate more total tonnage.

Say, for example, you can typically deadlift 250 pounds for eight reps. You could load 285 to 300 pounds on the bar and perform four two-rep clusters, resting 15 to 30 seconds between, to complete the same eight reps with roughly 15 to 20 percent more weight.

The main difference between rest-pause and cluster sets is that cluster sets strategically use rest to achieve a preplanned number of reps, often at a higher weight. Rest-pause sets have you take a few breaths after reaching failure to push past what you can normally do rep-wise. Cluster sets are likely superior to rest-pause sets for building strength.

Instead of resting and then doing more reps once you reach failure, you can perform forced reps, where your spotter provides just enough assistance to help you complete a few more reps with good form. Forced reps are usually done on exercises where a spotter can easily help; think the bench press or certain machine exercises, not deadlifts or heavy back squats.

While you’re technically pushing past failure, you don’t have control over how much assistance your spotter provides; this can vary from workout to workout or even rep to rep. You can, however, control the eccentric portion of the contraction after the spotter has helped you, so if you’re doing forced reps, it’s a must to lower the weight slowly to get the most from these. Forced reps can be a useful occasional technique if you have an experienced spotter who knows how much assistance to provide; because they’re forcing you to acclimate to increased time-under-tension with a weight that you know is challenging.

#4843. Tesla’s $10B solar factory could get 35 years of tax breaks in Texas

Tesla’s proposed $10 billion “Project Crystal Sun” solar factory in Texas could get up to 35 years of local tax breaks on its equipment, according to the four agreements Fort Bend County commissioners approved on Thursday.

The vote was 4-0. And Tesla still hasn’t committed to building the plant in Texas.

As we first reported in August, Tesla applied for a 10-year school property tax limitation under the state’s JETI program, through Lamar CISD and the Texas Comptroller. The plan is a vertically integrated solar plant near Richmond, southwest of Houston, that would make everything from silicon ingots to finished modules, with commercial production targeted for Q1 2029.

Lamar CISD approved the school tax piece in September. The county was next.

On October 22, the commissioners court approved items 25A to 25D on its agenda: a Chapter 312 tax abatement, a Chapter 381 incentive agreement, a foreign trade zone agreement with a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT), and a “true up” PILOT agreement. Interim County Judge Daniel Wong abstained because his engineering firm has worked with Tesla.

Each agreement covers a different slice of Tesla’s tax bill, and together they run for decades.

The Chapter 312 agreement abates 100% of county property taxes on Tesla’s equipment and other tangible personal property at the plant for 10 tax years. The clock starts in tax year 2029 by default, but Tesla can move it to the first year after production starts, as late as 2031 without needing the county’s approval.

Tesla’s JETI application splits the $10.1 billion into $1.52 billion of real property and $8.6 billion of personal property, mostly production equipment.

Land and buildings aren’t part of the deal. Anything that isn’t eligible for the abatement, including the land and buildings, stays “fully taxable at all times,” according to the agreement.

Inventory goes through the foreign trade zone deal instead. Tesla’s site would be part of Port Freeport’s Foreign-Trade Zone No. 149, which exempts eligible inventory from local property tax. In exchange for the county not objecting, Tesla agreed to make PILOT payments, set at “zero dollars or 0%” of the forgone taxes for as long as the abatement is in effect.

When the abatement ends, the Chapter 381 agreement takes over. Tesla starts paying county taxes on its equipment, and the county pays 90% of them back as an annual grant for 20 years. The county keeps 10% for its general fund.

Inventory follows the same pattern. After the abatement, Tesla’s FTZ payment rises to 10% of the taxes that would otherwise apply.

There’s one more lever. If Tesla averages at least 12,000 employees for any two consecutive years during the first decade, the first five years of the rebate period become a 100% grant, and the rebate period stretches from 20 to 25 years.

That pushes the agreement out to Project Year 35. It’s also 2,288 jobs above the 9,712 Tesla says it will create.

To keep the tax breaks, Tesla has to start construction by June 30, 2027, begin “regular commercial production of solar cells” by December 31, 2030, and invest $10 billion by the later of December 31, 2031 or two years after production starts. Force majeure and “ERCOT Delay” provisions can extend those dates.

The jobs ramp is 2,500, 5,000, 7,500, then 9,712 employees by the fourth year of operations, with an average compensation of $55 per hour. Tesla gets the full abatement as long as it hits 90% of the headcount target, which is about 8,741 people.

The penalties are mild. Missing a jobs or wage target for one year only costs Tesla that year’s break, and two misses in a row lets the county terminate the agreement. Full recapture of abated taxes, plus a possible 15% penalty if they aren’t repaid within 60 days, is reserved for “Material Defaults” like missing the $10 billion investment, blowing the construction deadlines or abandoning the plant for 12 months.

Under the Chapter 381 deal, grants from earlier years can’t be clawed back for a headcount shortfall.

The county’s floor is small. The true-up agreement only guarantees that Fort Bend collects at least $2 million a year, and 25% of the taxes Tesla pays on its real property, the county’s 10% share and the FTZ payments all count toward that total.

For scale, Tesla’s own consultant, Kroll, estimated in the JETI filing that the project would pay $276.5 million in Fort Bend County general taxes over 38 years without incentives, peaking at $16.2 million in 2030. That estimate lumps land, buildings and equipment together. The equipment portion is the one the county just agreed to give back, for most of those years.

In its application, it says the economics of the Fort Bend site are “not competitive” with an unnamed site in another state without the JETI limitation and local abatements. The competing state is redacted in a confidential supplement.

None of the documents state a production capacity. The only big number is a quote from Elon Musk at Davos in January, cited in the application: “The SpaceX and Tesla team, both separately, are working to build to 100 GW a year of solar power in the U.S., of manufactured solar power.”

For comparison, Qcells is spending $2.5 billion on its ingot-to-module campus in Cartersville, Georgia, where a 3.5 GW cell line started production this year. Crystal Sun’s budget is four times that.

Tesla has been here before. New York spent $950 million on the Buffalo factory for Tesla’s solar business, and when the solar plans fell apart, Tesla turned to things other than solar to meet its employment requirements, including data labeling for Autopilot. Tesla did announce production of a new solar panel in Buffalo last year.

We want this factory to happen. A US plant making its own ingots, wafers, cells and modules would be rare, and it’s one of the few parts of Tesla’s business that still lines up with the mission it used to talk about before its “awesome abundance” pivot based on AI.

But corporate America loves its tax breaks. For 10 years, Tesla pays no county tax on the $8.6 billion of equipment that makes up most of the project. For the next 20, it gets 90% of it back. In return, the county’s guaranteed minimum is $2 million a year, on a $10 billion plant. And Tesla still hasn’t said it’s coming.

That’s how site selection works now. Companies file, collect offers from several states, and the county that bids the most wins. Fort Bend’s economic development director, Carlos Guzman, told ABC13 the county “would’ve been eliminated from consideration” without these agreements. Hard to argue with that, and it’s exactly why these deals keep getting richer.

That bonus for extra workers looks like an invitation to gaming (if things get that far). Paying people for make-work for a couple of years could yield tax breaks well exceeding their combined wages.

The protections are thin too. One bad year costs Tesla a year of breaks, and past rebates can’t be clawed back over a headcount shortfall, even though the county’s goal is obviously long-term employment.

Then there’s the equipment. Reuters reported in March that Tesla was in talks to buy $2.9 billion of Chinese solar equipment, and its supply chain is already caught in a patent fight between Chinese suppliers.

The state still has to sign off on the school-tax piece. After that, it’s on Tesla. Is it actually building in Texas, or is Fort Bend’s offer just leverage against the other state? From what I’m hearing, Tesla is set on the Houston-area location.

Tesla wants to start making solar panels in Texas by 2029, but you don’t have to wait that long to go solar at home. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4841. Hormone Therapy May Help Improve Menopause Brain Fog, Mood Changes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT), also known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), helps manage various menopause symptoms.

Currently, MHT is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help relieve hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and dyspareunia (pain during sex).

However, recent research has found that MHT may also help improve mental symptoms like “brain fog” and mood changes.

Other research also found that MHT does not affect dementia risk. This research followed the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on these products, which suggested they may increase the risk.

Together, these studies show that MHT may help people experiencing menopause in ways not previously realized and that it is generally safe to use.

Research published in Scientific Reports on September 1 suggests that an estrogen hormone treatment that combines estriol and progesterone may help ease the symptoms of brain fog during menopause.

Brain fog may involve memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking.

Just about two-thirds of women experience cognitive difficulties, like brain fog, during the menopausal transition. However, there is currently no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved treatment for these symptoms.

This study was an observational case series that followed 20 menopausal women with an average age of 53. Each participant was given a baseline assessment for cognitive symptoms prior to treatment.

They were then treated for 12 months with a customized regimen of estriol and progesterone.

Estriol is a natural form of estrogen that occurs during pregnancy and has been used in Europe and Asia to treat other symptoms of menopause.

After 12 months, the participants reported significant reductions in:

“Estrogen plays a well-documented role in protecting the brain, yet there are still no approved type and dose of treatment that specifically targets the cognitive symptoms so many women experience during menopause,” Rhonda Voskuhl, MD, neurologist, member of the Comprehensive Menopause Center at UCLA Health, and senior study author, said in a press release.

“Women are often told to simply live with brain fog, when in fact there is a neuroscience basis for it, and potentially a way to address it. That gap in care is what motivated us to look more closely at estriol,” Voskuhl said.

This was a small, preliminary case series without a placebo group or randomization. More research is needed to confirm the benefits for cognitive symptoms.

A study published September 9 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society, showed that hormone therapy may help improve mood changes in women in midlife.

The researchers noted that mood disturbances, such as depression, irritability, anxiety, and mental exhaustion, affect up to 68% of women during menopause.

“The erratic changes and loss of estrogen associated with this hormonal transition can lower serotonin and dopamine levels, which [are] associated with depression and cognitive changes, including poor concentration, brain fog, and memory loss,” said Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included 260 individuals with an average age of 52 years. Just over half of the participants had a history of anxiety or depression, and 24% were using an antidepressant medication at the start of the study.

Each participant completed the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) both before and after initiating hormone therapy for FDA-approved indications, such as hot flashes and night sweats.

The average follow-up during the study was 4.5 months. Between the baseline and the follow-up, there was a significant reduction in the MRS psychological scores. The percentage of participants with severe mood symptoms decreased from 62.3% to 24.6%.

Treatment response didn’t appear to differ by age, menopausal stage, psychiatric history, or antidepressant use. These findings suggest that hormone therapy may help improve mood symptoms in midlife, especially for those with higher severity of symptoms before treatment.

“This study supports the evidence that starting hormone therapy for the typical disruptive symptoms of menopause may bring collateral benefits, including improvement in mood,” Ross said. “Communicating with your healthcare provider is always best to manage your symptoms and prepare yourself properly for this next stage of life.”

For decades, women have been warned about the serious potential risks associated with menopause hormone therapy (MHT). This included an FDA “black box” warning citing complications like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

However, a recent meta-analysis commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) that included data from more than a million women, and was published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, found that MHT neither increased nor decreased dementia risk.

“The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” Melissa Melville, a PhD candidate and aging researcher in the Department of Clinical Health Psychology at the University College London, and first author of the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

In the same interview, Melville stressed that the importance of this work is twofold: for clinicians, there is an urgent need for higher-quality research, and for patients, decisions about MHT should be guided by symptoms and well-established benefits and risks.

#4840. Why It's Difficult to Be a Good Leader

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

When I conduct a workshop or extended program on leadership development, I often start by asking participants to identify the various characteristics of “good leaders.” Regardless of the audience, their lists are typically similar. In other words, the characteristics that define good leaders are not a secret, and there is general agreement as to what those characteristics are. I then follow with a question: “If this isn’t a secret, why don’t we see more actual leaders who exhibit these characteristics?”

Of course there are several viable answers to that question, but one important answer that gets overlooked is polarities that are inherent in leadership within an organization. What’s a polarity? Imagine a continuum, anchored at each end by a competing goal. As you invest more in reaching one of the goals, it’s like a pendulum swinging toward that end of the continuum, and you risk failing to reach the other goal. That is a polarity, and the trick is to continually and intentionally manage where you are on the continuum, recognizing that focusing more at one end tends to starve achievement of the goal at the other end.

As an example, a common polarity that many employed individuals face is the work-family polarity. The more time and energy devoted to work tends to result in negligence of one’s family, and vice versa. In a sense, “work-life balance” implies maintaining a midpoint position on the continuum. In reality, work or family often receives more than 50 percent of one’s time and energy due to what is needed in each domain at the time. Perhaps the ultimate goal of “life success” rests on not neglecting work or family for too long.

What about leaders in organizational settings? They commonly face a number of polarities, including these:

I imagine there are additional polarities, and perhaps some that are specific to each setting, but managing even this set listed here represents a monumental achievement. Leaders frequently notice a deficit in some area, perhaps followers regularly working in ways that do not align with the organization’s priorities. We might say that the leader’s pendulum had swung too far toward allowing autonomy. Because it’s now a problem, the unfortunate tendency is to swing too far in the other direction. In this case, the leader may take a heavy hands-on approach, which ends up frustrating followers as they complain of being micromanaged.

Just as leaders commonly focus on instances where a pendulum swung too far in one direction within the polarity, followers do as well. In the example of too much autonomy, at least some followers likely felt as though they did not receive enough direction or supervision. Just like Goldilocks and the Three Bears, the trick is finding and maintaining the area within the polarity that feels “just right.” Unfortunately, what constitutes “just right” varies across individuals.

So what can leaders do? Identify the prominent polarities they must navigate, and work on resisting the temptation to swing too far in one direction when trying to rectify a situation in which the other end of the continuum had been overly emphasized. I also suggest being explicit in explaining to followers the concept of polarities and the inherent tension the leader faces in each one. The hope is that followers begin to notice when a polarity is becoming out of balance and can alert leadership.

Perhaps you’re not a leader, and instead feel as though you are at the mercy of polarities over which you have little (if any) control. In that case, you now know about polarities and have that construct with which to better understand at least some of the problems you encounter at work. That knowledge doesn’t remove the negative effects of being too far toward one end of a continuum, but hopefully it provides the ability to recognize that leaders face difficult polarities. Because leaders frequently have not heard of the concept and the dynamic that polarities explain, it may be helpful for you to share this post with the leaders you think may benefit from it.
